# HiringItaly – full text

## 13th and 14th Month Pay in Italy: When and Why They Are Paid
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/13th-14th-month-pay-italy-cash-flow.html
Summary: How Italy's 13th and 14th month pay work, why employers owe them, and how to plan cash flow when annual pay arrives in extra installments.
If you hire in Italy, you will meet two terms early: the thirteenth month and the fourteenth month. They are called “tredicesima” and “quattordicesima” locally. Many US teams read them as bonuses. They are not. They are deferred pay that employees have earned through regular work.
This article explains what they are, why they exist, and how to plan for them in your budget.
What they are   The thirteenth month is an extra installment of salary paid on top of the regular monthly payments. The fourteenth month works the same way, but it is not universal. Whether an employee gets it depends on the national collective agreement that applies to the role and the industry.
The key point is that these amounts are part of annual pay. A contract might quote a gross annual salary. That figure already includes the extra installments, and it is split across more payments than the calendar has months.
This is different from a discretionary bonus. You cannot skip it in a weak year. You cannot tie it to a target. It is owed by default, and it is owed to every employee covered by the relevant agreement.
Why they exist   The practice comes from Italian labor tradition and is now set mainly through collective bargaining. Unions and employer associations negotiate the terms for each sector. The result is a standard structure of annual pay that employees and employers both expect.
For employees, the extra installments act as a forced savings mechanism. They arrive at predictable points in the year, often when household costs are high. Workers plan holidays, school costs and tax payments around them.
For employers, the rule is simple. The agreement sets the structure, and you follow it. There is little room to negotiate it away in an individual contract.
When they are paid   Timing also follows the collective agreement. The thirteenth month is commonly paid near the end of the year. The fourteenth month, where it applies, is commonly paid around the summer. Your agreement may set different dates, and some contracts spread the amounts into regular monthly payslips instead of paying them as lump sums.
Before you plan anything, confirm three things for each hire:
Which collective agreement applies to the role. Whether the fourteenth month is included. Whether the extra installments are paid as lump sums or spread across the year. These answers change your cash profile more than most people expect.
The effect on cash flow   Here is where finance teams get caught out. A US company is used to paying salary in an even rhythm. Italian payroll is often uneven. In months where an extra installment lands, the payroll run is larger than usual.
The extra pay also carries related costs. Employer social contributions and other payroll charges apply to these amounts, so the cost of each installment is higher than the net amount the employee sees. A budget built on a simple monthly salary will understate the real cost of the role.
There is also an accrual issue. The employee earns the thirteenth and fourteenth month pay gradually through the year, even though the cash goes out later. If you only book the expense when it is paid, your monthly results will look better than reality for part of the year and worse at the payment date. Good practice is to accrue the cost month by month.
A few habits help:
Budget on annual cost, not monthly salary. Take the full annual package, including extra installments and employer charges, and divide it across the year for planning. Accrue monthly. Set aside the cost as it builds up, so no payroll run produces a surprise. Mark the heavy months in your cash forecast. Treasury should know which months carry larger outflows before they arrive. Check what happens at exit. When an employee leaves mid-year, the portion of extra pay earned up to that point is generally still owed. Include it in any separation planning. Communicating with the candidate   Offers in Italy are often discussed in terms of gross annual salary. A candidate may ask how many payments that is divided into. Be ready to answer clearly. If your offer is a fixed annual number, say whether it already includes the extra installments. Confusion here leads to disputes later, and it can make an offer look smaller or larger than you intended.
It also helps to explain the structure to your US leadership. A hire with a given annual salary does not cost that figure divided evenly across the months. The pattern is lumpy, and that is normal.
What to do next   Treat the thirteenth and fourteenth month as fixed parts of compensation. Confirm the applicable agreement first. Then build your forecast on the full annual cost, accrue monthly, and flag the heavier payroll months in advance.
Done this way, the extra installments stop being a surprise. They become one more line in a predictable budget.

## At-will vs Italian employment: what US managers must unlearn
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/at-will-vs-italian-employment-what-us-managers-must-unlearn.html
Summary: At-will habits break in Italy. Learn how dismissal, notice, collective agreements and documentation change how a US manager hires, manages and exits staff.
If you manage in the US, you carry a default setting: either side can end the job at any time, for almost any reason. In Italy that setting does not exist. Most of the friction US teams hit comes from managing with the wrong default.
This article covers the mindset shifts. It is not legal advice. Your Italian counsel or employer of record should confirm the details for your case.
1. Employment is the default, not a favor   In the US, the burden sits with the employee. They stay as long as the company wants them.
In Italy, the burden sits with the employer. A permanent contract is the normal form of employment. Ending it needs a recognized reason, and you must be able to prove that reason if the employee challenges it.
So stop asking, “Do we still want this person?” Start asking, “Do we have a documented reason that Italian law accepts?”
2. “Not a fit” is not a reason   US managers often exit people for fit, attitude, or a change in strategy. Those words carry little weight in Italy.
Italian law looks for specific grounds. Broadly, these are serious misconduct, objective business reasons, or a subjective failure serious enough to justify ending the relationship. Each has its own standard. Each needs facts, dates, and records.
If a role is no longer needed, you must show that the need is real. You may also have to show you considered other options inside the company. A reorganization announced in a slide deck is not enough.
3. Documentation is the real management tool   In an at-will setting, a manager can act first and write later. In Italy the order flips.
Performance and conduct problems need a paper trail built over time. Clear written expectations, written feedback, and a record of support offered all matter. When a dispute arrives, a judge reads your file, not your intentions.
This changes daily habits. A quick Slack message saying “this is not working” does not count as a process. Your HR lead needs to own a consistent method for recording issues.
4. Discipline follows a procedure   For misconduct, you cannot simply tell someone to leave. The employee has the right to know the charge in writing and to respond before any sanction. Skipping that step can undo an otherwise valid decision.
Timing matters too. Act too slowly and you may be seen as having tolerated the behavior. Act too fast and you deny the right to respond. Managers need to learn this rhythm before they need it.
5. The collective agreement sits above your offer letter   US offer letters are built from scratch around the company’s preferences. In Italy, most employees fall under a national collective agreement (CCNL). It sets minimum pay levels, job classifications, working time, leave, notice periods, and more.
You cannot offer less than the agreement says. You also cannot ignore the classification system when you promote someone or change their duties. Which agreement applies depends on the sector and the work, and picking the wrong one is a common early mistake.
Expect the agreement to answer many questions you would normally settle in negotiation.
6. Notice runs both ways, and it is not a courtesy   At-will teams often treat notice as optional. In Italy, notice periods are set by the applicable agreement and are part of the deal. If you end a contract without a valid reason, or skip the required notice, you create a cost.
Employees must also give notice when they resign, so planning handovers is easier than in a pure at-will setting.
7. Probation exists, but it is not a loophole   A probation period can be agreed in writing at the start. It gives both sides more freedom to part ways. But it only works if it is set up correctly and the employee is actually evaluated on the real duties. A vague or late clause can fall apart. Treat probation as a real review window with clear goals, not as a shortcut.
8. Remedies are different   In the US, a wrongful termination claim is rare and narrow. In Italy, an unjustified dismissal can lead to financial compensation, and in some situations reinstatement. The outcome depends on the type of defect and on the company.
The practical point is simple. A bad exit is not a quiet settlement. It can become a long, public, and expensive dispute.
9. Change is slower, so hire more carefully   Because exits take care, hiring decisions carry more weight. Define the role in writing. Check the classification. Use a structured interview process. Agree the probation terms. Many problems that look like firing problems are really hiring problems.
What to do on day one   Name one owner for employment records. Confirm the correct collective agreement before making an offer. Write job descriptions that match the classification. Give feedback in writing, early and often. Ask your local advisor before any exit conversation, not after. The shift in one sentence   In the US, you manage by freedom to leave. In Italy, you manage by obligation to justify. Teams that accept this early hire better, document better, and rarely face the dispute they feared.

## Background and Reference Checks in Italy: What Employers Can and Can't Ask
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/background-reference-checks-italy-what-is-allowed.html
Summary: US employers expect broad background checks. Italy limits what you can ask and verify. Here is what is allowed, what is not, and how to stay compliant.
US hiring teams are used to a standard routine. Run a background check, call references, search social media, ask about past jobs and personal history. In Italy, much of that routine is restricted. Privacy rules and labor protections limit what an employer may ask a candidate, and what it may find out about them.
This article explains the main boundaries. It is a practical overview, not legal advice. Confirm your process with Italian counsel before you roll it out.
The basic rule: relevance to the job   Italian law sets a simple test. You may collect information only if it is needed to judge whether the person can do the job. The Workers’ Statute bars employers from investigating a candidate’s political, religious or union views. It also bars questions on facts that are not relevant to professional skills. The EU data protection regime (GDPR) adds the principle of data minimization. You collect what you need and nothing more.
This applies before the hire, during the interview stage, and during the employment relationship.
What you can ask and verify   You can ask about things tied directly to the role:
Work history, job titles and responsibilities. Education, degrees and professional certifications. Skills, languages and technical experience. Availability and notice period at the current employer. Professional licenses required for the position. You can verify credentials, but do it openly. Ask the candidate for the diploma or certificate, or ask for their agreement to contact the issuing institution. Do not go around the candidate.
What you cannot ask   Avoid these topics in interviews, forms and screening tools:
Political opinions, religion and union membership. Health conditions, disabilities and medical history. Pregnancy, plans to have children and marital status. Sexual orientation and ethnic origin. Personal habits and private life unrelated to the job. Some of these are special categories of data under GDPR. Others are protected by anti-discrimination rules. A single careless question in an interview can create exposure, even if you never use the answer.
Criminal records   This is where US teams are most often surprised. In Italy, an employer cannot freely demand a criminal record check. Data on criminal convictions can be processed only where the law specifically allows it. For most roles, there is no such basis. Some regulated positions are the exception, for example roles involving minors or certain financial functions.
Do not make a clean record a blanket condition of every offer. If a role truly needs it, confirm the legal basis for that role first.
Health checks   An employer should not ask candidates about their health. Medical fitness is handled through the workplace health surveillance system. A designated occupational physician carries out the assessment, and the employer receives only the outcome on fitness for the job. The employer does not get the diagnosis.
Reference checks   Calling a former employer is not forbidden. But it needs care.
Tell the candidate you will contact references. Prefer references the candidate names and agrees to. Keep questions to job performance and dates of employment. Do not contact the current employer without the candidate’s clear consent. It can put their job at risk. Do not ask a referee about health, family, union activity or private conduct. A former employer also has duties. It should not share personal data about a past employee without a proper basis. Expect many Italian employers to confirm only basic facts, such as role and tenure. Do not read this as a red flag.
Social media and online searches   A quick look at a public professional profile is usually fine. A deep search into a candidate’s personal accounts is not. What you find may reveal protected information, such as religion, opinions or health. Once you have seen it, you carry the risk. If you use online sources, limit them to professional material, and keep a record of why the information was relevant.
Credit checks and third-party screening   Credit and financial checks are hard to justify for most roles. Using an outside screening vendor does not remove your responsibility. The vendor acts for you, so you need a data processing agreement, a clear scope, and a check that its methods respect Italian rules. Many standard US packages include items that do not fit here. Strip them out.
Transparency toward candidates   Give every candidate a privacy notice. It should say what data you collect, why, how long you keep it, and who sees it. Keep candidate data only as long as the hiring process needs it. Delete the files of rejected candidates on a set schedule. If you transfer data to the US, for example to a headquarters HR system, you need a valid transfer mechanism.
A practical checklist   Replace your US background check package with an Italy-specific version. Train interviewers on the questions they must not ask. Limit screening to what the role needs, and document the reason. Get the candidate’s agreement before any reference call or credential check with third parties. Do not request criminal records unless the law allows it for the role. Publish a candidate privacy notice and a retention schedule. Keep health matters with the occupational physician. The takeaway   Italy does not ban checks. It asks that every check be needed, proportionate and open to the candidate. If your process follows that logic, you can hire well and stay compliant.
Before you plan your first Italian hire, try the cost calculator.

## Benefits Italian Tech Candidates Expect Beyond Salary
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/benefits-italian-tech-candidates-expect.html
Summary: What Italian tech candidates expect beyond salary, by seniority, and how US employers can build a benefits package that fits the local market.
Salary gets the first call. Benefits decide the second one.
US founders hiring in Italy often assume a strong base pay closes the deal. It rarely does on its own. Italian tech candidates compare the whole package. What they expect depends a lot on seniority.
What everyone expects   Some things are baseline. Candidates at every level assume them. Missing them signals that you do not know the market.
A proper written contract with clear terms, role and reporting line. The statutory protections and paid leave that come with Italian employment. Social security and pension contributions paid correctly and on time. A clear notice and probation framework. These are not perks. They are the floor. If you hire through an Employer of Record (EOR), they come built in, which removes one source of doubt for candidates who have never heard of your company.
Junior candidates: stability and learning   Junior engineers, analysts and support staff want two things above the rest: security and growth.
Many are early in their careers and have seen friends move between short contracts. A permanent contract from a foreign company matters more to them than a perk list. They also look for structured learning.
What works for this group:
A permanent contract, not a chain of short ones. A named mentor and a clear first-year plan. A training budget they can actually use, for courses, books and conferences. Meal vouchers or a similar daily benefit, which are common and easy to compare. Flexible hours, even if the role is mostly on site. Juniors rarely negotiate hard. They do compare offers closely, and small, concrete benefits tip the choice.
Mid-level candidates: flexibility and health   Mid-level people have options and know it. They often have a family, a mortgage or a partner with a job in the same city. Their questions shift from learning to life fit.
What they ask about:
Remote or hybrid work, and whether it is a real policy or a favor. Supplementary health insurance, ideally covering family members. Flexible working hours and time off beyond the legal minimum. Equipment, a home office allowance and coworking access. A clear path to a senior title. Supplementary health cover carries real weight here. Italy has public healthcare, but many professionals still want private options for speed and choice. A plan that covers family is valued more than a small salary bump.
Remote work is the other big filter. Candidates will walk away from a role that demands daily office presence in a city they do not want to live in. If your team is fully remote, say so early.
Senior candidates: total package and autonomy   Senior engineers, managers and specialists judge the offer as a whole. They want to see how each part is structured, not only the headline number.
What matters to them:
Equity or a long-term incentive, explained in plain terms, with clear tax treatment. A bonus with transparent rules, not a vague promise. Supplementary pension contributions. Autonomy over how and where they work. A seat at the table on product and technical decisions. Support for conferences, speaking and open source work. Equity is where US employers most often stumble. A plan written for US employees may not translate cleanly to an Italian employment relationship. Seniors know this. If you cannot explain how it works for them in Italy, they will discount it to zero. Get local advice before you put it in an offer.
Relocation and international hires   Some of your best candidates may not live in Italy yet. Others may be Italians returning from abroad. Both groups ask about practical support.
Expect questions about:
Help with housing in the first months. Visa and residence paperwork for non-EU hires. Registration with local services. Tax and social security status in the first year. A clear answer here builds trust fast. Vague promises do the opposite.
How to build the package   Do not copy a US benefits plan. Do not try to match every perk a large local employer offers either. Pick a few that fit your team and do them well.
Start with the legal floor and make sure it is correct. Add the daily benefits candidates compare most, such as meal vouchers and flexible hours. Offer health cover that includes family if your budget allows. Be explicit about remote and hybrid rules. For senior roles, put the incentive structure in writing and have it reviewed locally. Then tell candidates about it. Many companies offer decent benefits and hide them in a long document. Put the package in the first conversation, not the last.
The cost side   Every benefit has a price, and the employer cost in Italy is higher than the salary line. Contributions and mandatory items add on top. Before you promise anything, model the full cost per hire, so the package you offer is one you can sustain.

## Biweekly US Payroll vs Monthly Italian Payroll: What Changes for Cash Flow
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/biweekly-us-payroll-vs-monthly-italian-payroll.html
Summary: US teams pay biweekly. Italy pays monthly. See how the difference affects your cash flow, your forecasts and what your Italian hires expect.
If your US team is paid biweekly, you are used to a steady rhythm. Money leaves the account every other week. Employees see a deposit on a fixed Friday. Finance plans around it.
Italy works differently. Employees are normally paid monthly. That sounds like a small detail. It is not. It changes your cash flow, your accruals and what your new hire expects on pay day.
This article covers the practical differences. It does not replace advice on your specific contract or collective agreement.
The basic difference   In the US, biweekly payroll is common. Pay periods are short. Each check is a smaller slice of annual pay. Some months contain an extra pay run, and finance teams know to plan for it.
In Italy, the standard is one payslip per month. The employee receives their net salary once, usually at or near the end of the month. The payslip covers the whole month and shows gross pay, withholdings, social contributions and net pay.
There is no extra pay run in some months. Each month looks the same on the calendar.
What this means for your cash flow   Larger single outflows. A monthly run moves a bigger amount at once. Your treasury needs to hold enough cash on the payment date. If your US payroll is spread across the month, the Italian run will feel lumpy by comparison.
Contributions and taxes follow a monthly cycle. Employer social contributions and employee withholdings are tied to the monthly payroll. They are due on a schedule after the pay month closes. Your payroll provider or EOR should give you a calendar. Build it into your forecast so these dates do not surprise you.
Fewer pay runs, more predictability. One run per month is simpler to reconcile. You close the books on one payroll, not a mix of partial periods. For many finance teams this is easier once the first cycle is done.
Accruals work differently. With biweekly pay, some salary expense is earned but unpaid at month end. With monthly pay in arrears, the gap can be larger. Check how your accounting treats this so your month-end close stays accurate.
Additional payments beyond the monthly salary   Many Italian employment contracts include more than the regular monthly payment. Collective agreements often provide extra salary payments at set times of the year, and certain amounts are accrued for the employee over time and settled when employment ends.
The details depend on the collective agreement that applies to the role. Do not assume your US compensation structure maps over. Ask for the full annual cost, not just the monthly figure. Cash flow is lumpy in the months when these extra payments fall due.
This is where US teams most often underestimate the real cost. A salary quoted as an annual number and divided by the pay periods you are used to will not match what you actually pay.
What employees expect   Your Italian hires will not expect a biweekly deposit. They know monthly pay and plan their finances around it. Rent, loans and household bills line up with one monthly income.
Three expectations matter most.
Reliability on the pay date. A late payment is a serious problem. Employees count on the money arriving when it always does. Set the date once and keep it.
A clear payslip. The monthly payslip is a formal document. Employees read it. They expect to understand each line. If you work with a provider, make sure payslips are available and explained in a way your hire can follow.
No pressure to move to biweekly. Some US founders ask whether they can match their home schedule. It is rarely worth it. The monthly rhythm is the local norm, and your employee will not see biweekly pay as a benefit. It may only create extra admin.
How to prepare   Map the pay calendar. Fix the monthly payment date and the dates for contributions and withholdings. Share it with finance. Forecast the full annual cost. Include the extra payments and the amounts accrued over time. Do not forecast from base salary alone. Align your accounting. Decide how to accrue salary at month end so reports stay consistent across the US and Italian entities. Fund the account early. Make sure cash is in place before the pay date, since the amount is larger than a single biweekly run. Explain the schedule to your hire. A short note on when they will be paid and what the payslip shows avoids confusion in the first month. Practical takeaway   Monthly pay is not worse than biweekly. It is different. Your cash moves in bigger steps, your calendar has fewer pay events, and your employee plans around one reliable date.
Treat the Italian schedule as a local standard. Build your forecast around it from the first day. Your finance team will thank you, and your new hire will start with confidence in how they are paid.

## Bringing a Non-EU Hire to Italy: The Work Permit Process Step by Step
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/non-eu-hire-italy-work-permit-process.html
Summary: How a sponsored non-EU hire moves from quota and work authorization to visa and residence permit in Italy, in the order each step happens.
You found the right person. They live outside the EU. Before they can start in Italy, three separate documents have to line up: the work authorization, the entry visa and the residence permit. Each one is issued by a different office. Each depends on the one before it.
This guide walks through the sequence for a sponsored hire.
The order at a glance   Check whether a quota slot exists for the role and the worker’s nationality. The employer applies for work authorization (the nulla osta). The worker applies for the entry visa at an Italian consulate. The worker arrives and signs the stay contract. The worker applies for the residence permit. Skip or reorder any of these and the file stalls.
Step one: check the quota   Most sponsored non-EU hires depend on the annual entry quotas, known as flussi. The current framework is the DPCM of 02/10/2025, which covers the 2026-28 period.
For 2026, the non-seasonal quota is 43300 entries. It is split by category:
25000 for nationals of the countries listed in article 6, paragraph 2, letter a. 18000 for nationals of countries with cooperation agreements. 300 for stateless persons and refugees. The worker’s nationality decides which bucket applies. A candidate from a country with no agreement and not on the list may have no path through the quota at all. Check this before you make an offer, not after.
Some categories sit outside the quotas. We have not verified the current rules for seasonal work or for out-of-quota routes, so confirm those with an adviser before you rely on them.
Step two: the employer applies for the nulla osta   The employer, or its Italian representative, files the request online with the Sportello Unico per l’Immigrazione. This is the one-stop immigration desk at the local prefecture.
Expect to provide:
The job offer, with role, pay and working hours. Proof of the employer’s capacity to pay the salary. Proof of suitable housing for the worker. The collective agreement (CCNL) that governs the role. A foreign company with no Italian entity cannot easily act as the sponsor. This is where many founders get stuck. The sponsor must be an employer with a legal presence in Italy. An Employer of Record can fill that role while you build your own entity, or instead of building one.
If the file is approved, the desk issues the nulla osta. This is the permission to bring the worker in. It is not yet a visa.
Step three: the visa   With the nulla osta in hand, the worker applies for a work visa at the Italian consulate in their country of residence. The consulate checks the nulla osta, the passport and the supporting documents. It may also ask for proof of the worker’s qualifications.
A few practical points:
The visa application is personal. The worker must usually appear in person. The visa is tied to the approved job. It does not allow a change of employer or role. Documents issued abroad often need translation and legalization. Start those early. When the visa is granted, the worker can travel to Italy.
Step four: arrival and the stay contract   After entry, the worker and the employer go back to the immigration desk. There they sign the stay contract (contratto di soggiorno). It confirms the employment terms that the authorization was based on.
At this point the worker also needs an Italian tax code (codice fiscale). It is required for the contract, for payroll and for the permit application.
The employer must also notify the start of the employment through the mandatory online communication. Your payroll provider normally handles this.
Step five: the residence permit   The visa only gets the worker through the border. To stay and work, they need the residence permit (permesso di soggiorno). They must apply within the legal deadline after arrival. The application is filed through the postal kit system, followed by an appointment at the police headquarters (Questura) for fingerprints and identity checks.
Until the card is printed, the receipt from the application serves as proof that the process is under way. In practice, the card arrives well after the worker has started. Plan for that gap in your onboarding and your payroll set-up.
Where files fail   Most delays come from the same few causes:
Applying in the wrong quota category. Housing or income evidence that does not match the offer. A job description that differs between the application and the contract. Missed deadlines after arrival. Keep the paperwork consistent from the first form to the last. Every document is checked against the others.
What to decide first   Before you start, settle three questions. Who is the sponsoring employer in Italy? Which quota category does the candidate fall into? Who owns the deadlines after arrival?
If you can answer all three, the rest is a checklist.

## Budgeting for Workplace Injury Insurance in Italy: Office Roles vs. Field Technicians
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/workplace-injury-insurance-italy-budget-by-role.html
Summary: Why an office role and a field technician carry different INAIL injury premiums in Italy, and how to budget for each before you hire.
If you hire in Italy, workplace injury insurance is not a flat add-on. It depends on what the person actually does. A finance analyst at a desk and a technician who installs equipment at customer sites will not cost you the same.
This article explains why, and how to build the line into your hiring budget.
Who provides the cover   In Italy, workplace injury and occupational disease cover runs through INAIL, the national insurance body. Employers pay the premium. The employee does not. It is mandatory, and it applies from the first day of work.
For a US team, the closest comparison is workers’ compensation. The logic is similar. Higher-risk work costs more to insure.
How the premium is built   The premium is not set per person. It is set per type of work. Each activity is classified under a rate table, and the rate is applied to the payroll of the people doing that activity.
The table in force is the 2019 tariff. The rules for applying it changed in 2026, so older guides may be out of date. We cover what changed below.
In practice, three things drive the final number:
The classification of the work the person performs. The payroll amount for that person. The employer’s own injury record over time. The first one is where role type matters most.
Office role: low exposure   A person in finance, HR, sales operations or software development who works at a desk sits in a low-risk classification. Injuries are rare and usually minor. The rate reflects that.
For budgeting, treat this as a small line item. It will not move the total cost of an employee in any major way.
Field technician: higher exposure   A field technician drives to sites, handles tools and equipment, and works in environments you do not control. Injuries are more likely and can be more serious. The classification is higher, and so is the rate.
The same salary can therefore produce a noticeably larger insurance cost for a technician than for an office employee. The gap comes from the rate, not from the pay.
Mixed roles need care   Many roles are not clearly one or the other. Think of a sales engineer who spends part of the week in an office and part at customer plants. Or a project manager who visits construction sites.
Classification follows the real activity. It does not follow the job title. If you label someone “account manager” but they spend most days on a production floor, the risk profile is not that of an office worker. Describe the actual duties when you set up the role. A wrong classification can lead to corrections later, and corrections cost more than getting it right at the start.
What changed in 2026   There is one update worth knowing. The 2019 tariff stays in force, but the way it is applied was modified in 2026, with the measure published in June.
Two points matter for planning:
A new bonus table now links the reduction to the number of worker-years and to an accident index known as ISAR. For insurance positions that are not statistically significant, the fixed reduction is now 13%. It was 5%. The second point mostly affects small positions, where there is too little data to measure the employer’s record in a meaningful way. If you start with a small team in Italy, this may apply to you.
Do not build your budget on the reduction, though. Whether it applies depends on your insurance position and your record, and a new team has no record yet. Budget at the full rate first. Treat any reduction as a later saving.
How to budget by role   A simple approach works well.
List each planned role and describe the real daily work, including travel and site visits. Mark each role as office, field, or mixed. Ask for the classification that fits the real activity, not the title. Apply the rate to the expected payroll for that role. Keep the reduction out of the base case. Then review the numbers when the team grows. A company that starts with office staff and later adds field technicians will see its average insurance cost per head rise. That is normal. It is better to expect it than to find it in a quarterly review.
Why it matters for the business case   Injury insurance is only one part of employer cost in Italy. It sits next to social security contributions, severance accrual and other items. But it is the one that changes most with job content rather than with salary.
This is why a flat percentage on top of salary can mislead. If your plan mixes desk roles and field roles, model them separately. The result is closer to what you will actually pay.
Summary   Injury premiums depend on the type of work, not the job title. Office roles carry low rates. Field technicians carry higher ones. Mixed roles follow their real activity. The 2019 tariff is in force, and the 2026 changes affect how reductions work. Budget at the full rate and treat reductions as upside. Want to see what this means for your own roles? Try the cost calculator.

## Building Career Paths for Italian Employees in US-Led Teams
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/career-paths-italian-employees-us-led-teams.html
Summary: How US-led companies can give Italian hires real growth paths, and avoid turning them into a remote outpost with no future.
You hired well in Italy. The person is skilled, motivated and productive. Then, a year later, they leave. The exit interview says the same thing it always says: nowhere to go.
This is the remote outpost trap. A team member sits in another country, works in another time zone, and slowly drops out of the company’s promotion logic. Nobody decided this. It just happens when growth paths are designed around the people in the headquarters.
Here is how to avoid it.
Why the trap forms   US-led teams tend to promote what they see. Managers notice the person who speaks up in the hallway, joins the late call, or answers fast on chat. An employee in Italy is often offline when the decisions get made. Over time, the work is the same but the visibility is not.
There is a second cause. Many US companies have no written definition of what each level means. Promotions run on trust and proximity. That works poorly across borders, and it works worst for people who are far from the center.
The fix is not a special Italy program. The fix is to make growth rules explicit for everyone, then check that they work in Italy.
Write down the levels   Start with a career ladder. For each role family, define the levels in plain terms. What scope does the person own? What decisions can they make alone? What impact do they have beyond their own tasks?
Keep the language about outcomes, not hours or presence. If a level requires “strong executive presence,” rewrite it. Say what you actually need: clear written updates, sound judgment on tradeoffs, the ability to lead a project without close supervision.
Then share the ladder with every employee. Italian hires should see it on day one, not discover it at review time.
Give real ownership, not leftover work   Outposts often get the stable, well-defined tasks. The new, risky and visible projects stay at headquarters. That caps growth.
Do the opposite on purpose. Assign Italian team members to projects with clear business results. Let them present the work to leadership. Let them own a product area, a customer segment or a region, such as Southern Europe.
Ownership is what makes a promotion case. If the person never owned anything, the case is empty.
Make the work visible in writing   Time zones make live visibility hard. So build visibility into documents.
Ask for short written project updates in a shared place. Record decisions and the reasons behind them. Keep promotion cases in writing, with examples of impact. Share wins in channels everyone reads, not in private chats. Written work travels across time zones. It also helps your US-based staff, who benefit from the same habits.
Fix the meeting schedule   If every important meeting happens at a time that suits only the US, the Italian team member will always be a guest. Rotate times where you can. Record the sessions and share notes. Move decisions out of live meetings and into written proposals with a comment window.
Also plan for the cost of being late in the day. Do not make the same person take the late call every week. Share the burden or protect their evenings.
Connect them to a manager who can advocate   A manager’s job in a promotion cycle is to argue for their people. A distant manager who rarely interacts with the report will argue weakly.
Hold regular one-on-ones that are about growth, not only status. Ask what the person wants in the next stage of their career. Set goals together. Make sure the manager attends calibration or promotion discussions with evidence in hand.
If the manager has several remote reports and a large local team, check that the remote ones are not at the bottom of the attention list.
Offer mobility, not only stasis   Some Italian employees will want to move into leadership. Others will want to become deep specialists. Some may want a stint at headquarters or in another office. Offer all of these paths where the business allows.
A lateral move or a short assignment abroad can signal that the company sees the person as part of the whole. If you plan relocation or visas, handle them early with your Employer of Record (EOR) or advisors, so the person is not left waiting.
Review pay and titles on the same terms   An Italian employee should be evaluated against the same ladder as a US colleague. Titles should mean the same thing. Pay will differ by local market, but the logic for raises and promotions should not. If the process is different, people will notice, and trust will go.
Check the results   Track simple signals. Are Italian employees promoted at a similar rate to peers? Do they hold visible projects? Do they stay? Ask in surveys whether they see a future at the company.
If the answers are weak, change the process before you lose the next person.
The short version   An outpost is a team without a path. Remove the causes: unclear levels, hidden work, distant managers and meeting schedules built for one time zone. Give real ownership, write things down, and apply the same growth rules everywhere.
Then the Italian hire stops being a remote exception and becomes a core part of the team.

## Company Cars, Phones and Laptops in Italy: Which Equipment Perks Are Taxable
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/italy-company-cars-phones-laptops-taxable-benefits.html
Summary: How Italy taxes company cars, phones and laptops. Learn when equipment is a tool of work and when it becomes a taxable fringe benefit for the employee.
You hire in Italy. You want to hand your new employee a laptop, a phone and maybe a car. The question is simple. Does the employee pay tax on it?
The answer depends on one test: who benefits from the use. Italian payroll treats equipment as either a tool of work or a benefit in kind. The first is not taxed. The second is added to the employee’s taxable pay.
The basic rule   Anything the employer gives that has value for the employee is, in principle, income. Italy calls these items fringe benefits. They are taxed as if they were salary, and they also count for social security contributions.
There is an exception for items the employee needs to do the job. A tool that exists only for work is not income. It is a business cost for the employer.
The line is use, not ownership. The company can own the device and still create a taxable benefit if the employee uses it freely for private life.
Laptops   A laptop used for work is a tool of work. The employer buys it, owns it and the employee uses it to do the job. No taxable benefit arises.
The picture changes if the employee can keep the laptop for personal use with no real work restriction. Or if the employer later gives it to the employee. That transfer is a benefit and it is taxable, unless it falls under the allowance described below.
Good practice:
Keep the device on the company asset register. Put the work purpose in a written equipment policy. Record the handover and the return. Phones   The same logic applies to mobile phones. A company phone with a company plan, issued for work, is a tool of work. Occasional private calls do not turn it into pay in practice.
The risk comes from mixed arrangements. For example, the employer pays the personal phone bill of the employee, or covers a family plan. Those payments are a benefit and are taxable.
If you want to avoid doubt, keep two things separate. Business lines belong to the company. Private costs stay with the employee.
Company cars   Cars are the item that creates real tax. A car given for business use only is not a benefit. In reality that is rare, because most employees drive the car home and use it on weekends.
When the employer allows private use, the car becomes a taxable benefit. This is called a car for mixed use. Italy does not look at your actual costs. It uses a conventional value set by an official table, based on the car and a standard yearly distance. The employee is taxed on that value, less any amount the employee pays back to the company.
Two points matter for planning:
The taxable value comes from the official table, not from your lease invoice. A cheap lease does not lower it. Fuel cards and other running costs paid for private use can add to the benefit. Companies often choose between a car with private use and a higher salary. Run both numbers. The car creates a taxable value for the employee and a cost for you. The result is not always better than cash.
The annual allowance for benefits   Italy lets employers give certain benefits tax-free up to a yearly threshold. According to the source we checked, the threshold is 1,000 EUR per year in the general case. It is 2,000 EUR per year for employees with dependent children.
This matters for equipment in one case. If you give a device or other goods for personal use, the value can fall within the threshold and stay tax-free. If the total of all such benefits goes over the threshold, the full amount becomes taxable, not just the excess.
Two cautions. This figure comes from a press review, so treat it as secondary. Confirm the current threshold and its conditions with your Italian payroll provider before you build a policy around it. Also, the threshold is shared across all benefits of the employee, so a gift card, a phone handover and other perks all count toward the same limit.
What this means for payroll   A taxable benefit is not a problem. It is a payroll step. The employer must:
Value the benefit. Add it to the monthly pay for tax and contribution purposes. Show it on the payslip. The cost is real for both sides. The employee sees higher taxable income. You may owe higher employer contributions on that amount.
A short checklist   Decide if the item is for work only or also for private use. Write that down in an equipment policy signed by the employee. For cars, ask payroll to calculate the conventional value before you make an offer. Track all other benefits against the yearly threshold. Review the policy when a role or family situation changes. US teams often assume a company device is free of tax everywhere. In Italy the answer depends on use. A clear policy removes most of the risk.

## Company Welfare Plans in Italy: Flexible Benefits Explained
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/italy-company-welfare-plans-flexible-benefits.html
Summary: How welfare plans and flexible benefits work in Italy, what the tax-free fringe benefit thresholds are, and how platforms help employers run them.
Italian employees expect more than a salary. Many expect a welfare plan. If you hire in Italy, you will hear the terms “welfare aziendale” and “flexible benefits” early. This article explains what they mean and how to use them without creating a tax problem.
What a welfare plan is   A welfare plan is a set of goods and services an employer gives to staff on top of pay. Examples include supermarket and fuel vouchers, public transport passes, school and childcare costs, health services, gym memberships and supplementary pension contributions.
The reason it exists is tax. Cash salary is taxed heavily and carries social contributions. Some benefits in kind can be given with much lighter tax treatment, or none at all. The employee keeps more value. The employer often pays less than it would to deliver the same value in cash.
The fringe benefit threshold   The simplest rule to know is the fringe benefit threshold. Goods and services that an employer provides to employees do not count as taxable income up to an annual limit.
The figures from the source we use are:
EUR 1,000 per year in the general case. EUR 2,000 per year for employees with dependent children. If the total value of the benefits goes above the threshold, the whole amount becomes taxable, not only the excess. That is the detail that surprises most foreign employers. Track the total per employee.
These limits are set by law and can change. Confirm the current rules with your payroll provider before you publish a benefits policy.
What “flexible” means   Flexible benefits means the employee chooses. The employer sets a budget per person. The employee spends it from a catalog. One person picks childcare. Another picks transport. A third picks a health check.
This matters for a few reasons:
A young single employee and a parent of school-age children value different things. Choice makes a modest budget feel larger. The employer controls the total, so cost stays predictable. How welfare platforms work   Most companies do not run this by hand. They use a welfare platform. It is a web portal and app, usually run by a specialist provider.
The usual flow:
The employer defines the budget and which categories are allowed. The platform credits each employee with a balance. The employee logs in and chooses services or vouchers. The platform keeps the records and passes the data to payroll. The records are the useful part. Tax treatment depends on the type of benefit and on proof that it was used for the permitted purpose. A platform keeps that trail in one place. Your payroll team and your auditors will want it.
Platforms usually charge a fee, often built into the cost of the vouchers or services. Ask for the full cost in writing before you sign.
Where welfare comes from   There are two common sources.
Company policy. You decide to offer a benefits budget to all employees or to a defined group. You set the rules. This is the easiest route for a small foreign employer.
Collective agreements. Many national collective labor agreements (CCNL) already require some welfare provisions, such as supplementary health cover or pension contributions. If your employees fall under such an agreement, you may owe these benefits regardless of your own policy. Check which agreement applies to each role.
Common mistakes   Ignoring the threshold. Going over it turns the full amount into taxable income. Treating all employees the same. The higher limit applies to employees with dependent children. You need to collect and verify that information. Copying a US benefits package. Health insurance, retirement plans and stock options work differently in Italy. A package that is generous in the US can be poor value here. No written policy. If benefits are given with no clear rule, they can be challenged later, both by tax authorities and by employees. Choosing a platform on price alone. Look at the catalog, the payroll integration and the reporting. What to do before you hire   Decide your budget per employee first. Then check which collective agreement applies, because it may already set a floor. Then choose whether to offer a flexible catalog through a platform or a smaller fixed set of benefits.
If you hire through an Employer of Record, ask how welfare is handled. A good EOR can run the plan inside payroll, apply the right agreement and keep the records. You still decide the budget. They handle the mechanics.
Welfare is a tool, not a cost center. Used well, it raises take-home value for the employee and keeps your total spend under control.

## Documents an Italian New Hire Needs Before Day One
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/documents-italian-new-hire-needs-before-day-one.html
Summary: A checklist of what to collect from a new hire in Italy before they start: tax code, ID, IBAN, residence, work authorization and more.
A late start in Italy is rarely about the contract. It is about a missing document. A tax code that does not exist yet, an expired ID, or a bank account in the wrong name can hold up the registration of a new hire and the first payroll.
This checklist covers what to collect, why each item matters, and what to do when the hire does not have it yet.
Tax code (codice fiscale)   Every employee in Italy needs a codice fiscale. Payroll, social security registration and the mandatory employment notification all depend on it.
Most Italian residents already have one. Foreign hires often do not. The tax code is issued by the Italian tax authority, and a person abroad can usually request it through an Italian consulate. Someone already in Italy can request it at a tax office.
Ask for the tax code early. If the hire has to apply, build that time into your start date.
Identity document   You need a valid copy of an identity document. For Italian and EU citizens, that is a national ID card or passport. For others, it is a passport, plus the permit described below.
Check the expiry date now. A document that lapses a few weeks after the start creates a problem later, especially for non-EU hires whose permit depends on the passport.
Work authorization for non-EU hires   EU citizens can work in Italy without a permit. Hires from outside the EU need the right to work before they begin. Depending on the case, that means an entry visa for work followed by a residence permit, or an existing permit that allows employment.
Do not let anyone start before this is in place. Working without authorization exposes the employer, not only the employee. This is the item with the longest lead time, so start it first.
Residence and address   Collect the hire’s residence address and, if different, their current address. Residence is a legal status registered with the local municipality. It affects tax treatment, local forms and some benefits.
A hire who is relocating may not have a registered address yet. That is normal. Note the temporary address, record the planned move, and update the file once the registration is done. Registering residence often takes a while after arrival, so do not wait for it before you onboard.
Bank details   Get an IBAN for an account held in the employee’s own name. Salary cannot go to a third party’s account, and a joint account should be confirmed with the employee in writing.
A new arrival may not have an Italian account. An account in another SEPA country can work for the first payments, but ask your payroll provider before promising it. Collect the IBAN as text, not a screenshot, and have the employee check it twice.
Health card and social security data   Italian residents hold a health card (tessera sanitaria). It is not needed to run payroll, but it is useful to have on file. New arrivals will usually register for the national health service after they have residence, so do not block onboarding on it.
If the hire has worked in Italy before, ask for any social security details they have. If they come from another EU country, ask whether they hold documents that show their coverage there. This helps avoid gaps and double coverage.
Family and tax situation   Italian payroll applies tax relief for dependent family members. To apply it correctly, the employee must declare who qualifies. Ask for the details of a spouse, children or other dependents, and a signed declaration where your payroll provider requires one.
If the hire skips this, payroll will still run. It will just apply the standard treatment, and the employee may have to claim the difference later. Tell them this up front.
Previous employment   If the hire changed jobs this year, ask for the tax certificate from the previous employer. It lets payroll account for income already earned. Without it, the tax calculation can be off.
Also confirm any notice period or non-compete obligations. These are not documents for payroll, but they decide whether the start date is realistic.
Qualifications and medical fitness   Some roles need proof of a degree, a license or a professional registration. Ask for copies and check them against what you advertised.
Certain jobs also require a medical fitness check and safety training before work begins. Ask your local adviser whether the role needs them. Office jobs often have lighter requirements than field or lab roles, but the answer depends on the duties.
Signed contract and privacy forms   The employment contract must be signed and the employee should receive it in a language they understand. Add the privacy notice and any consent forms required for processing personal data. Send them with the contract, not on the first morning.
A simple way to run it   Send one request list as soon as the offer is accepted. Group it by lead time: work authorization and tax code first, then address and bank details, then everything else. Track each item by name and owner. Chase the slow items weekly.
The documents are routine once you know them. The delay almost always comes from asking late.

## Electronic vs Paper Meal Vouchers in Italy: Which Should You Offer?
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/electronic-vs-paper-meal-vouchers-italy.html
Summary: Electronic meal vouchers carry a higher daily tax-free limit than paper ones in Italy. See how the two formats compare on tax treatment and employee preference.
Meal vouchers, called buoni pasto, are one of the most common benefits in Italian employment. Many employees expect them. If you hire in Italy, you will need to decide which format to offer: paper or electronic.
The choice affects your payroll cost and how your team feels about the benefit. This article compares the two on tax treatment and employee preference.
Why the format matters   In Italy, meal vouchers are not treated like ordinary salary. Up to a daily limit, the value is usually exempt from income tax and social contributions. That makes them an efficient way to give employees more value than the same amount paid as cash wages.
The exemption has a ceiling. Anything above the daily limit is treated as normal taxable pay. The ceiling is different for each format.
Tax treatment: the daily limits   According to current reporting on the latest budget law, the daily limit for electronic vouchers is 10.0 EUR per day. For paper vouchers it is 4.0 EUR per day.
The gap is large. Electronic vouchers allow more than double the tax-free value per working day. The source is a secondary one, so check the figures with your payroll provider before you set up a plan.
Here is what that means in practice:
Electronic: you can give a higher daily value before any tax or contribution applies. Paper: the tax-free room is much smaller. A voucher worth more than the limit pushes the excess into taxable pay. For a finance team, the point is simple. The same benefit budget goes further with electronic vouchers. You pay less in employer contributions on the benefit, and the employee keeps more net value.
Employee preference   We do not have survey data to cite here, so this section sticks to what is easy to observe.
Employees generally like electronic vouchers because they are easy to use. The balance sits on a card or an app. There is nothing to carry, count or lose. Many workers also value being able to see the remaining balance at any time.
Paper vouchers have some friction. Employees receive booklets and hand them over at the till. Some shops limit how many vouchers they accept in one purchase, and some do not take them at all. Lost or damaged vouchers are hard to replace.
There is one point in favor of paper. Some older or less digital workers are used to it and find it familiar. If your team is small and local, this may matter.
For most foreign companies hiring remote or hybrid staff, electronic is the easier fit. It works for people who split their time between home and office, and it requires no physical distribution.
Admin and operations   Electronic vouchers are also simpler for you to run.
No printing or shipping. Balances are loaded digitally each month. Cleaner records. The provider reports usage, which helps your payroll and finance teams. Easier for remote staff. You do not need to send anything to an employee’s home. Paper vouchers need physical handling. Someone has to order, deliver and track them. For a company without a local office, that is extra work with little benefit.
Which one should you offer?   For most US companies hiring in Italy, electronic vouchers are the better default. They have a higher tax-free limit, they are easier for employees to use, and they take less effort to manage.
Paper may still make sense in a narrow case. For example, you might inherit an existing arrangement, or your workforce may have a clear preference for it. Even then, the lower limit means less tax-free value per day.
Before you decide   Three checks will keep you out of trouble:
Confirm the current daily limits with your payroll advisor. Rules can change with each budget law. Check whether your collective agreement sets a minimum voucher value or eligibility rules. Decide whether vouchers are part of the base offer or an addition. Put it in writing in the employment contract or a company policy. Meal vouchers are a small line in the offer letter, but they shape how competitive your package looks to Italian candidates. Getting the format right costs nothing and saves tax.

## Ending Employment in Italy: Resignation, Notice and Termination Basics
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/ending-employment-italy-resignation-notice-termination.html
Summary: How employment ends in Italy: resignation, notice, dismissal and final pay. A plain overview for US founders, HR, finance and legal ops teams.
Hiring in Italy is the easy part for many US teams. Ending a job is where surprises show up. The rules are not hostile to employers, but they are formal. Process matters, and so does documentation.
This guide covers the basics. It is not legal advice for a specific case. It gives you the map so you ask the right questions early.
The main ways employment ends   Most exits fall into a few groups:
The employee resigns. The employer dismisses the employee. Both sides agree to part ways. A fixed-term contract reaches its end. The employee retires. Each path has its own steps, costs and risks. Resignation is usually the simplest. Dismissal by the employer is the one that needs the most care.
Resignation   An employee who wants to leave must follow a formal process. A casual email or a chat with a manager is not enough. Resignation is submitted through an official digital procedure, so the company can rely on a clear record that the choice was the employee’s own.
After that, the employee works through the notice period. Notice is not a courtesy in Italy. It is a duty on both sides, and its length usually comes from the national collective agreement that applies to the role. The length can differ by sector, seniority and contract type. Your payroll provider or EOR should confirm the right period before you plan a handover.
If the employee leaves without serving notice, the employer can generally claim an indemnity in place of the missing notice. If the employer wants the person to stop working right away, it can often pay in place of notice. Check how your agreement handles this.
Dismissal by the employer   Italy does not work like at-will employment in the US. An employer cannot simply end the relationship because it no longer wants the person. There has to be a recognized reason, and the employer has to be able to show it.
In broad terms, reasons fall into three types:
Misconduct. Serious behavior by the employee that breaks trust. The employer must follow a formal disciplinary process, including a written charge and a chance for the employee to respond. Business reasons. An objective need linked to the organization, such as a role that no longer exists. The employer may need to show it cannot place the person elsewhere in the company. Other grounds. Some situations, such as long absence for illness beyond the allowed limit, have their own rules. Also know what is off limits. Dismissal tied to discrimination, to pregnancy or family leave, or to an employee exercising a legal right is treated very seriously. Some of these cases are void, not just costly.
A dismissal must be communicated in writing. The letter should state the reason clearly when the law requires it. Vague or late letters are a common cause of lost disputes.
Agreed exits   Many companies prefer a mutual agreement. Both sides sign terms for the exit, often with a payment on top of what is already owed. This can cut the risk of a later claim. To protect the company, the agreement often needs to be signed in a way the law recognizes, such as before a labor office or union representative. A private paper alone may not hold up.
Fixed-term contracts   A fixed-term contract ends on its date, but the rules around renewals and extensions are strict. If you extend or renew too often, or without a valid reason where one is required, the contract can turn into a permanent one. Track end dates and decisions well in advance.
What the employee is owed at the end   On exit, the final pay usually includes more than the last salary. Expect to settle:
Unused vacation and leave. Accrued pro-rata items such as extra monthly salary payments, where the contract provides them. The end-of-service payment that builds up during employment in Italy. Any notice indemnity, if it applies. Finance teams often miss the end-of-service payment because it does not exist in many US setups. It is a real liability that grows over time. Budget for it from the start.
Practical steps for foreign employers   Read the applicable collective agreement before you hire. It drives notice and many exit terms. Keep written records of performance issues and any warnings. Do not tell an employee verbally that they are out. Use the formal steps. Talk to local advisors before you start any dismissal, not after. Plan the final pay run early, so nothing is left open. Remember equipment, access and data. Close accounts on the exit date, not before the process is complete. The bottom line   Ending employment in Italy is manageable when you treat it as a process. Know the reason, follow the form, keep the paper trail and budget for the full cost of exit. Surprises come from skipping steps, not from the rules themselves.

## Equity and Stock Options for Italian Employees: A Primer
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/equity-stock-options-italian-employees-primer.html
Summary: How US equity plans meet Italian employment: tax, payroll, contracts and filings. A high-level primer for founders, HR, finance and legal ops.
You want your Italian hires to own a piece of the company. That is a fair goal. It is also where many US teams hit surprises. A plan that works well in the US does not carry over unchanged. This primer covers the main points to check before you grant anything.
The core issue: the plan is yours, the employment is Italian   A US equity plan is written under US corporate and securities rules. An Italian employee works under Italian employment, tax and social security rules. Both sets of rules apply at the same time. Neither one switches the other off.
So the question is never just “can we grant options in Italy?” Usually you can. The real questions are how the grant is taxed, who withholds, and how it fits the employment contract.
Equity is usually treated as pay   In the US, many teams think of equity as an investment upside. In Italy, equity given because of a job is generally treated as compensation in kind. That has consequences.
Income tax can arise on the benefit the employee receives. Social security contributions can apply to that benefit as well. The employer, not the employee, is often responsible for withholding and reporting. The exact treatment depends on the type of award, the moment of the taxable event, and the terms of the plan. Stock options, restricted stock units and direct share purchases can each be handled differently. Do not assume they follow the same path.
The cash problem   This is the most common practical issue. An employee may owe tax when they receive shares or exercise options. But the shares may be illiquid, especially in a private company. The employee has a tax bill and no cash to pay it.
In the US, companies often solve this with net settlement or sell-to-cover. These tools may or may not fit your plan, and they may need extra steps in Italy. Decide early how tax will be funded. Then write it into the plan documents.
Who withholds: the local employer question   If you employ people in Italy through your own Italian entity, that entity runs payroll. It must withhold tax and contributions on the equity benefit and report it. That means your US team has to send grant, vesting and valuation data to Italian payroll on time. Late data creates late withholding.
If you use an Employer of Record (EOR), the EOR is the legal employer and runs payroll. The same data flow still applies. The EOR needs accurate information on each grant, each vesting event and each exercise. It also needs to know who pays the tax cost when it is due. Agree this in writing before the first grant, not after.
Valuation matters   For private companies, the value of the shares drives the taxable amount. You need a defensible valuation process, and you need to share the result with Italian payroll. A weak or undocumented valuation can cause disputes with the tax authorities later.
Employment law touches equity too   Equity terms sit next to the employment contract. A few points deserve attention:
Vesting and termination. Italian employment law is protective of employees. Forfeiture clauses that look standard in the US may need review for an Italian worker. Plan terms as pay. If equity is seen as part of regular pay, it can affect other entitlements. Draft the plan so it is clear that awards are discretionary and separate from base pay, where that is the intent. Language and clarity. Give employees plan documents they can understand. Provide an Italian version where useful. Unclear terms are more likely to be read against the employer. Data and consent. Equity administration shares personal data with US providers. Handle that under EU data protection rules. Securities and filing questions   Offering shares to employees can also raise securities-law questions, in the US and locally. Many employee plans qualify for exemptions or simplified treatment, but this should be confirmed for your plan and your structure. Some arrangements also involve reporting by the employee, such as declaring foreign-held assets. Tell your people this early. Surprises here fall on them personally.
Alternatives some companies use   If a standard option plan is hard to run, there are other routes. Companies sometimes use phantom equity or cash-settled awards that track share value. These can reduce securities and ownership complexity. They have their own tax and drafting issues, so they are not a free shortcut. The right choice depends on your stage, your cap table and how much administration you can handle.
A practical checklist   Decide the award type before you promise anything in an offer letter. Confirm the tax and social security treatment with local advisers. Plan how the employee will fund tax at the taxable event. Set up a data flow from your equity platform to Italian payroll. Document the valuation method. Review forfeiture, leaver and discretionary-award wording against Italian employment law. Tell employees what they will need to report and when. Do not promise in the offer letter   A common mistake is to put a headline equity number in an offer letter before anyone has checked the Italian side. Candidates compare offers. If the real after-tax result is lower than they expected, trust suffers. Keep early messages accurate and general. Share details once the plan has been reviewed for Italy.
Bottom line   Equity for Italian employees is workable. It needs planning on tax, payroll, valuation and contract language. Treat it as part of total compensation cost, not as a free add-on. Get local advice on your specific plan before the first grant.

## Expense Reimbursements in Italy: Per Diems, Receipts and Tax Treatment
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/expense-reimbursements-italy-per-diems-receipts-taxable.html
Summary: How travel and expense claims move through Italian payroll, and what decides whether a reimbursement is taxable or not.
Expense claims look simple until they hit payroll. In Italy, the way you pay a reimbursement decides whether it is taxed. It also decides whether it carries social contributions. A claim that is handled well costs the employee nothing. A claim that is handled badly can turn into taxable pay for the employee and extra contributions for you.
This article explains how the flow works and where US teams usually get it wrong.
The basic principle   A reimbursement repays a real business cost. It is not pay for work. Italian payroll treats the two very differently.
If the employee spent money on behalf of the company and can prove it, the repayment is generally not part of taxable income. If the money is paid without proof, or paid as a fixed amount that does not match a rule, it can be treated as ordinary pay. Then it is taxed and contributions apply.
So the question is never just “was it a business expense?” The question is “can we document it in the way Italian rules expect?”
Three ways to reimburse   Italian practice usually sorts travel and expense payments into three groups.
Documented reimbursement. The employee pays, keeps the receipt, and submits it. The company repays the exact amount. This is the cleanest route for flights, hotels, train tickets, taxis and client meals.
Flat per diem. The company pays a fixed daily amount for a trip instead of collecting receipts. This is common for meals and small costs while traveling. The tax result depends on the rules for the type of trip and on the amount paid. Part of a per diem can stay outside taxable income. Any amount above the allowed level is taxable.
Mixed approach. The company pays hotel and transport against receipts and adds a flat amount for meals. Many employers prefer this because it cuts paperwork but keeps the large costs fully documented.
The trip location matters too. Rules differ between travel within the employee’s usual work area, travel elsewhere in Italy and travel abroad. Your payroll provider should classify each trip before the payment is processed.
What counts as a valid receipt   In Italy, a receipt is not a casual photo of a card slip. Payroll needs a proper tax document. In practice that means an invoice or a fiscal receipt that shows the supplier, the date and the amount. A card statement alone usually does not meet the standard.
A few habits help:
Ask the supplier for a proper invoice or fiscal receipt at the time of purchase. Submit claims soon after the trip, not months later. Keep the original or a clear digital copy, as your provider requires. Tie each claim to a trip, a date and a business reason. If the supporting document is missing, do not assume payroll will accept the claim. Without it, the amount may have to be taxed as pay.
How a claim moves through payroll   The flow is short, but each step matters.
The employee submits the claim with documents and a short note on the purpose. Someone on your side approves the business need. Payroll checks the documents and classifies each line as non-taxable or taxable. The payment goes out with the monthly payslip. Non-taxable items appear as a separate line. Records are kept in case of an audit. Timing is the part founders miss. Expense claims should reach payroll before the monthly cut-off. A claim that arrives late waits for the next cycle. Employees notice this quickly, so set a clear deadline and repeat it.
Where things go wrong   Paying through a US system. A reimbursement sent from a US expense tool never touches Italian payroll. The employee may receive it as untracked income. That creates a compliance gap for both sides.
Treating a stipend as a reimbursement. A fixed monthly amount for home office or phone costs, paid with no receipts, is usually taxable pay. Calling it a reimbursement does not change that.
Mixing personal and business costs. Add-ons such as a personal meal on a business trip need to be separated before the claim is submitted.
No written policy. Without a policy, every claim becomes a debate. Write down what is covered, what proof is needed, and which per diem approach you use.
A simple policy to start with   Keep it short. State which costs are covered. State that receipts must be proper Italian tax documents. State whether meals use a flat per diem or actual cost. Set a monthly submission deadline. Name who approves claims. Share it with every new hire in Italy on day one.
The practical takeaway   Reimbursements in Italy are not hard, but they are not informal. Proof, classification and timing decide the tax result. Run every claim through Italian payroll, keep your policy clear, and confirm the treatment of each trip type with your payroll provider before you pay.
