## Hiring your first sales rep in Italy: from job post to first quarter
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/hiring-first-sales-rep-italy-eu-expansion.html
Summary: A walk-through for US founders hiring a first sales rep in Italy, from the job post and offer to onboarding and the first quarter, using an Employer of Record.
You have product-market fit in the US. Now you want a rep on the ground in Italy to open the EU market. You have no Italian entity and no local HR. This is how the path usually runs, step by step, when you use an Employer of Record (EOR).
Before the job post   Decide what the role is. A first rep in a new market is not a pure closer. They will prospect, run demos, handle local procurement questions and feed product feedback home. Write that down. It shapes the profile you search for.
Also decide where the rep sits. Many Italian sales hires work from home or from a coworking space in Milan, Rome or another hub. Pick the location based on your customers, not on habit.
Fix the pay structure early. Italian candidates will ask about fixed salary, variable pay and benefits. A clear split between base and commission helps. Vague promises of equity or a bonus to be defined later put off good people.
Writing the post   Post in Italian and in English. Say what the product does, who the buyer is and what the rep owns. Mention that the role is employed through an EOR. Candidates in Italy are used to a formal employer, so explain it in one plain sentence: the EOR is the legal employer, and you direct the daily work.
Avoid long lists of buzzwords. Strong sellers read for three things: the market, the territory and the pay. Give them those.
Interviews and the offer   Run interviews in your normal way, with one adjustment. Ask a local advisor or your EOR to check how the role maps to a collective agreement. In Italy, the national collective agreement for the sector sets minimum pay, working time, leave and notice rules. It is not optional. Your offer has to sit on top of it.
This surprises many US teams. At-will employment does not exist here. Terms are written, and changes later are harder than in the US. Get the contract right before the candidate signs.
Your EOR drafts the employment contract in Italian, aligned with the right agreement. You review the commercial terms: targets, commission plan, territory, reporting line. Keep the commission plan in a separate document so you can update it without reopening the contract.
Between acceptance and day one   Once the candidate accepts, the EOR registers the employment with the Italian authorities, sets up payroll and arranges the mandatory insurance and social security. You do not form an entity. You do not open a bank account in Italy. You do not hire a payroll provider.
The candidate may be serving notice at a current employer. Notice periods in Italy can be long, and they depend on the old contract. Ask early and plan for it. A start date that slips is normal. Do not treat it as a warning sign.
Send equipment ahead of time. A laptop, a phone and access to your CRM should be ready before the first morning.
The first weeks   Onboarding a remote rep in a new country needs more structure than a US hire. Plan the first weeks like this:
Give them a written ramp plan with clear goals for learning, pipeline and first meetings. Pair them with a US colleague for product and process questions. Set a weekly call that stays on the calendar. Share your best case studies and translate the ones that matter for Italian buyers. Do not expect closed deals right away. Enterprise cycles in Italy can be slow, and trust matters. Local references help a lot.
The first quarter   By the end of the quarter, judge the rep on activity and learning, not only on revenue. Look at these signals:
Is the pipeline filling with the right accounts? Are prospects taking meetings in Italian, and is the pitch landing? What objections come up that you did not hear in the US? Is pricing and contract language working for local buyers? This is also when you review the commission plan. If the targets were set without local data, adjust them with the rep. Do it openly and in writing.
Payroll will have run each month by now. Check the payslips with your EOR so you understand what the total cost looks like. Many founders find the full employer cost higher than the salary figure they first had in mind. Better to learn that in the first quarter than in the budget review.
What you should have at the end   A working rep with a compliant contract. A repeatable process for the next hire. Real data on what it costs to employ someone in Italy. And an answer to the question that started this: does the market respond to your product?
If yes, you can hire a second rep, add a customer success role or think about a permanent entity later. If not, you learned that without setting up a company first.

## How a US SaaS Company Built an Engineering Hub in Italy Without an Entity
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/us-saas-remote-engineering-hub-italy-without-entity.html
Summary: A scenario for US founders: how a SaaS company can build a remote engineering hub in Italy through an Employer of Record, without setting up a local entity.
This is a scenario, not a case study. It shows how a US SaaS company can build an engineering hub in Italy without opening a local company. The steps are the ones most teams follow.
The starting point   A US software company has a product that is growing. The engineering team is stretched. The founders want strong backend and platform engineers, and they want them in a time zone that overlaps with both the US East Coast and their European customers.
They look at Italy. The talent pool is deep. Engineers there are used to working with distributed teams. The cost of senior talent is lower than in San Francisco or New York.
The obstacle is not hiring. The obstacle is the paperwork behind hiring.
The first instinct: set up a subsidiary   Most founders start here. They ask a lawyer how to incorporate in Italy. They learn that an entity needs a registered address, a legal representative, a bank account, accounting, payroll registration and social security enrollment. Each step has its own office and its own language.
None of this is impossible. But it takes time, and it assumes the company already knows the hub will work. At this stage, nobody knows that yet.
The team is also worried about a second risk. If they hire an Italian resident as a contractor and manage them like an employee, they may create a misclassification problem. Italian labor rules are protective of employees. A contractor arrangement that looks like employment can be challenged.
So the company wants real employment contracts, but not a real entity. That is the gap an Employer of Record fills.
The second path: an Employer of Record   An Employer of Record (EOR) is a local company that becomes the legal employer of your people. You choose the person. You direct the daily work. The EOR signs the Italian employment contract, runs payroll, handles tax withholding and social security, and keeps the employment file in order.
For the US company, this changes the project. It no longer needs to build a legal and administrative structure first. It needs to find the right engineer.
How the hub grows   The first hire. The company picks a senior engineer who can work independently and who will help interview the next people. The EOR prepares a contract that follows the national collective agreement for the sector. The engineer gets a proper Italian employment contract, with the protections and benefits that come with it. The company does not draft any of this itself.
The first months. Payroll runs every month through the EOR. The engineer receives a normal Italian payslip. The US finance team receives one invoice from the EOR, not a set of local filings. That makes budgeting simple.
The next hires. Once the first engineer is settled, hiring gets easier. The engineer refers former colleagues. The company adds a second and a third person to the hub. Each new hire follows the same process. No new setup is needed.
Relocation and visas. Some candidates live outside Italy. If the company wants to bring a non-EU engineer to Rome or Milan, the EOR can support the visa process and the move. The company does not need to sponsor from a foreign entity.
What the US team still owns   An EOR does not replace management. The US company still owns the work.
It sets goals, reviews code and gives feedback. It decides who to hire, promote or let go, within the rules of the contract. It protects its intellectual property through the agreements signed at hiring. It keeps clear notes on how the engineer works, so the relationship stays that of an employee and employer. The EOR owns the compliance side. The company owns the product and the team culture.
When the entity makes sense   The hub eventually reaches a size where an entity may be worth it. The signs are simple. The team is large and stable. The company plans to stay in Italy for the long term. Leadership wants a local manager, a local office or local sales activity.
By then the company has real data. It knows what the hub costs, how well it performs and how hard it is to hire there. The decision to open an entity is made with facts, not guesses. Many companies move their EOR employees onto their own entity at that point. The people stay. Only the legal employer changes.
The lesson from the scenario   The company did not skip Italy’s rules. It used a partner that already works inside them. That let the hub start with real contracts, real payroll and real engineers, without building a legal structure for a team that did not exist yet.
If you are planning something similar, start by modeling the full cost of an Italian hire. Include salary, employer contributions and the EOR fee, so the numbers are clear before you commit.

## How Italian Income Tax Brackets Affect a Job Offer in 2026
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/italian-income-tax-brackets-job-offer-2026.html
Summary: Italy taxes salary in three brackets: 23%, 33% and 43%. Here is how they shape the gross-to-net gap in an offer, and where the extra relief fades.
You make an offer in gross salary. Your candidate thinks in take-home pay. In Italy, the gap between the two depends on how income tax brackets work. This article explains the brackets and what they mean when you set a number.
We cover personal income tax (IRPEF) only. Social contributions and local surtaxes are separate and are not covered here.
The three brackets   Italy taxes personal income in three slices. Each slice has its own rate.
Annual taxable income Rate Up to EUR 28,000 23% EUR 28,000 to EUR 50,000 33% Above EUR 50,000 43% The rates are marginal. They apply only to the part of income that falls inside each slice. A person who earns above EUR 50,000 does not pay 43% on everything. The first EUR 28,000 is still taxed at 23%. The next slice, up to EUR 50,000, is taxed at 33%. Only the income above EUR 50,000 is taxed at 43%.
This is the most common misunderstanding in cross-border offers. Candidates sometimes fear that a raise will push them into a bracket where they take home less. That does not happen with marginal rates. A higher salary always means more net pay from the bracket system alone.
What this means for your offer   The same raise is worth less at higher levels. Each extra euro of salary is taxed at the rate of the bracket it lands in. A raise inside the lowest bracket keeps most of its value for the employee. A raise that lands above EUR 50,000 is taxed at 43%. If you want the candidate to feel a real increase in net pay, the bracket they sit in matters.
Crossing a threshold changes the economics. The step from 23% to 33% at EUR 28,000 is a large one. The step from 33% to 43% at EUR 50,000 is just as large. If an offer sits close to either line, a small change in gross pay can change how much of the next euro the employee keeps.
US salary logic does not transfer directly. A US candidate used to a flat view of withholding may compare a gross figure to their current one and conclude the offer is low. In Italy the same gross figure turns into net pay through a different structure. Show the candidate the net result, not just the gross number.
The extra relief that fades   There is one more piece that matters for mid-range salaries. Employees with income in the range of EUR 20,000 to EUR 32,000 get an additional tax relief of EUR 1,000 per year.
Above EUR 32,000, this relief does not stop at once. It decreases gradually and reaches zero at EUR 40,000.
This has a practical effect. Between EUR 32,000 and EUR 40,000, the employee is in the 33% bracket and is also losing the extra relief. The real burden on each additional euro in that band is higher than the 33% rate suggests. A raise in this range feels smaller than the bracket table implies.
If you are hiring in this range, keep this in mind. A modest increase in gross pay may not move net pay as much as the candidate expects. Run the numbers before you promise a specific result.
How to use this when you build an offer   Decide on gross and check the net. Start from the gross figure. Then work out what the candidate actually takes home. Know where the number lands. Check which bracket the top part of the salary falls in. Check whether the extra relief applies in full, is fading, or is gone. Be careful near the thresholds. At EUR 28,000, EUR 32,000, EUR 40,000 and EUR 50,000 the tax treatment of the next euro changes. A small adjustment can matter more than it looks. Explain it plainly. Candidates in Italy know their own tax system. Candidates abroad do not. A short note that shows gross, tax and net removes most of the friction. What to remember   Italian income tax has three brackets: 23%, 33% and 43%. The rates apply to slices of income, not to the whole salary. An additional relief of EUR 1,000 applies for income between EUR 20,000 and EUR 32,000. It fades to zero between EUR 32,000 and EUR 40,000. The fade makes raises in the EUR 32,000 to EUR 40,000 band less effective than the headline rate suggests. The figures here come from a secondary source. Check them against the current official tax rules before you finalize any offer.

## How Long It Takes to Hire in Italy With an Employer of Record
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/how-long-to-hire-in-italy-with-eor.html
Summary: What happens between a signed offer and the first payroll when you hire in Italy through an Employer of Record, and what speeds up or slows down the timeline.
You found your candidate. The offer is signed. Now the question every founder and HR lead asks: how long until this person is on payroll and working legally in Italy?
The honest answer is that it depends on a few inputs you control and a few you do not. This article walks through the timeline from signed offer to first payroll when you use an Employer of Record (EOR). It shows where time goes and what you can do to shorten it.
We do not quote fixed day counts here. Italian onboarding depends on the role, the contract type, the collective agreement that applies and the worker’s own situation. Anyone who promises a single number for every case is guessing.
What an EOR changes about the timeline   Without an EOR, you would set up a local entity before you could hire. That means registrations, a local bank account, social security and tax accounts, and a payroll provider. Each step has its own queue.
With an EOR, the legal employer already exists. It already has the registrations and the payroll process. Your hire becomes an employee of that entity, and you direct the daily work. The setup phase mostly disappears. What remains is the work specific to your hire.
Stage 1: Intake and contract drafting   The clock starts when you send the signed offer and the hire’s details. The EOR needs the basics: role, start date, salary, working hours, work location and the employee’s personal data.
The EOR then maps the role to the right national collective agreement. This matters in Italy. The agreement sets minimum pay levels, notice periods, extra monthly payments and leave rules. It shapes the employment contract.
This stage is fast when your information is complete. It slows down when the job description is vague, the salary is not final, or the role could fit more than one collective agreement. Send a clear job description and a firm compensation figure on day one.
Stage 2: Contract review and signature   The EOR sends the employment contract to the employee. Italian contracts are written in Italian, and the employee should be able to read and understand what they sign. Good providers supply an English version for your records.
Time here depends on the employee. If they are currently employed, they may need time to resign and serve notice. That notice period often sets your real start date. Italian notice periods can be long for senior roles, and they follow the rules of the employee’s current agreement. Ask the candidate early what notice they owe.
Stage 3: Right to work and documents   For an EU citizen, this stage is simple. The EOR collects identity documents, tax code and bank details.
For a non-EU citizen who is not yet in Italy, this is the stage that decides your timeline. Work authorization and visa steps involve government offices and consulates. The EOR can prepare and submit the files, but it cannot control how long the offices take. If your hire already lives in Italy with a valid permit to work, the process is much shorter.
If you plan to hire someone who needs a visa, tell your EOR before the offer is signed. Better still, ask about this during candidate selection.
Stage 4: Mandatory registrations   Before the start date, the EOR must notify the relevant authorities of the new employment. It also registers the employee for social security and insurance. This is routine for an EOR and happens inside its existing accounts.
The key rule is simple. These notifications must be in place on time for the start date. That is why a late start-date change or late documents can push the start back. Plan the start date after the paperwork is complete, not before.
Stage 5: First payroll   Payroll in Italy runs on a monthly cycle. Your first payroll depends on when the employee starts relative to the payroll cut-off. A hire who starts just after a cut-off may wait for the next cycle. A hire who starts well before it will usually be paid in the same cycle, with a partial period.
Ask your EOR for the cut-off date and the pay date. Then choose a start date with that calendar in mind.
What speeds things up   A complete, accurate intake form on the first day. A clear job description that maps to one collective agreement. A candidate who is already in Italy with the right to work. Early questions about notice periods. A start date chosen around the payroll calendar. What slows things down   Visa or work permit needs. Long notice periods at the candidate’s current employer. Salary changes after contract drafting begins. Missing personal documents. Last-minute changes to the start date. The practical view   Think of the timeline as a chain. The longest link sets the pace. For most EU-based hires, that link is the candidate’s notice period. For non-EU hires, it is usually the work authorization process. The EOR’s own steps are the shortest part, because the legal employer and payroll are already in place.
To plan well, ask your EOR for a written timeline for your specific hire before you sign the offer. A good provider will show you each stage and tell you which ones depend on third parties.
Before you commit to a start date, check what the hire will cost you in total. Try the cost calculator to estimate your full employment cost in Italy.

## How New Employees in Italy Register with the National Health Service
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/register-italy-national-health-service-new-employee.html
Summary: How employees and their families sign up for Italy's public healthcare: what to bring, who handles it, and what to expect once enrolled.
Italy has a public health system called the Servizio Sanitario Nazionale, or SSN. Employees who work in Italy pay into it through payroll contributions. In return, they and their families can use public care. For a US company hiring its first person in Italy, this is one of the first practical questions the new hire will ask.
This article explains how registration works, what the employer does, and what families should expect.
What the SSN covers   The SSN gives access to a family doctor, specialist visits, hospital care, emergency treatment, and many diagnostic tests. Some services are free at the point of use. Others carry a small co-payment, known as a ticket. What you pay depends on the service, the region, and the person’s circumstances.
Healthcare in Italy is run largely at the regional level. The basic framework is national, but the booking systems, forms and waiting times differ from one region to another. A new hire in Milan may see a different process than one in Naples or Palermo.
Who is eligible   Employees working legally in Italy are generally entitled to enroll. This covers Italian citizens, EU citizens and non-EU nationals who hold a valid residence permit for work. Enrollment is tied to legal residence and employment, not to citizenship.
Family members can usually be enrolled as dependents. This typically includes a spouse or partner and children. Non-EU families need their own valid residence documents. The exact paperwork depends on the family’s status, so it is worth checking with the local office early.
The documents you need   Before anything else, the employee needs a tax code, called the codice fiscale. Italy uses it for almost every administrative step, including health registration. Many new hires get it early in the onboarding process.
The usual documents are:
A valid passport or identity card. The codice fiscale. The employment contract or proof of employment. A residence permit, for non-EU nationals. Proof of address in Italy, such as a lease or a residency registration. Documents showing family ties, if dependents will be enrolled. Non-EU families may need translated and legalized civil records. Ask the local office what it will accept.
Where to register   Registration happens at the local health authority, the Azienda Sanitaria Locale, usually shortened to ASL. Each area of Italy has its own. The employee registers with the ASL that covers their place of residence.
Many offices let you start online. Others require an in-person visit. Some accept an appointment booking only. Check the website of the relevant ASL before going.
At registration, the employee is entered in the system. The ASL then issues a health card, the tessera sanitaria. The card carries the person’s tax code. It is used at pharmacies, clinics and labs.
Choosing a family doctor   After enrollment, the employee picks a family doctor, the medico di base. Children generally get a pediatrician instead. The choice is made from a list of doctors in the area who are accepting patients.
The family doctor is the main contact for everyday care. They treat common illnesses, write prescriptions, and refer patients to specialists. In most cases, you need this referral to book a specialist visit under the public system.
A good family doctor can make the system much easier to use. New residents should not be afraid to switch if the fit is poor.
Using the system day to day   Once enrolled, a typical visit works like this:
The patient books an appointment with the family doctor. The doctor issues a prescription or referral, often in electronic form. The patient books the specialist or test through the regional booking system, or at a pharmacy that offers the service. The patient pays any co-payment and attends the visit. Pharmacies play a bigger role in Italy than many Americans expect. They give advice, fill prescriptions, and often handle bookings.
For emergencies, the hospital emergency room, the pronto soccorso, is open to everyone. Triage decides who is seen first.
Waiting times and private care   Public care has real limits. Waiting times for some specialist visits and tests can be long, especially in busy regions. Many Italians use private clinics for faster access. Some employers offer supplementary health insurance as a benefit, which can cover private visits and reduce waiting.
This is a point worth raising with new hires from the US. They may expect an insurance card and a short wait. The Italian model works differently. It is broad and affordable, but it asks for patience and paperwork.
What the employer should do   The employer does not register the employee with the SSN directly. But a good employer makes the process easier.
Help the employee get the codice fiscale before the start date. Provide a clear employment contract and proof of employment. Explain that payroll contributions fund the public system. Share a short guide to the local ASL and how to book. Consider supplementary insurance for faster private access. This support has a real effect on retention. A new hire who feels lost with healthcare in the first weeks is more likely to feel unsettled overall. This matters most for people relocating with a family.
Common mistakes   The most common problem is delay. Employees wait to register until they are sick. Then they find that the card and the doctor assignment take time. Start early.
Another mistake is assuming the process is the same everywhere. It is not. Always check the rules of the specific region and ASL.
A third is forgetting dependents. Families should be enrolled together, so children and partners can access care from the start.
In short   Italy’s public health system is open to employees and their families. Registration needs a tax code, valid documents and a visit to the local ASL. After that, a family doctor becomes the entry point to care. Employers cannot do the registration for the employee, but they can remove most of the friction.

## How to Build a Fully Loaded Cost Model for Your First Italian Hire
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/fully-loaded-cost-model-first-italian-hire.html
Summary: A step-by-step spreadsheet method for US controllers to model the true cost of a first hire in Italy, from gross pay to employer contributions and insurance.
A US offer letter names a salary. An Italian payroll names a cost. The gap between them is where budgets break. This guide gives you the spreadsheet logic to close that gap. A controller can build it in an afternoon.
Start with the right mental model   In Italy, the gross salary is not what the company pays in total. The employer owes contributions on top of it. The employee also has contributions withheld from the gross. Those are different flows. Keep them in separate blocks of your sheet, or you will double count or miss something.
Think of the model as layers. Each layer sits on the one below it.
Layer 1: the inputs tab   Create a tab called Inputs. Put every assumption there and nowhere else. Formulas elsewhere should only point to these cells.
You need:
Gross annual salary in euros. The applicable national collective agreement (CCNL) for the role. The INAIL risk classification for the job. The EUR/USD rate you use for budgeting. The start date, so you can prorate the first year. Add a column next to each input for source and date. If a number has no source, mark it red. This habit saves you at audit time.
Layer 2: the contribution base   Create a tab called Contributions. The first cell is the taxable base for social security. For a simple salaried role, this starts from gross pay. Your CCNL may define what counts and what does not, so check it before you lock the base.
The pension line (called IVS in the Italian system) is the clearest example of the two-flow logic.
Employer IVS: 23.81% of the taxable base. Employee IVS: 9.19% of the taxable base. The employer share is a real cost on top of gross. Build it as = base * employer_rate. The employee share is withheld from the gross. It reduces net pay. It does not increase your cost. Build it as a separate line and exclude it from the total employer cost.
These rates come from secondary sources. Treat them as working values. Before you finalize a budget, confirm them against the current INPS circulars. Store the confirmation date in the source column.
IVS is not the only employer contribution. Other INPS items can apply depending on the sector, company size and contract type. Create a row for each and leave the rate empty until you have confirmed it. An empty cell is better than a guess, because it shows up as an open item.
Layer 3: workplace injury insurance   Add an INAIL block below the contributions. INAIL is the national workplace injury insurer. The premium depends on the risk classification of the job, not on your company’s home country or industry.
The tariffs currently in force are the 2019 ones (DI 27/02/2019). The way they are applied was changed by a ministerial decree dated 02/04/2026 and published on 03/06/2026. So do not copy a rate from an old article and assume it holds. Build the row with two cells: the rate and the application rule. Fill both from the current INAIL source for your classification.
For a desk role the premium is usually small compared with pension contributions. Even so, keep the line. A small line that is missing is still an error.
Layer 4: the items outside payroll   A fully loaded model includes more than contributions. Add these as separate rows, each with its own status column:
Severance accrual (TFR). Italy requires employers to set this aside during employment. Model it as an accrual, not as a cost that appears only at exit. Additional monthly pay periods required by the CCNL. Many agreements call for more than twelve payments a year. Check yours and reflect it in the annual gross. Paid leave and holiday cost. Model the cost of absence coverage if the role needs it. Benefits such as meal vouchers or supplementary health cover, if the CCNL or your policy includes them. Equipment, software and workspace. One-time costs: onboarding, local payroll setup and any relocation. Not every row needs a number on day one. Every row needs an owner and a status: confirmed, estimated or open.
Layer 5: the total and the checks   On a Summary tab, add up gross salary, employer contributions, INAIL and the accruals. That is your annual employer cost in euros. Convert to dollars with the rate from Inputs.
Then add three checks.
Ratio check: total cost divided by gross salary. This is your loading factor. Compare it with the factor you saw in other quotes. If it differs a lot, find the reason row by row. Open items count: a cell that counts rows still marked open. The budget is not final until it reads zero. Sensitivity: change gross salary and the exchange rate and see what moves. The contribution lines scale with pay. The exchange rate moves everything. Keep it auditable   Use one formula per row, copied down. Avoid hard-coded numbers inside formulas. Log the date you last checked each rate. When a rule changes, as the INAIL application rules did, you will know which cells to revisit.
What to do next   Build the Inputs tab first. Then fill the pension line, since it is the most certain part. Leave unconfirmed items open and visible. A model with honest gaps beats a model with confident guesses.
When your sheet is ready, try our cost calculator and compare it with your own numbers.

## How to Convert a Contractor Into an Italian Employee
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/convert-contractor-to-italian-employee.html
Summary: A practical sequence for moving a freelancer in Italy onto payroll: what to check first, what to sign, and how to time the switch without gaps.
Many US companies start in Italy with a freelancer. It is fast and it works. Then the relationship grows. The person works set hours, uses your tools, reports to your managers and has no other clients. At that point the contractor setup is a risk, and moving the person onto payroll is the clean fix.
This guide covers the steps and the order to do them in.
Why the switch matters   Italian authorities look at how the work is actually done, not at what the contract says. If the person is integrated into your team and takes direction from you, the arrangement can be reclassified as employment. That can bring back-pay of contributions and other claims. Converting on your own terms is cheaper and calmer than being forced to later.
It also helps the person. Employees get social security coverage, paid leave, sick pay and notice rights that a freelancer does not have. Frame the conversation around that.
Step 1: Review the current relationship   Start with facts. Write down how the person works today.
Who sets the schedule? Who assigns the tasks? Do they work only for you? Do they use your equipment and email? How long has the engagement lasted? This tells you how urgent the change is. It also gives you a record of the starting point. Share it with your Italian counsel or provider before you draft anything.
Step 2: Decide who will employ them   You have two main routes.
The first is to set up your own Italian entity and run payroll yourself. This makes sense when you plan to hire several people and want a long-term presence. It takes time to set up and needs ongoing local admin.
The second is to use an Employer of Record (EOR). The EOR becomes the legal employer in Italy. It handles the contract, payroll, contributions and compliance. You direct the daily work. This is usually the faster route for a single hire or a small team, and it lets you test the market before committing to an entity.
Pick the route first. Everything else depends on it.
Step 3: Choose the contract terms   Italian employment is shaped by national collective agreements. The one that applies depends on your sector and the role. It sets minimum pay levels, job grades, working hours, leave and notice periods. You cannot go below it.
Work out three things:
The correct collective agreement and job grade for the role Whether the contract is open-ended or fixed-term Whether a probation period applies and how long the agreement allows it Open-ended is the normal default. Fixed-term contracts have limits and conditions, so ask before you choose one.
Expect the gross salary to be different from the old freelance fee. A freelancer pays their own taxes and contributions out of the fee. An employer pays additional contributions on top of salary. Build the new package from total employer cost, not from the old invoice amount.
Step 4: End the contractor agreement   Do not run both arrangements at once. Overlap strengthens the case that the work was always employment.
Check the termination terms in the existing contract. Agree an end date with the contractor in writing. Settle the final invoices. Make clear in the document that the new employment contract replaces the old working relationship going forward.
The contractor may also need to close or pause their freelance tax registration. That is their decision, and they should speak to their accountant.
Step 5: Complete the pre-hire formalities   Italy requires the employer to notify the authorities of a new hire before the person starts. The employment contract should be signed and in place before the first working day. The employer also registers the employee with the social security and workplace insurance bodies.
If the person is not an EU citizen, check their right to work before anything else. A permit tied to self-employment does not automatically cover employment. Your EOR or counsel can tell you what is needed.
Step 6: Plan the timing   Work backwards from the start date you want.
First, settle the review and the choice of employer. Then agree the offer with the person. Then sign the employment contract and file the hire notification before day one. Set the contractor end date to the day before the employment start date, so there is no gap and no overlap.
If you use an EOR, much of this runs in parallel because the provider already has the entity and the payroll set up. If you open your own entity, expect the setup to be the longest part. Do not promise a start date to the person until the legal employer exists.
Pay attention to payroll cut-offs. Ask your provider when payroll closes, so the first payslip is correct and on time.
Step 7: Onboard as an employee   On day one the person is an employee. Give them an employee handbook, a clear job description and a named manager. Confirm how leave, sick days and expenses work. Update their tools and access to match their new status.
Keep the paperwork from the whole change in one folder: the review, the signed termination, the contract and the filings. If anyone asks later, you can show a clean, well-timed transition.
A short checklist   Document how the person works today Choose your own entity or an EOR Set the collective agreement, grade and contract type Price the role on total employer cost End the freelance agreement in writing File the hire notification and register the employee before the start date Check work authorization for non-EU workers Align the end and start dates with no gap and no overlap None of this is hard, but the order matters. Do it in sequence and the conversion is routine.

## How to Convert a USD Budget into a Competitive Italian Gross Salary
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/convert-usd-budget-to-italian-gross-salary.html
Summary: Work backwards from a USD budget to an Italian gross salary offer. Learn how IRPEF and INPS shape take-home pay so you neither overpay nor underbid.
You have a budget in dollars. Your candidate thinks in euros, and in net monthly pay. The offer you write must be a gross annual figure in euros. Getting from one to the other is where most US teams go wrong.
This guide works backwards from the budget. It shows what sits between a gross offer and what the person actually receives.
Start with the right question   Most founders ask: “What salary can we afford?” That is only half of it. Two numbers matter:
Total employer cost. This is your budget ceiling. It includes the gross salary plus employer-side contributions and other mandatory costs. Net pay to the employee. This is what the candidate compares against other offers. The gross salary sits between the two. Your job is to pick a gross figure where the total cost fits your budget and the net pay is competitive.
Step one: fix the budget in euros   Convert your USD budget to euros at a rate you can defend. Use a recent rate and add a margin for movement. A budget that works at today’s rate may not work after a currency swing. If your cost base is in dollars, build a buffer into the offer instead of renegotiating later.
Then subtract the employer-side costs to find the gross salary your budget can carry. Employer contributions are paid on top of gross pay. They are not part of it. Many first-time Italian employers forget this and treat the budget as if it were the gross figure. That is how teams end up overpaying or running over budget.
Your cost calculator will do this step for you. The point here is to see the logic: budget, minus employer costs, equals the maximum gross.
Step two: see what the employee loses   A candidate will not judge your gross figure in isolation. They will estimate what lands in their bank account. Two deductions drive that.
Social security. The employee’s share of INPS pension contributions (IVS) is 9.19% of the taxable base. It is withheld from the gross salary every month.
Income tax. Italy taxes personal income under IRPEF, with rising brackets:
Annual income (EUR) Rate Up to 28,000 23% 28,000 to 50,000 33% Above 50,000 43% These are marginal rates. Each rate applies only to the slice of income inside that bracket. A person earning above 50,000 does not pay 43% on everything. They pay 23% on the first slice, 33% on the next, and 43% only on the part above 50,000.
Local surtaxes and any deductions also apply, so treat the brackets as the core of the estimate, not the whole of it.
Why the brackets matter for your offer   The jump from 33% to 43% changes how much an extra euro of gross is worth to the candidate. Once a salary is in the top bracket, each additional euro of gross delivers less net than it did lower down. That has two practical effects.
First, a small gross raise near a bracket line buys little net pay for the employee. It still costs you the full amount plus employer contributions. Pushing the offer across a threshold is often poor value.
Second, a gross figure just below a threshold can be more competitive than it looks. The candidate keeps a larger share of each euro.
Before you commit, run your target gross through the brackets and see where it falls.
Avoid the two common mistakes   Overpaying. This happens when a US team converts a dollar salary directly into euros and calls it the gross. Italian gross pay is usually not a one-to-one match with a US base salary. Employer contributions and the tax structure change the picture. A direct conversion can leave you well above the market rate for the role, or well above what your budget can carry.
Underbidding. This happens when a team quotes a gross that looks fine in dollars but delivers a thin net after INPS and IRPEF. The candidate runs the numbers, sees the take-home, and walks. They compare net, not gross.
A simple working method   Set the total budget and convert it to euros with a safety margin. Subtract employer-side costs to find the maximum gross. Apply the employee’s INPS share of 9.19% to that gross. Run the remaining taxable amount through the IRPEF brackets. Read the resulting net pay against the market for the role. Adjust the gross up or down until cost and net both make sense. If the net is too low to compete, you have three honest options. Raise the budget, narrow the role, or offer non-cash value the candidate cares about. Do not hide the gap with a gross number that looks good on paper.
Keep the offer honest   Share the gross figure in the offer, and be ready to explain the net. Candidates in Italy expect to talk about take-home pay. A clear, accurate estimate builds trust early and avoids surprises on the first payslip.
Verify the rates before you finalize any offer, since tax and contribution rules can change. The figures above come from published secondary sources, not from a payroll run.

## How to Design a Benefits Package for Italian Employees
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/design-benefits-package-italian-employees.html
Summary: Build an Italy benefits package that employees value and that stays tax-efficient: meal vouchers, fringe benefits, welfare and how to structure them.
US companies tend to copy their home benefits plan when they hire in Italy. It rarely works. Italian employees compare offers differently. They look at take-home pay, meal support, family help and time off. A well-built package costs you less and feels bigger to the employee.
This guide shows how to prioritize perks Italians value and that are tax-efficient.
Start with what the law and the contract already give   Italy sets a lot by default. National collective agreements (CCNL) define minimum pay, extra monthly payments, leave and notice. Many also include supplementary health or pension funds. You do not choose these. You build on top of them.
So your first task is to find the CCNL that applies to your role and sector. Then read what it already provides. Offering a perk that duplicates it wastes budget. Offering one that sits below it creates a compliance problem.
Use tax-efficient benefits instead of extra salary   In Italy, a raise is expensive. Employer contributions and employee income tax both reduce its value. Some benefits are treated more kindly. Money spent there reaches the employee at a better ratio.
Two tools matter most.
Electronic meal vouchers   Meal vouchers are a standard expectation in Italy. Many candidates ask about them in the first call. Electronic vouchers have a higher tax-free daily limit than paper ones. A secondary source reports the electronic limit at EUR 10 per day.
This is easy to run. You pay per working day. Employees use the card in shops and restaurants. It signals that you understand local practice.
Check the details with your payroll provider before you promise anything. Limits change with budget laws, and your CCNL may set its own rules.
The fringe benefit allowance   Italian rules let employers give certain goods and services up to an annual threshold without the value counting as taxable income for the employee. A secondary source reports the following thresholds:
EUR 1,000 per year in the general case EUR 2,000 per year for employees with dependent children The higher figure matters. Many of your hires will be parents. A family-aware package uses that room.
These thresholds are annual and per employee. Treat them as a ceiling for the whole tax-free fringe budget, not a per-benefit amount. Track what you give across the year.
Pick perks Italians actually value   A good package fits local life. These categories tend to land well.
Meal support. Covered above. It is low cost and widely understood.
Family and education support. Contributions toward school costs, childcare and similar needs often fit within welfare arrangements. Employees with children notice this the most.
Health coverage. Public healthcare exists, but many employees like a private layer for faster access. Supplementary health plans are common and well regarded.
Supplementary pension. Pension planning matters in Italy. A contribution to a pension fund shows long-term commitment. Check how it interacts with any fund your CCNL already names.
Time and flexibility. Italians value time off and predictable hours. Flexible schedules and remote days cost little and carry real weight, especially for parents.
Transport and commuting help. Useful in big cities. Often simple to administer.
What to skip or rethink   Some US staples do not translate.
Equity alone is hard to value for local staff. If you use it, explain it plainly and pair it with cash benefits. A large cash perks stipend is less efficient than structured welfare. It may be fully taxable. Unlimited time off sounds generous but can read as vague in a country where leave is clearly defined. A simple way to build the package   Identify the CCNL and list what it already covers. Set your total budget per employee, including employer cost. Fill the tax-efficient layer first: electronic meal vouchers, then fringe benefits up to the annual threshold. Add health or pension contributions where the contract allows. Use salary only for the remainder. Document the plan so payroll can apply it correctly. This order matters. Salary is the most expensive way to deliver value. Use it last.
Keep it easy to explain   In offer letters, show the whole package in plain terms. Name the meal voucher value. State the fringe allowance. Say what the CCNL gives on top. Candidates in Italy compare these lines. A clear breakdown builds trust.
Also review the package every year. Limits and rules change. A plan that was efficient last year may leave room unused this year.
Work with local payroll   Benefits in Italy look simple until you run them. Rules differ by contract, by employee situation and by the type of benefit. Have a local payroll or employer-of-record partner confirm each element before launch.

## How to Explain Net Pay to an Italian Employee
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/explain-net-pay-italian-employee.html
Summary: A plain guide for managers on walking an Italian employee through gross-to-net: pension contributions, income tax brackets and the employment tax credit.
Your new hire in Italy looks at the payslip and asks why the net is so far from the gross. You need a clear answer. This guide gives you one.
The short version: the gross salary goes through two main steps. First, the employee’s pension contribution comes out. Then income tax is calculated on what remains, and a tax credit reduces that tax.
Start with the order of the steps   In Italy, gross-to-net follows a fixed sequence. Explain it in that order and the payslip stops looking random.
Gross salary. Social security contribution paid by the employee. Taxable income (gross minus that contribution). Income tax (IRPEF) by bracket. Employment tax credit, which lowers the IRPEF. Net pay. Write these on a slide or in a short email. Employees remember a list better than a paragraph.
Step one: the pension contribution   The employee pays a share of pay into the national pension system through INPS. The pension (IVS) rate for employees is 9.19% of the taxable base for contributions.
Tell the employee what this is for. It builds their state pension and related cover. It is not a fee. It also reduces the income on which tax is calculated, which many people do not know.
A note on scope: other contributions and local items can appear on a payslip. This article covers the main mechanics. Your payroll provider can explain any extra line.
Step two: income tax by bracket   IRPEF is progressive. That means different slices of income are taxed at different rates. It does not mean the whole salary is taxed at one rate.
The national brackets are:
Up to 28,000 euros a year: 23%. From 28,000 to 50,000 euros: 33%. Above 50,000 euros: 43%. The most common mistake is thinking that crossing a threshold taxes the full salary at the higher rate. It does not. Only the part of income above the threshold is taxed at the higher rate. Say this out loud in the conversation. Employees who earn near a threshold often worry about a raise for exactly this reason.
Step three: the employment tax credit   After IRPEF is calculated, employees get a tax credit for employment income. It is subtracted from the tax, not from the salary. This is why the effective tax rate is lower than the bracket rate.
The credit depends on income:
Up to 15,000 euros: 1,955 euros, with a minimum of 690 euros (1,380 euros for fixed-term contracts). From 15,000 to 28,000 euros: 1,910 euros plus 1,190 euros scaled by how far income is below 28,000, over a range of 13,000. From 28,000 to 50,000 euros: 1,910 euros scaled by how far income is below 50,000, over a range of 22,000. An extra 65 euros applies for income between 25,000 and 35,000 euros. Above 50,000 euros: no credit. Two points matter for the conversation. The credit shrinks as income rises. And above 50,000 euros it is gone. A manager does not need to recite the formula. You need to say that the credit exists, that it falls with income, and that payroll applies it automatically.
How to run the conversation   Use the employee’s own payslip. Generic examples feel abstract. Go through the real lines one by one.
Separate gross from cost. The employee sees gross and net. The company sees total cost. Do not mix the two. If the employee asks what the company pays, answer that separately.
Do not promise a net figure from memory. The net depends on the contract type, the income level and the payroll calculation. Give the method, then let payroll produce the number.
Explain what changes with a raise. A raise moves part of income into a higher bracket only for the portion above the threshold. At the same time, the tax credit may fall. Both effects are normal. Tell the employee before the raise lands, not after.
Offer a follow-up. Some people need time with the numbers. Say they can come back with questions after they have read the payslip at home.
What to avoid   Do not say “the state takes a percentage” as if it were one flat rate. There are several steps. Do not quote a net salary you have not checked. Do not treat the pension contribution as a tax. The employee gets something for it. Do not skip the tax credit. Without it, the explanation does not add up. A script you can use   “Your gross salary is the starting point. First, your pension contribution comes out. Then we calculate income tax on the rest, by bracket. Each bracket only applies to the slice of income inside it. Finally, a tax credit for employees reduces the tax. What is left is your net pay.”
That is enough for most first conversations. Go deeper only if the employee asks.
Want to see how gross, contributions and total cost fit together for a hire in Italy? Try the cost calculator.

## How to Get an Italian Tax Code (Codice Fiscale) for a New Hire
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/italian-tax-code-codice-fiscale-new-hire.html
Summary: How to get a codice fiscale for a new hire in Italy, with practical routes for residents and non-residents and tips to avoid payroll delays.
Every employee in Italy needs a codice fiscale. It is the personal tax identifier. Payroll, social security filings, the employment contract registration and the employee’s own tax position all depend on it. If your new hire does not have one, you cannot complete onboarding.
This guide covers the practical routes. The right one depends on where the person lives today.
What the codice fiscale is   The codice fiscale is an alphanumeric code. It is built from the person’s surname, first name, date of birth, sex and place of birth. The Italian tax authority, the Agenzia delle Entrate, issues it and keeps the register.
You will find many free online calculators that produce a code from these data. Do not treat their output as official. A calculated code can be wrong, and it may not exist in the register. Only a code issued by the tax authority or an authorized body counts. Ask your hire for the official certificate or card, not a screenshot from a calculator.
Why the employer cares   You need the code before the first payroll run. You also need it for the mandatory notice of hire and for monthly social security reporting. A missing or mistyped code causes rejected filings. Fixing them later costs time and often needs a correction procedure.
Check the code against the passport or ID. A single wrong letter in a surname or a swapped birth date is the most common error.
Route one: the hire lives in Italy   Most residents fall into one of these cases.
Italian citizens. Most already have a code, often issued at birth. Ask for the health card or the tax card. If they cannot find it, they can get a certificate from the tax authority’s website or at a local office.
Foreign nationals living in Italy. They can apply in person at a local office of the Agenzia delle Entrate. They bring a valid passport or ID document and complete the application form. For non-EU citizens, the residence permit or proof of permit application is usually also needed. The office issues the code on the spot in most cases.
Someone with digital access. If the person already has a digital identity such as SPID, many services are available online. This helps with downloading certificates for an existing code. First-time issuance for foreigners is usually easier in person.
Tell your hire to book an appointment early. Some offices have limited slots and busy periods.
Route two: the hire lives abroad   This is the common case for companies hiring from the US or elsewhere before the person moves. There are three practical options.
Italian consulate abroad. Italian consulates can issue a codice fiscale to foreign nationals who live outside Italy. The person applies with a passport copy and the application form. Processing times and requirements vary by consulate, so check the local page first. This is often the best choice when the hire needs the code before arrival.
At the visa stage. For non-EU hires who need a work visa, the code is often requested as part of the visa and permit process. Confirm with the consulate what they require in your case. Do not assume it happens automatically.
On arrival in Italy. If timing allows, the hire can apply at a local tax office after landing. This works, but it delays payroll setup until the person is physically in Italy and has an appointment.
Italian citizens living abroad. If they are registered with the Italian registry of citizens abroad, AIRE, they may already have a code. If not, the consulate or a municipal office can help.
Can the employer or a representative apply?   In some cases a delegate can submit the request on behalf of the applicant. This usually needs a signed delegation and a copy of the applicant’s ID. Rules differ by office and case, so check with the specific office before relying on it. A local representative or your Employer of Record can often handle the follow-up, which saves your team from chasing offices in another time zone.
Documents to collect from the hire   A valid passport or national ID Full legal name as shown in the passport, with accents and middle names Date and place of birth, including country Address of residence, in Italy or abroad For non-EU citizens in Italy, the residence permit or permit receipt Common mistakes   Using an unofficial calculated code. Entering the name differently from the passport. Waiting until the start date to ask for the code. Forgetting that a hire abroad may need a consulate appointment with a long lead time. Mixing up the personal code with a company tax number. They are different identifiers. A simple plan   Ask for the code as soon as the offer is signed. If the person already has one, collect the official certificate. If not, choose the route by location: tax office for residents, consulate or arrival appointment for those abroad. Verify the final code against the passport before it goes into payroll.
A tax code is a small step, but it sits on the critical path. Starting early removes a common source of delay.

## How to Give Feedback Across US and Italian Communication Styles
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/feedback-us-italian-communication-styles.html
Summary: US feedback is direct and explicit. Italian feedback is often contextual. Here is how to bridge both styles with your Italian team without losing clarity.
You hired someone in Italy. You gave clear feedback. Nothing changed. Or the reverse: your Italian manager gave you a careful, gentle update, and you missed that it was a warning.
This is rarely about skill or effort. It is about two different ways of saying hard things. Once you see the difference, you can work with both.
Two styles, two assumptions   US feedback is usually direct. You say what worked, what did not, and what to change. The words carry the message. A good manager is clear, and clarity is seen as respect.
Italian feedback often relies on context. The message sits in the tone, the timing, the setting and the relationship. A direct criticism, especially in front of others, can feel harsh or even personal. A good manager protects the relationship first and then raises the issue, often indirectly.
Neither style is better. Each one assumes the listener will fill in the gaps in a certain way. Problems start when the listener fills them in the other way.
What goes wrong   A US founder says, “This report needs work.” In the US, that is a mild note. An Italian employee may hear it as a sharp judgment and go quiet.
An Italian team lead says, “Maybe we could look again at this section.” To them, that is a clear request. A US founder may read it as a suggestion and move on.
Both sides acted in good faith. Both sides misread the other.
Rules for US managers giving feedback in Italy   Do it in private. Public correction damages trust fast. Use a one-to-one call or meeting.
Open with the relationship. Take a moment to ask how things are going. This is not wasted time. It sets the frame in which your feedback will be heard.
Be specific, but frame it as shared work. Say “Let’s look at how we can make this section stronger” instead of “This section is wrong.” Then name the exact change you need.
Do not hide the point. Softening is fine. Vagueness is not. If you need something fixed, say what, and say by when. Your Italian colleague will respect a clear request delivered with care.
Pair criticism with real recognition. Mention what the person does well, and mean it. Skip the formula of praise, criticism, praise. It reads as scripted.
Check understanding. Ask, “What would you change first?” Their answer shows you whether the message landed.
Rules for reading Italian feedback as a US manager   When an Italian colleague raises something, treat soft wording as a real signal.
“It might be complicated” often means “this will not work as planned.” “We could consider” often means “I think we should.” A long pause or a change of subject can mean disagreement. When you sense hesitation, ask a follow-up in private. Try, “What concerns do you have?” or “What would make this easier?” Give them room to be honest without losing face.
Set the rules together   The most useful step is to talk about the gap itself. In a new team, say it openly:
“I tend to be very direct. It is not meant as criticism of you. If something I say sounds harsh, tell me. And please tell me directly when you see a problem.”
This does two things. It gives your Italian colleagues permission to be more explicit with you. It also signals that your bluntness is a style, not a verdict.
Agree on a few habits:
A regular one-to-one where feedback goes both ways. A shared way to flag urgency, such as a word or a label, so a soft tone never hides a real deadline. A written follow-up after any serious conversation, so the agreed actions are clear to everyone. Written feedback needs extra care   Email and chat remove tone. A short, direct message that feels efficient in the US can feel cold in Italy. Add a greeting. Add a sentence of context. Keep the request itself plain and easy to find.
For anything sensitive, speak first and write after. A call lets you adjust as you go. The written note then confirms what you both agreed.
Performance problems   If the issue is serious or repeated, do not rely on hints. Be explicit and calm. Describe the facts, the effect on the work, and what must change. Keep a record of what was said. Italian employment rules shape how formal steps must be handled, so involve your local HR or employment partner before any formal action.
The goal   You are not trying to become Italian, and your team is not trying to become American. You are building a shared style: clear enough for the US side, respectful enough for the Italian side. Teams that do this well move faster, because people say what they mean and hear what is meant.

## How to Handle Salary Raises and Promotions on Italian Payroll
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/salary-raises-promotions-italian-payroll.html
Summary: A step-by-step view of how a raise or promotion moves from approval to the payslip and the contract addendum when you employ people in Italy.
A raise in Italy is not just a number change in your HR system. It touches the employment contract, the collective agreement, payroll and sometimes the employee’s job level. If you skip a step, you get payslip errors and disputes later.
This guide walks through the process in the order it should happen.
Start with the decision, in writing   Before anything reaches payroll, record the approval. Keep it simple and internal:
The employee’s name and current role. The new gross salary, or the new role and the salary that goes with it. The effective date. Who approved it and why. The effective date matters more than most teams expect. Payroll is built around a monthly cycle. A change agreed late in the month, but meant to apply earlier, forces a manual adjustment. Decide the effective date with the payroll calendar in mind.
Check the collective agreement   Most Italian employees are covered by a national collective agreement. It sets minimum pay for each job level and defines what each level means. This is where a promotion differs from a plain raise.
A raise keeps the same role and level. The pay goes up, but the contract terms otherwise stay put.
A promotion changes the duties, and often the contractual level. The new level has its own minimum pay, its own description and sometimes different rules on notice or other terms. Check that the new salary does not fall below the minimum for the new level.
Also check whether the employee already receives pay above the minimum. Some companies treat that extra amount as absorbable, meaning a later increase can be set against it. Others do not. If your original contract says nothing, ask your payroll provider how it has been treated so far. Do not assume.
Decide how the raise is structured   A raise can take different forms. The most common are an increase in base pay or a separate fixed allowance. Each has a different effect on other items calculated from base pay, such as severance accrual and some paid leave calculations.
This is why the structure should be chosen deliberately, not left to whoever updates the spreadsheet. Ask your payroll provider or labor consultant to confirm what the structure changes downstream before you commit.
Prepare the contract addendum   In Italy, a change to the terms of employment should be documented. For a raise or promotion, that usually means a short addendum to the employment contract, or a letter of variation signed by both sides.
A good addendum states:
The new gross salary and how it is structured. The new role and level, if there is a promotion. The effective date. That all other terms remain unchanged. Write it in Italian, and add an English version for the employee if useful. Have a local advisor review it. The signed document goes into the employee file and a copy goes to payroll.
Do not rely on an email thread as the only record. Emails get lost, and they rarely carry the detail a payroll audit or a later dispute will ask for.
Send the data to payroll on time   Payroll closes before the payslip is issued. Your provider will have a cutoff for changes. If the addendum and the new figures arrive after that cutoff, the change slips to the next cycle, and the difference has to be paid as a catch-up.
Send payroll these items together:
The signed addendum. The effective date. The new level and job title, if any. Any change to allowances or other recurring items. Sending everything in one package avoids the back and forth that causes most delays.
Review the first payslip carefully   When the first payslip with the change arrives, check it against the addendum. Look at:
Gross pay matches the agreed figure. The job level and title are correct. Any retroactive amount is shown and explained. Net pay looks reasonable given the change in taxes and social contributions. A higher gross salary does not raise net pay by the same amount. Tax and contributions take a larger share as pay rises. Tell the employee this before the payslip arrives, so the net figure is not a surprise.
Update your own records   After the payslip checks out, update your internal systems: HR records, budget forecasts and any cost reports. If you use a headcount or cost model for Italy, refresh it with the new salary. Employer contributions and accruals move with the salary, so the true cost of the raise is higher than the gross increase alone.
A short checklist   Approve in writing, with an effective date. Check the collective agreement and the level. Choose the pay structure on purpose. Draft and sign the addendum. Send one complete package to payroll before the cutoff. Verify the first payslip. Update your cost forecast. Done in this order, a raise or promotion is routine. Done out of order, it creates corrections that take weeks to clear.

## How to Make a Job Offer in Italy That Closes
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/how-to-make-a-job-offer-in-italy-that-closes.html
Summary: A practical guide to structuring an Italian job offer, timing it well, and explaining gross versus net pay so candidates say yes.
A strong offer in Italy is not just a number. It is a clear package, sent at the right moment, with pay explained in terms the candidate actually thinks in. Most US teams lose candidates on the last point.
Anatomy of an offer that closes   Keep the written offer short and complete. A candidate who has to ask what is missing starts to doubt the employer.
Include these items:
Job title and level. In Italy the level often drives pay minimums and notice terms, so it matters more than the title. Gross annual salary. State it as a yearly figure. This is the number Italian candidates compare across offers. Collective agreement. Name the national collective agreement (CCNL) that applies. It sets minimum pay, working hours, leave and notice. Candidates and their advisers will look for it. How pay is paid out. Many contracts pay the annual salary over more monthly payments than a US team expects. Say so in the offer, so the candidate does not do the math wrong. Variable pay. Bonus or commission terms in plain words: what triggers them, how they are measured, when they are paid. Benefits. Meal vouchers, health cover, equipment, remote work terms. List what is real. Do not promise what you have not approved. Start date and probation. Give a target start date and say that a probation period applies, as the contract will set out. Conditions. Right to work, references, signed contract. Say them once, calmly. The offer letter is not the contract. The Italian employment contract follows, in Italian, and should match the offer line by line. Any gap between the two is where trust breaks. Tell the candidate early that the contract will be in Italian, and offer a plain English summary.
Present gross and net together   US teams talk in gross. Italian candidates think in gross for comparison, but they budget in net. If you only give one, you leave a question open.
Give both. Lead with the gross annual figure, then give an estimated monthly net. Label the net as an estimate and say what it assumes.
The gap between the two comes from personal income tax (IRPEF) and the employee’s social security contributions. IRPEF is progressive. These are the national brackets, as reported by a secondary source:
Income up to 28,000 EUR per year: 23%. Income from 28,000 to 50,000 EUR: 33%. Income above 50,000 EUR: 43%. The rates apply to each slice of income, not to the whole salary. A candidate earning above 50,000 EUR does not pay 43% on everything. Say this out loud, because many people assume the top rate hits the full amount.
These brackets are only part of the picture. Deductions, social contributions and local surcharges change the final net. That is why you should show an estimate, not a promise, and why the person who prepares it should know Italian payroll.
Explain the employer side too   A gross salary is not your full cost. Employer contributions and other mandatory items sit on top. Your finance team needs the total cost, and your candidate does not need it. Keep the two views apart. The candidate sees gross and net. Finance sees total employer cost.
If you mix them, you get two bad outcomes. The candidate sees a large number and expects a large net. Or finance sees the gross and underbudgets.
Timing   Speed matters, but so does sequence.
Verbal first. Call the candidate before sending anything in writing. Share the gross figure and the main terms. Listen for hesitation. Written offer soon after. Send it while the call is fresh. A long gap reads as doubt. Give a real decision window. Candidates in Italy often owe notice to their current employer and may want to talk to family or an adviser. A deadline that is too tight feels like pressure and often backfires. Name one contact. One person answers questions about pay, benefits and the contract. Mixed answers from several people cost you the hire. Move to the contract quickly once they accept. The period between acceptance and signature is when a competing offer can still land. Common mistakes   Quoting a net figure without saying how you got it. Using a US-style total compensation sheet with stock and bonuses mixed into one number. Leaving out the collective agreement. Sending an English contract draft as if it were the final document. Letting different people give the candidate different numbers. A simple check before you send   Ask three questions. Could the candidate explain this offer to their partner in two minutes? Does the gross match the contract draft? Does finance agree on the total cost? If any answer is no, fix it first.
An offer that is clear, consistent and honest about net pay closes more often than a higher number with gaps in it.

## How to Monitor Employees in Italy Without Breaking Privacy Rules
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/monitor-employees-italy-privacy-rules.html
Summary: Which employee tracking tools are allowed in Italy, which need a union or labor office agreement, and what notice you must give your staff.
Many US companies bring their usual monitoring setup to Italy. Time trackers, laptop agents, GPS on vehicles, email scanning. Some of it is fine. Some of it can lead to fines and to evidence you cannot use in a dispute.
This guide explains where the line sits and what you need to do before you switch a tool on.
The basic rule   Italy protects workers from remote control of their activity. Two layers apply at the same time.
The Workers’ Statute limits tools that can monitor employees, even if monitoring is not their main purpose. The GDPR and the Italian privacy code govern how you collect and use the personal data those tools produce. You must satisfy both. Passing one does not excuse the other.
What usually needs an agreement   If a tool is installed for organizational, production or safety needs, and it can also monitor workers, you need prior approval. You get it in one of two ways.
A collective agreement with the works council or the union representatives in the company. Where there is no representation, or no deal, an authorization from the labor inspectorate. Typical examples:
CCTV cameras in workplaces. Software that logs activity, screens, keystrokes or application use. Systems that record location or movement through badges or sensors. Tools that scan email content or browsing history beyond basic security. This step comes first. If you install the tool before you have the agreement or authorization, the setup is not compliant, even if you fix the paperwork later.
A foreign employer with a small team in Italy often has no union representation. In that case the labor inspectorate route is the normal path. Plan time for it before your start date.
What does not need an agreement   The law makes an exception for tools that employees use to do their job, and for tools that record attendance and access. Examples:
A company laptop and the standard business software on it. A company email account and phone used for work. Badge or clock-in systems that record arrival and departure. This exception is narrower than it looks. A laptop is a work tool. A hidden agent on that laptop that captures screens is not. Once a tool goes beyond what the job needs, you are back in the agreement zone.
GPS is a common trap. A GPS device on a delivery van used to route and schedule work may need an agreement. A GPS app that tracks a salesperson all day for control purposes is harder to defend. Ask what the tool is for, and whether a lighter option does the same job.
Notice is always required   Even when no agreement is needed, you must tell employees how monitoring works. Give them a clear written policy that covers:
Which tools you use. What data they collect. How the data is used, and for what purposes. How long you keep it. Who can see it. How employees can exercise their data rights. Write it in plain language. Give it to every employee in Italian, and keep proof that they received it. A policy buried in a handbook does not count.
If you want to use the data in a disciplinary matter, this notice matters a lot. Data collected without proper information may not be usable.
Privacy principles you must follow   The GDPR sets the frame for every tool.
Legitimate purpose. Define why you monitor. Security, safety and protecting company assets can qualify. General curiosity about productivity does not. Proportionality. Use the least intrusive method that meets the goal. Blanket, continuous monitoring is hard to justify. Minimization. Collect only what you need. Do not read private messages or personal browsing if a log of security events is enough. Impact assessment. Systematic monitoring of staff often calls for a data protection impact assessment. Do it before launch. Retention limits. Delete data when the purpose ends. Practical checklist before launch   List every tool that touches employee activity, including those bundled in your global IT stack. Sort them into work tools, attendance tools and everything else. For the “everything else” group, start the agreement or authorization process. Switch off or limit features that are not needed in Italy. Many global platforms let you do this by region. Draft the monitoring policy and the employee notice. Run the impact assessment where required. Brief your managers. They must not look at data outside the stated purpose. Remote and hybrid work   The same rules apply when people work from home. Home monitoring raises the privacy stakes, because the line between work and private life is thin. Webcam checks, screenshots and always-on tracking are high risk. Measure outcomes and deliverables instead of watching screens.
What this means for a foreign company   Your headquarters policy probably does not fit Italy as it stands. Your global IT team may have rolled out tools that cannot be used there without an approval step. Check this before the first hire starts, not after.
When you hire through an employer of record, the local employer can help you align your tools and notices with Italian practice. You still need to decide what you monitor and why.
