## How to Onboard an Italian Employee Remotely: A Day-by-Day First-Week Plan
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/onboard-italian-employee-remotely-first-week-plan.html
Summary: A practical day-by-day plan for onboarding a new hire in Italy remotely, from pre-start paperwork to the first Friday check-in.
A remote hire in Italy can feel settled by Friday or lost by Wednesday. The difference is usually preparation. This plan gives you a day-by-day structure for the first week, plus what to finish before Monday.
Before Monday: close the gaps   Most first-week problems start before the first day. Check these items by the Friday before the start date.
The signed employment contract is in the employee’s hands, in Italian, with an English copy if they want one. The mandatory registrations with the Italian authorities are filed. Confirm this with your payroll or Employer of Record (EOR) partner. Do not assume it happened. The applicable national collective agreement (CCNL) is identified. It drives leave, notice, and many pay details. Laptop, accounts, and a password manager invite are ready. The employee has a named buddy and a named manager. Send a short welcome note with the schedule for the week. People relax when they know what comes next.
Monday: arrival and access   Keep Monday light. The goal is that the employee can log in and knows who to ask.
Start with a video call from the manager. Cover the week’s plan, not the company strategy. Confirm that the equipment works and every account opens. Walk through the payroll and benefits basics. Explain how payslips arrive and who to contact with questions. Share the privacy notice and any data protection forms. Italy takes employee data seriously, so handle this on day one. End the day with a short check-in. Ask what was confusing. Tuesday: role and people   Tuesday is about context.
Give a clear picture of the role. Write down what success looks like at the end of the first month. Introduce the team in small video calls, not a single large one. Pair the employee with the buddy for an informal hour. Let them ask basic questions without feeling judged. Share the team calendar, meeting rhythm, and where decisions get made. If your team is mostly in the US, agree on overlap hours today. Italy is many hours ahead of US time zones, so set a window that works for both sides and write it down.
Wednesday: tools and first task   By midweek, the employee should do real work.
Run a hands-on session on your core tools and workflows. Assign a small, finishable first task with a clear owner and deadline. Cover the health and safety basics that apply to the role, including home workstation guidance for remote staff. Your EOR partner can tell you what training is required and how to deliver it. Review the company handbook. Flag where local rules differ from your home-country defaults, such as working time and leave. Thursday: expectations and compliance habits   Thursday is for the conversations that are easy to skip.
Hold a first one-to-one with the manager. Review goals and how feedback will work. Explain how to request leave and report sickness. Italian practice has its own steps, so give written instructions. Cover working hours and how you will respect time off. Be explicit that no one is expected to answer messages late in the evening. Explain expense rules and how reimbursement works. Write these down. A short page in the shared drive beats a long call that nobody remembers.
Friday: review and next steps   Close the week with a feedback loop.
Review the first task together. Praise what worked and be specific about what to change. Ask the employee for honest feedback on the onboarding. What was missing? What was too much? Set goals for the following weeks and book the recurring one-to-ones. Confirm that all signed documents are returned and filed. Send a brief summary of the week to the employee, the buddy, and your HR or finance contact. Common mistakes to avoid   Treating the hire like a contractor. An Italian employee has statutory rights and a defined contract. Do not run onboarding as if it were a freelance engagement. Skipping the local paperwork check. Late or missing registrations create problems that are hard to fix later. Overloading Monday. Too many meetings leave the new hire tired and silent. Forgetting the language. Provide key documents in Italian. Offer English summaries where helpful. No named point of contact. Remote staff need one person who answers fast. Who owns what   Split responsibilities clearly. The manager owns the role and the work. The buddy owns the small questions. HR or your EOR partner owns contracts, registrations, payroll, and compliance. Finance owns the budget and the cost view. When each person knows their part, nothing falls between the cracks.
A strong first week does not need to be complicated. It needs a plan, a calendar, and people who show up. Follow the structure above and your new hire in Italy will know the job, the team, and the rules by Friday.

## How to Pick Job Level and Classification Under an Italian Collective Agreement
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/italy-job-level-classification-collective-agreement.html
Summary: How Italian collective agreements classify roles, how to pick the right level, and why a wrong classification turns into pay claims and disputes later.
When you hire in Italy, you do not set the job level freely. A national collective agreement (CCNL) sets it. Each agreement has its own classification system. Your job is to match the role to the right level. If you get it wrong, the cost shows up later.
This article explains how levels work, how to choose one, and how a wrong choice becomes a dispute.
What a classification system does   Every CCNL groups jobs into levels. Each level has a written description of duties, autonomy, and responsibility. Each level also carries a minimum pay floor and, in many agreements, other rights tied to it. These can include notice periods, leave rules, and allowances.
Above the levels sit the broad categories. Italian law recognizes executives (dirigenti), middle managers (quadri), white-collar employees (impiegati), and blue-collar workers (operai). The collective agreement then splits these into its own levels.
The level is not a title. It is a legal fit between what the person actually does and the description in the agreement.
Step 1: Choose the right agreement   The level only makes sense inside the right CCNL. The agreement usually follows the sector of the employer’s main activity, such as commerce, metalworking, IT services, or chemicals. A US company with a software team may assume one agreement applies. Another may fit the real activity better.
Pick the agreement first. Then pick the level. If the agreement is wrong, every level choice after it is also wrong.
Step 2: Read the level descriptions, not the job title   A “Senior Engineer” in San Francisco may be a different job from a “Senior Engineer” in Milan. The CCNL does not care about the title on the offer letter. It cares about the tasks.
For each role, write down:
The daily tasks. Who the person reports to. Whether they supervise others. How much they decide alone. What training or experience the work requires. Then compare this list against the level descriptions. Pick the level whose description matches the real work. Do not pick the level that matches the salary you want to pay.
Step 3: Test the role against the level above and below   A good check is to read the neighboring levels. Ask whether the person does anything described in the higher level. If they do it regularly, the higher level may apply. Ask whether anything in the lower level fits better. This keeps you from guessing.
Be careful with mixed roles. Many startup roles combine tasks. A person may code, lead a small group, and talk to clients. Italian practice usually looks at the prevailing tasks. If higher-level tasks are a real and continuing part of the job, they matter.
Step 4: Record the choice   Put the level in the employment contract. Keep a short internal note that explains why this level fits. Include the job description and the clause of the agreement you relied on. If the role changes, review the level again.
This note costs little. It can be very useful in front of a labor judge.
How mis-classification becomes a dispute   The common failure is under-classification. A company gives a senior role a low level to keep pay close to the floor. Everything works for a while. Then the employee leaves, or is dismissed, or the relationship turns sour.
At that point the employee can claim that the real duties matched a higher level. If a court agrees, the company may owe the pay difference for the whole period. It may also owe the effects on severance pay (TFR), social contributions, and other items that depend on pay. The claim grows with every month of employment.
Other patterns cause trouble too:
Title inflation. Giving a manager title to a role that does not meet the manager definition. It can create expectations and rights you did not plan for. Role drift. The person was hired for one job and slowly took on bigger duties. The level stayed the same. Copying a US grade. Mapping an internal US band directly to an Italian level without reading the agreement. Wrong agreement. Using a cheaper or more familiar CCNL that does not fit the actual business. These disputes are hard to defend because the standard is factual. The court looks at what the person did. Your contract label does not settle it.
Practical rules   Keep the rules simple.
Choose the agreement by the real activity. Choose the level by real duties. Document the reasoning at hiring. Review the level when duties change. Do not use level as a negotiating tool on pay. If you want to pay more, you can pay above the floor at the correct level. Paying above the minimum is safe. Placing someone at a lower level than their work deserves is not.
Working with local help   A payroll or employment advisor in Italy knows how each agreement is read in practice. An Employer of Record (EOR) can also handle this for you. It helps map the role to the agreement and level, then keeps the file in order. Either way, send a real job description, not just a title.
Getting classification right at the start costs a short conversation. Getting it wrong can cost much more later.

## How to Plan a Work Permit Timeline Around Italy's Annual Quotas
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/work-permit-timeline-italy-annual-quotas.html
Summary: Italy caps non-seasonal work entries each year. Learn how quotas shape hiring plans for non-EU talent and how to build a realistic permit timeline.
If you plan to hire someone from outside the EU in Italy, the calendar matters as much as the candidate. Italy does not issue work entry permits without limit. It sets annual quotas. Your hiring plan has to fit them.
This article explains how the quota system affects timing and how to build a plan that does not stall.
What the quotas are   Italy sets entry quotas through a government decree known as the Decreto Flussi. The current one is the DPCM of 02/10/2025. It covers the 2026-28 period and sets the ceilings year by year.
For 2026, the non-seasonal quota is 43300 entries. It is split like this:
25000 entries for nationals of the countries listed under art. 6, paragraph 2, letter a. 18000 entries for countries that have signed cooperation agreements with Italy. 300 entries for stateless persons and refugees. The figures above come from a secondary source reporting on the decree. Seasonal and out-of-quota categories are not covered here. Check the decree text or ask your advisor before you rely on them.
Why this changes your hiring plan   A quota is a cap. Once the places are used, they are gone for that year. That has three practical effects.
Nationality matters. Most of the 2026 places are tied to the country of the candidate. A candidate from a country on the art. 6 list draws on one pool. A candidate from a country with an agreement draws on another. A candidate from a country in neither group may have no route at all through the quota system.
Role type matters. The quota figures above are for non-seasonal work. If the job is not seasonal, this is the pool that applies. If your role might fall in another category, confirm it before you promise a start date.
Other routes exist. Some profiles enter outside the quota system. Examples include certain highly skilled workers and intra-company transfers. These follow their own rules and their own timing. If your candidate qualifies, you may avoid the quota calendar altogether. Do not assume it. Have the route confirmed first.
Build the plan backwards   Start from the date you need the person working in Italy. Then work back through each step.
Confirm the route. Decide whether the hire falls under the quota or outside it. This decides everything that follows. Confirm the candidate’s country. Check which pool applies and whether it is open to that nationality. Prepare documents early. Contracts, employer details and candidate documents take time to assemble. Do this before the quota window opens, not after. Submit when the window opens. Quota places are limited. Being ready on the first day gives you the best chance. Allow for the consular step. After the Italian authorities approve, the candidate still has to obtain an entry visa abroad. Then comes the arrival formalities in Italy. Add buffer. Each step can run late. Plan the start date with room to spare. Do not set a start date first and hope the permit follows. The permit sets the start date.
Common mistakes   Promising a start date too early. Founders often tell a candidate to resign and be ready in a few weeks. Quota-based entry rarely moves that fast. Give the candidate a realistic range and update it as steps clear.
Treating the quota as a formality. It is not. Places run out. A late or incomplete application can mean waiting for the next year’s allocation.
Hiring first, checking eligibility later. Check nationality and route before you make an offer. An offer you cannot support wastes time on both sides.
Ignoring the multi-year view. The decree covers 2026-28. If you expect to hire more than one person from abroad, plan the whole period. Spread the hires so each one has its own window and its own paperwork.
Where an Employer of Record helps   An Employer of Record (EOR) in Italy can employ the worker on your behalf. It handles the payroll, the contract and the local compliance. It does not change the quota rules. The same limits apply. What an EOR gives you is a local entity that knows the process and can prepare the paperwork before the window opens.
This matters most when you have no Italian entity. Without one, you may not be able to act as the sponsoring employer at all. An EOR can fill that role while you decide whether to set up your own company.
A simple checklist   Is the candidate from a country in one of the quota pools? Is the role non-seasonal? Could another route apply instead of the quota? Are the documents ready before the window opens? Does the start date include time for the visa and arrival steps? Have you told the candidate a range, not a promise? If you can answer all six, your timeline is realistic. If you cannot, fix that before you commit to a date.

## How to Run Month-End Payroll Inputs for an Italian Team
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/month-end-payroll-inputs-italy-manager-guide.html
Summary: What a manager must send to payroll each month for an Italian team: overtime, absences and expenses, how to send them, and when. Plain steps, no jargon.
Payroll in Italy runs on inputs. The payroll team does not guess what happened in your month. It processes what you send. If an input is late or unclear, the payslip is wrong or delayed, and the employee notices.
This guide covers what a manager must send, what each input needs to say, and when to send it.
Why the timing matters   Payroll closes on a fixed calendar. After the cutoff, the data is locked and checked. A change that arrives later does not vanish. It moves to the next cycle as a correction. Corrections cost time, confuse employees and create extra work for finance.
Ask your payroll provider for the cutoff calendar at the start of the year. Put the dates in your team’s shared calendar. Treat the cutoff like a board deadline.
The three inputs   Most months, three things change a payslip: overtime, absences and expenses. Everything else is usually stable. Start with these.
1. Overtime   Overtime in Italy is governed by the law and by the national collective agreement (CCNL) that applies to the employee. The agreement decides what counts as overtime, how it is paid and what limits apply. So you cannot copy your home-country rules.
Send these details for each employee:
The dates worked. The hours worked beyond the normal schedule. Whether the hours fell on a night, a Sunday or a public holiday. Who approved the hours, and when. Get approval before the work, not after. Payroll will ask for it. A short email from the manager is enough if your policy allows it. Do not send a round total with no dates. Payroll cannot apply the right rate to a total.
If the employee prefers time off instead of pay, say so. Some agreements allow it. Payroll needs to know which route you chose.
2. Absences   Absences are the input with the most variety. Each type is treated differently for pay and for social contributions. Common types are:
Paid vacation. Paid leave for permits. Sickness. Maternity and paternity leave. Unpaid leave. Public holidays that fall on working days. For each absence, send the employee name, the type, the first and last day, and any document that supports it. Do not label sickness as vacation to keep things simple. The two have different effects on pay and on state benefits.
Sickness has its own rules. The employee must report it, and a medical certificate is filed through an electronic system. Your role as manager is to tell payroll the days off as soon as you know them. Do not wait for month-end to mention a long illness.
For planned absences, send them as soon as they are approved. Payroll can then track balances all year. At month-end you only confirm.
3. Expenses   Expense reimbursements need clear support, because the tax treatment depends on what the cost was and how it was documented.
For each claim, send:
The employee name. The date and the business purpose. The amount and the currency. The receipt or invoice, readable and complete. Any travel details, such as the destination and the reason for the trip. A receipt alone is not enough. A meal receipt with no purpose may be treated as pay. Ask employees to add a one-line note when they submit. As manager, approve the claim before it reaches payroll. Payroll checks the paperwork. It does not judge whether the spend was needed.
Send all claims for the month together, with one list. Do not send them in pieces across several days.
A simple monthly routine   Use the same rhythm every month. Routine removes most errors.
Near the end of the month: remind your team to submit hours, absences and expense claims. Before the cutoff: review each item. Check dates, approvals and receipts. At the cutoff: send one consolidated file to payroll. Use a shared template, so fields are always in the same place. After processing: read the draft payroll summary if you receive it. Look for anything unexpected, such as a missing overtime payment or a wrong absence. Keep a copy of what you sent. If an employee asks a question about a payslip, you can answer from the record.
Common mistakes   Sending hours without dates. Mixing absence types. Approving overtime after the fact. Sending receipts with no business purpose. Sending changes after the cutoff and expecting them to be in the same payslip. Using several channels, such as chat, email and calls, with no single source of truth. Who owns what   The manager owns the facts: who worked, who was absent and what was spent. Payroll owns the calculation and the filings. Finance owns the budget view. When each side keeps to its role, the cycle is short and quiet.
If you employ people in Italy through an Employer of Record, the provider runs payroll and filings for you. You still send the same three inputs. The provider tells you the cutoff and the format, and you meet them.
Want to see what an Italian hire costs before you start? Try the cost calculator.

## How to Run One-on-Ones With Italian Employees
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/one-on-ones-italian-employees.html
Summary: A practical guide for US managers on one-on-ones in Italy: how to give feedback, set a rhythm, and build trust with Italian team members.
You hired someone in Italy. You want to run one-on-ones the way you do at home. Most of it will carry over. Some of it needs adjusting. This guide covers feedback style, cadence and trust.
Start with relationships, not agenda   US managers often open a one-on-one with the agenda. Status, blockers, next steps. In Italy, that can feel cold, especially early on.
Spend the opening minutes on the person. Ask how things are going. Ask about their week. Do not turn it into a ritual or a script. Listen and respond like you mean it.
This is not wasted time. In many Italian workplaces, trust comes before candor. People share problems with managers they feel they know. If you skip the human part, you get polite updates and little else.
Then move to the work. The shift will feel natural if you have built the opening well.
Feedback style   Direct feedback is common in US teams. “This did not work, here is why” is normal. In Italy, the same words can land harder than you intend, particularly in front of others or in writing.
A few habits help:
Give critical feedback in private, in the one-on-one, never in a group channel. Be specific about the work, not the person. Name the task, the outcome and what you expected. Say what went well in plain terms. Do not use praise as padding before a hit. People notice. Ask for their read before you give yours. “How do you think that went?” often surfaces the problem on its own. Do not soften so much that the message disappears. Italian professionals value clarity too. They want to know where they stand. The goal is not gentler feedback. The goal is feedback that comes with respect and context. Say the hard thing, say it clearly, and say it to the right person in the right setting.
Praise needs care as well. Public recognition can be welcome, but generic cheerleading rings hollow. Name what the person did and why it mattered.
Cadence   Pick a regular rhythm and keep it. Consistency matters more than frequency. A one-on-one that is moved or canceled again and again tells the employee they are low priority.
Some practical points:
Fix the day and time, and protect it. Hold the meeting by video or in person. Avoid turning it into a chat thread. Keep a shared running document. Both sides add topics before the meeting. Notes from the last session stay visible. Time zones are a real issue. If you are in the US and your employee is in Italy, find a slot that does not push them late into their evening. Rotate the burden if your team is spread out. Respect time off. Italians take their leave seriously, and August in particular can be quiet. Plan your rhythm around it instead of pushing against it. If you manage remotely, the one-on-one may be the only time you hear what is really happening. Treat it as the core of the relationship, not an item to clear.
Building trust   Trust grows from small, repeated acts. Do what you said you would do. Follow up on questions. Share context about company decisions, not just instructions.
A few things matter in particular for a US company with an Italian hire:
Explain the why. Italian employees often want to understand the reasoning behind a goal, not just the goal. Give the background. Be clear on expectations. Say what good work looks like. Vague targets cause more friction than blunt ones. Respect boundaries. Evening messages and weekend requests can erode trust fast. Hold to working hours unless something is truly urgent. Ask about development. Ask what they want to learn and where they want to go. Then act on it where you can. Admit mistakes. If you got something wrong, say so. It earns more credit than you expect. Your employee may also be working under an arrangement where an Employer of Record handles local employment administration. That does not change who manages the work. You still own the day-to-day relationship. The one-on-one is yours.
A simple structure   You do not need a complex format. This works:
Open with a human check-in. Let the employee raise their topics first. Cover your own topics, including feedback. Talk about growth, workload and support. Close by confirming actions and who owns them. Write the actions down and share them. Review them at the next meeting.
What to watch for   Silence is not agreement. If your employee says “va bene” and offers nothing else, ask a more open question. “What would make this easier?” works better than “Any concerns?”
Pay attention to what is not said. A drop in energy or shorter answers can signal a problem long before it becomes a resignation.
Adjust over time. Every person is different, and no cultural guide replaces learning how your own employee communicates. Ask them directly how they prefer to receive feedback. Most people will tell you.

## How to Set Up a Productivity Bonus Plan for Your Italian Team
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/productivity-bonus-plan-italy-tax-treatment.html
Summary: Structure goals for an Italian productivity bonus so it can qualify for the 1% substitute tax. Practical steps for US founders, HR and finance teams.
A productivity bonus in Italy can be taxed far more lightly than regular pay. But the favorable treatment depends on how you build the plan. A bonus you decide on at year end, with no clear goals, is just extra salary. This guide shows how to structure goals so the bonus has a real chance of qualifying.
What the tax benefit looks like   Italian rules allow a substitute tax on productivity bonuses. Based on the figures we have, the rate is 1%. It applies to bonuses up to €5,000 per employee. There is also an income limit for the employee. The figure we found is €80,000, and it comes from 2025 data. We could not find confirmation that it stays the same for 2026. Treat it as provisional.
Our source for these numbers is a secondary one, a tax news site. Before you launch a plan, have your Italian payroll provider or labor consultant confirm the current rate, cap and income limit.
Compare this with an ordinary discretionary bonus. That bonus is taxed as normal employment income. The gap in net pay for the employee can be large. The gap in cost for you is smaller, but you still gain a better retention tool for the same budget.
The core idea   The benefit is tied to results, not to goodwill. The bonus must reward a measurable improvement in productivity, profitability, quality or efficiency. The plan must exist before the work is done. The result must be checkable after.
That shapes every step below.
Step 1: Define the goal before the period starts   Write the goal down at the start of the measurement period. Do not set targets after you know the outcome. Retroactive goals are the most common reason a plan fails a review.
Pick a period that fits your business. A calendar year works for many teams. Shorter cycles are fine if your numbers are reliable.
Step 2: Choose indicators you can measure   Use numbers that come from your own systems. Good examples:
Revenue or gross margin per team Output per hour or per project Defect rates or rework rates Customer response time or ticket resolution time Delivery against an agreed schedule Avoid vague goals such as “great attitude” or “strong collaboration.” Those are management judgments. They do not show a productivity gain.
Compare each indicator to a baseline. Record the baseline value at the start. A target of “improve” is not a target. A target of “move from the baseline to a stated level” is.
Step 3: Set the payout rule in advance   State how the bonus is calculated. Link the amount to the result. For example, define a threshold below which nothing is paid, a target level, and a maximum.
Keep the maximum for each employee within the €5,000 cap if you want the whole amount to benefit. Any part above the cap would be taxed in the ordinary way.
Do not mix this bonus with fixed payments. A bonus that is paid every year in the same amount, no matter the result, looks like salary.
Step 4: Put the plan in writing and get it agreed   The plan should be a formal document. It should name the indicators, the period, the baseline, the targets and the payout formula. In Italy, the way this document is agreed and filed matters for the tax treatment. This is where local advice is not optional. Ask your Italian adviser which agreement format applies to your company and what must be filed.
Share the plan with the team. People work toward goals they understand.
Step 5: Measure and keep the evidence   At the end of the period, calculate the results from your source data. Keep the reports. Keep the calculation. Keep the signed plan. If the tax authority asks questions, this file is your answer.
Pay the bonus only if the targets are met, and only in the amount the formula gives. Do not round up to be kind. A discretionary top-up breaks the link between result and reward.
Step 6: Check the employee’s income   The benefit has an income limit. Check each employee against it before payroll runs. Your payroll provider can do this. Employees above the limit receive the bonus under ordinary taxation.
Common mistakes   Setting goals after the period ends Using subjective criteria Paying the same amount every year regardless of results Skipping the written agreement Assuming last year’s rate and limits still apply What to do next   Draft your indicators and targets first. Then bring the draft to your Italian adviser with this checklist: current rate, current cap, current income limit, and the required agreement format. Build the budget from those confirmed numbers.

## How to Write a Job Post That Attracts Italian Candidates
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/job-post-italian-candidates.html
Summary: Write job posts that work in Italy: which language to use, how to frame salary and benefits, and which channels reach Italian candidates.
You can post the same job in New York and Milan. You will not get the same response. Italian candidates read job posts differently, look for different signals, and use different channels. A few changes to your post will help.
Write the post in Italian, or in both languages   Many Italian professionals read English well. Most still search for jobs in Italian. If your post is English only, you lose people who filter by Italian keywords. You also signal that the role is for a remote contractor, not a real local hire.
The best approach is a full Italian version with an English version below it. Do not machine translate and publish. A stiff translation reads as careless. Have a native speaker check it.
Use the Italian job title people actually search for. Some titles stay in English, such as Product Manager or Software Engineer. Others do not translate well. Check how Italian companies title the same role and copy that.
If the working language of the team is English, say so. Name the language level you expect. “Fluent English required” is clear. “Excellent communication skills” is not.
Be clear about the employer and the contract   Italian candidates want to know who employs them. A post from a foreign company with no Italian entity raises questions. Will they be on a proper payroll? Will they have the usual protections? Will they be paid on time?
Say it plainly. State that the role is a permanent employment contract under Italian rules, if it is. If you hire through an Employer of Record, say that the person will be employed in Italy and will work day to day with your team. This removes the main doubt.
Also state the collective agreement that applies, if you know it. Candidates in Italy expect this level of detail, and it shows you understand the market.
Frame salary the way Italians think about it   Most Italians talk about pay as gross annual salary. The common term is RAL, which stands for Retribuzione Annuale Lorda. Use it. State a gross annual figure or range in euros.
Do not quote a monthly net figure. Do not convert from a dollar number without checking it. A candidate who sees a dollar salary will convert it and compare it with local offers. If the number looks off, they will leave.
Explain how the annual figure is paid. In Italy, many contracts spread the annual amount over more monthly payments than twelve. If your structure differs, say so. Confusion here is a common reason offers fall apart late in the process.
Include a salary range. Posts without any pay information get fewer applications. Candidates assume the figure is low or negotiable in your favor. A range also saves time for both sides.
Mention the severance accrual (TFR) only if it matters to your pitch. It is standard, so it is not a selling point. The more useful message is that the package is complete and legal.
Show benefits that matter locally   US benefit lists do not always translate. Health insurance, for example, is less of a draw because public healthcare exists. A supplementary plan can still help, but do not lead with it.
What Italian candidates often care about:
Flexible or hybrid work, and clear rules on it Meal vouchers or welfare budgets Training and a clear growth path Stable contract terms Working hours that respect personal time Describe the rules, not the slogans. “Hybrid, with office days agreed by the team” is better than “flexible culture.”
Keep the tone plain   Italian professionals are wary of hype. Avoid phrases such as “rockstar,” “ninja,” or “fast-paced family.” They read as empty. Describe the work, the team, the tools, and the goals. Say who the person reports to.
Keep requirements honest. A long list of must-haves discourages good applicants. Separate what is required from what is useful.
Tell candidates what the process looks like. List the stages. Say how long you take to reply. Italian candidates often have a notice period to serve, so say early if you need a fast start.
Choose channels that perform   LinkedIn is the main channel for professional roles in Italy. Post there, and write the post in Italian. Ask your Italian team members or advisers to share it.
General job boards also work, especially for roles outside tech. Pick the ones Italian candidates already use, and avoid ones that only exist in your home market.
For junior and mid-level roles, university career services are worth the effort. Many schools run their own boards and events.
For technical roles, go where the community is. Local meetups, online groups, and open source circles are strong sources. A direct message from an engineer on your team often does more than any ad.
Referrals matter a lot. Italian professional networks are tight. If you have even one person in Italy, ask for introductions.
A short checklist   Italian text first, English second Local job title Clear employer and contract type Gross annual salary range in euros Specific benefits and work rules Plain tone, honest requirements Posted on LinkedIn plus one or two targeted channels Get these right and you will see better applicants and fewer drop-offs at the offer stage.

## INAIL in 2026: What Changes for Employers Hiring in Italy
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/inail-workplace-injury-insurance-2026-employers.html
Summary: INAIL premium rates stay on the 2019 tariffs, but the 2026 rules for premium reductions changed. See what US employers hiring in Italy should check.
If you hire in Italy, you pay for workplace injury insurance through INAIL. The 2026 changes do not touch the base rates. They change how employers can lower the premium they pay. This article covers what is confirmed, what is not, and what to check.
The base rates have not changed   The tariffs from 2019 are still in force. No new tariff table replaced them in 2026. If you budgeted INAIL costs on the current rates, that part of your model stays valid.
The change is in how the rules are applied. A ministerial measure dated April 2, 2026 changed the application rules. It was published on June 3, 2026. So the new rules are recent, and most employers have not yet seen them in a full premium cycle.
What is new: the premium reduction   INAIL can reduce an employer’s premium when its injury record is better than average. This is called the oscillation in reduction. The 2026 measure changes how it works in two ways.
1. A new Table A Bonus   There is now a new table called Table A Bonus. It uses two inputs:
The number of worker-years, shown as N in the table. The ISAR indicator. In plain terms, the size of your workforce and your injury indicator now feed into the same table. Your reduction depends on both.
2. A higher fixed reduction for small positions   Some insurance positions (PAT in Italian) are classed as not significant. For these, the fixed reduction is now 13%. It used to be 5%.
In practice, a company with a very small Italian headcount may now get a larger fixed reduction than before. The step from 5% to 13% is the most concrete number in this update.
What this means for a US company with a first Italian hire   Most foreign companies start with one or a few employees in Italy. That is the profile this change seems built for. Three points follow.
Do not assume the old discount. If your cost model uses the old 5% fixed reduction, it is out of date for positions classed as not significant.
Do not assume you qualify. We could not confirm from our sources how a position is classed as not significant. We also could not confirm how the new table sets its thresholds. Check these points before you put a saving into a budget.
Do not remove INAIL from your cost model. The reduction lowers a premium. It does not replace it. The base rates are the 2019 tariffs, and the reduction applies on top of them.
What we have not confirmed   Our information on the 2026 changes comes from a secondary source, not from the text of the measure itself. That limits what we can say. We have not confirmed:
The exact rules for the Table A Bonus. How ISAR is calculated. When each employer will see the new reduction on a premium notice. Read this article as a signal of what to ask, not as a final answer on your own premium.
What to check now   Your INAIL position. Find out whether your Italian position is treated as not significant under the new rules. Your cost model. Replace the 5% fixed reduction with the 13% figure only where it applies. Your payroll provider. Ask who files the INAIL declaration and how they will apply the new reduction. Your timeline. The measure was published on June 3, 2026. Ask when the new rules will first affect your premium. Why it matters for budgeting   Injury insurance is a small line next to salary and social contributions, but it is a recurring cost. A change in the discount moves your yearly figure. For a small team, a larger fixed reduction can be a real saving.
The safe approach is to model both cases. Use the lower figure as your base budget. Treat the higher reduction as an upside until your premium notice confirms it.
Bottom line   The 2019 tariffs are still the base. The 2026 change is in the reduction rules. There is a new Table A Bonus based on worker-years and ISAR. The fixed reduction for positions classed as not significant is now 13%, up from 5%. Confirm how your own position is classed before you count on it.

## Income Tax in Italy vs the US: Comparing the Layers in a Job Offer
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/income-tax-us-vs-italy-layered-comparison.html
Summary: US federal and state income tax versus Italian national IRPEF and municipal surcharges. How to compare the layers when you price an offer for a hire in Italy.
A US offer is usually quoted as a gross salary. The tax on it comes in layers. Italy works the same way, but the layers sit in different places. If you compare the two without lining them up, the numbers will mislead you.
This article gives you a simple frame. It does not give you a final net figure. That depends on the person and the city.
The US layers   A US employee pays federal income tax first. Most also pay state income tax on top. Some states charge none, others charge a lot. Some cities add their own tax as well.
So a US comparison starts with one question: which state, and which city. The same gross salary can produce very different net pay across the US.
The Italian layers   Italy also stacks taxes. The main one is the national personal income tax, called IRPEF. On top of it, the municipality where the employee lives charges a local surcharge.
The difference is where the choice sits. In the US, the state is the big variable. In Italy, the national schedule is the same for everyone. The city only adjusts the top layer.
IRPEF: three brackets   IRPEF is progressive. Each slice of income is taxed at its own rate.
Annual income slice Rate Up to EUR 28,000 23% EUR 28,000 to EUR 50,000 33% Above EUR 50,000 43% The rate applies only to the slice inside each bracket. Income above EUR 50,000 is taxed at 43% only for the part over that line. The first EUR 28,000 still pays 23%.
This matters for offers. A raise does not reprice the whole salary. It adds a slice at the marginal rate of the bracket where the salary lands.
The municipal surcharge   The municipal surcharge differs by city. Two examples show how much.
City Rate Exemption threshold Milan 0.8% EUR 23,000 Roma 0.9% EUR 14,000 Both cities use a single flat rate. Both have an exemption threshold below which the surcharge is not due. Rome charges a slightly higher rate. It also starts charging at a much lower income.
For a mid-level or senior hire, the gap between the two cities is small next to IRPEF. It is still a real line in the comparison, and it is easy to get right. Ask where the employee will live. Then check that city’s rate and threshold.
How to compare an offer   Use the same steps for both countries.
Fix the gross salary in the currency you are comparing. Apply the national layer. In the US, that is federal tax. In Italy, it is the three IRPEF brackets. Apply the local layers. In the US, that is state tax and any city tax. In Italy, it is the municipal surcharge for the employee’s city. Compare the marginal rate, not only the average. The marginal rate tells you what a raise or a bonus is worth after tax. A few cautions help.
Do not compare a US state with no income tax to Italy and stop there. The employer side and the social contributions also differ. They are outside this article. Italy has other surcharges besides the municipal one. They are outside this article too. Confirm them before you finalize a number. The figures above are from secondary sources. Check them against the official source before you put a number in a contract. What this means for your offer   For US founders, the main shift is this. Your candidate in Italy thinks in net pay after a progressive national schedule. The city adds a small flat layer. The result is clear once you separate the layers.
For finance and legal ops teams, keep the layers as separate lines in your model. One line for the national tax. One line for the municipal surcharge. This makes it easy to update a single rate without rebuilding the sheet.
For HR, show candidates the same breakdown. A gross figure with no layers invites doubt. A clear table builds trust.

## Interviewing Italian Candidates: Structure and Etiquette That Build Trust
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/interviewing-italian-candidates-structure-etiquette.html
Summary: How US teams can run interviews with Italian candidates: what to expect, how to structure each stage, and the small courtesies that build trust early.
Hiring in Italy starts with an interview that feels different from the US version. The format is not hard. But a few cultural habits change how candidates read you. Get them right and you earn trust before any offer is made.
Expect a more relational process   Italian candidates often judge the employer as much as you judge them. They want to know who they will work for, how the team treats people, and whether the company will still be around in a few years. A foreign company with no local presence raises extra questions. Answer them before they are asked.
Open the call with a real introduction. Say who you are, what the company does, and why you are hiring in Italy. Explain how the hire will be employed and paid. A short, clear note about your employment setup removes a lot of worry.
Greet properly and start formal   Use the candidate’s surname and a title at the start, unless they invite first names. Many Italians use a formal register with strangers. If your candidate switches to first names, follow them.
A few small points help:
Send the agenda and the names of the interviewers ahead of time. Start on time and say hello to everyone on the call. Allow a little general conversation before the questions begin. Skipping small talk can read as cold. You do not need long chats. A few friendly lines are enough.
Structure the conversation   A clear shape helps both sides, especially when the interview is in a second language.
Introduction. Present the company and the role. Let the candidate see the whole picture before they speak.
Background. Ask the candidate to walk through their career. Italian candidates often give context about their studies and earlier employers. Let them. Education and path matter in Italy, and it is part of how they show who they are.
Role-specific questions. Ask for concrete examples of past work. Follow up on details. Avoid trick questions and brainteasers. They tend to damage trust.
Their questions. Leave real room for them. Expect questions about team, growth, working hours, and stability.
Next steps. Say what happens after the call and when they will hear from you. Then keep that promise.
Language and tone   If the role needs English, test it in the interview, but be kind about it. Speak slowly, avoid idioms, and repeat key points in plain words. Many strong candidates are less fluent in a fast-paced call than in daily work.
In Italy, modesty and directness can sit side by side. Some candidates will not oversell themselves. Others will speak at length about the team and not about their own wins. Ask follow-up questions like “What was your part in that?” to get the detail you need.
Use video well   Most first interviews run on video. Keep your camera on, test your audio, and pick a quiet space. Be ready to switch to a phone call if the connection fails, and do not make the candidate feel at fault.
For senior roles, an in-person or in-office meeting can be a strong signal of commitment. If you cannot travel, bring a local contact or a senior leader on the call. Seeing a real person from the company helps.
Involve the right people   Candidates like to meet their future manager. Do not let the process sit only with HR or a recruiter. A founder or hiring manager on the call shows the role matters.
Keep the number of rounds reasonable. A long, unclear process makes people think the company is disorganized. Tell candidates the full process at the start.
Talk about pay and terms openly   Be ready to discuss compensation clearly. Italian candidates think in terms of gross annual pay, and often also in terms of extras such as additional monthly payments, benefits, and time off. Do not leave them to guess. If you work with an Employer of Record (EOR), explain that it handles payroll and compliance locally, so the candidate knows who issues the contract and the payslip.
Avoid pressure tactics. Exploding offers and vague promises hurt your reputation fast. Italian professional circles are small, and people talk.
Follow up with care   Send a short thank-you message after the call. Give feedback if you reject someone, even briefly. A polite, honest no is remembered, and rejected candidates often refer others to you later.
If you make an offer, put it in writing, explain each element, and give time to decide. Candidates may want to talk it over with family or a trusted adviser. That is normal.
What to remember   Be punctual, prepared, and warm. Explain your setup in Italy. Respect formality at the start. Give clear structure, honest answers, and a fair timeline. These habits cost nothing, and they separate employers people want to join from those they doubt.

## IP Assignment and Confidentiality for Italian Employees: Protecting Your Code
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/ip-assignment-confidentiality-italian-employees.html
Summary: How US companies protect code and inventions made by an Italian hire: what the law gives you by default, what to put in writing, and where contracts fall short.
US founders often assume Italy works like Delaware. You sign an invention assignment agreement on day zero and the company owns everything. In Italy the default rules are different. Some of them favor the employer. Some do not. You need to know which is which before your first engineer starts.
What the law gives you by default   Italian law does not leave employee work unowned. It sorts it into categories.
Service inventions. If the employee was hired to invent or research, and the pay reflects that, the employer owns the invention. The employee has no right to extra pay beyond salary. The employee keeps the right to be named as the inventor. That right cannot be waived.
Employee inventions made in the course of the job. If the employee invents something in the field of the employer’s business, but was not hired specifically to invent, the employer owns the invention. The employee is entitled to a fair payment for it, on top of salary. The amount depends on the value of the invention and what the employee contributed.
Occasional inventions. If the employee invents something that falls in the employer’s field but has no link to the role, the employee owns it. The employer has a right of first option to license or buy it, against a fair royalty. Other parties can be blocked while that option runs.
The lines between these categories are blurry. A backend engineer who builds a novel method at home on a weekend, using the company’s domain knowledge, can create a real dispute. Do not leave that to chance.
Software is treated differently   Software is mostly a copyright matter, not a patent matter. Italian copyright law gives the employer the economic rights in software created by an employee while performing duties or following the employer’s instructions. That is a strong default for code written as part of the job.
Two limits matter for a foreign company.
Moral rights, such as authorship attribution, stay with the individual. The default covers work done in the course of duties. Side projects, open source contributions and code written on personal time need clear contract language. Patents on software-related inventions follow the invention rules above. Treat the two tracks separately in your paperwork.
What to put in the employment contract   A US-style assignment agreement pasted into an Italian contract will not do the job. Use a clause drafted for Italian law, written in Italian, and signed as part of the employment agreement or a signed annex. A clear structure helps.
Define the role. State that the inventive and creative activity is part of the job description, and that the salary compensates it. This puts the work in the service invention category. Be honest here. If the role is sales, do not claim it is research. Assign economic rights. State that all economic rights in software, documentation, designs and databases created in the course of the job belong to the employer, worldwide and for the full legal term. Cover the gray zone. Say that work using company time, equipment, data or confidential information counts as company work, even if done outside hours. Require disclosure. Make the employee report inventions promptly and in writing. This starts the clock on your rights and gives you a record. List prior work. Ask the employee to list what they already own and bring to the job. This avoids later claims that your product contains their earlier code. Address inventor remuneration. For inventions outside the pure service category, decide how you will pay and say so clearly. A fixed premium or bonus structure agreed in advance reduces the risk of a later claim. Confidentiality   Every Italian employee already owes a duty of loyalty. That includes not using or disclosing business information in ways that hurt the employer. This duty exists without a contract and continues in some form after the job ends. It is not enough on its own.
Add a written confidentiality clause that does these things.
Defines confidential information in concrete terms: source code, architecture, customer lists, pricing, roadmaps. Applies during employment and after it ends, with no end date for trade secrets. Requires return or deletion of materials on exit. Sets rules for personal devices and personal cloud accounts. Italian law also protects trade secrets, but only if you take reasonable steps to keep them secret. Access controls, need-to-know permissions, and a written policy count as those steps. A confidentiality clause with no real internal controls is weak evidence in court.
Non-competes and post-exit protection   Italian law allows non-compete covenants, but with limits. They must be in writing, tied to a defined scope of activity, limited in time and geography, and paired with real payment to the employee. A vague or unpaid non-compete is unenforceable. If you want one, price it into your cost model from the start. Often a strong confidentiality clause plus good access hygiene gives more protection per euro.
Practical points for foreign employers   Who is the employer? If you use an Employer of Record, the EOR is the legal employer. The IP clauses must route rights to your company. Check that the EOR contract includes a clear assignment or license chain from the EOR to you. Without it, you may use code you do not formally own.
Contractors are a different case. Freelancers do not fall under the employee rules. Rights stay with the author unless transferred in writing. Never assume a contractor’s code is yours.
Keep records. Commit history, signed disclosures and dated approvals are your best evidence if a dispute arises.
Use local counsel. Have an Italian lawyer review the clause text. Small wording choices decide which category an invention falls into, and that decides who pays whom.
The short version   Italy gives employers real default rights over code and inventions made in the job. But the rules depend on the role, and the employee always keeps some rights and may be owed extra pay. Put the role description, the assignment, the disclosure duty and the confidentiality terms in writing, in Italian, under Italian law. Then back them with real internal controls.

## Italian CCNL explained: why every job maps to a collective agreement
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/italy-ccnl-collective-agreements-explained.html
Summary: Every job in Italy falls under a national collective agreement (CCNL). Learn what it sets, why it matters, and how it shapes your hiring terms.
If you hire in Italy, you will meet the term CCNL early. It stands for Contratto Collettivo Nazionale di Lavoro, or national collective labor agreement. It is the document that sets the baseline terms for most employees in a given sector.
US teams often expect to write an employment contract from a blank page. In Italy, that is not how it works. The collective agreement already covers many of the terms. Your individual contract sits on top of it.
What a CCNL is   A CCNL is negotiated between employer associations and trade unions for a specific sector. Commerce, manufacturing, tech services, logistics, hospitality and many others each have their own.
The agreement is not a law passed by parliament. It is a negotiated text. Yet in practice it acts as the reference standard for pay and conditions in that sector.
What it sets   The CCNL covers the core of the employment relationship. Typical topics include:
Job classification and levels Minimum pay for each level Working hours and overtime rules Paid leave and public holidays Notice periods when someone resigns or is dismissed Probation rules Sick leave and how it is supplemented Additional pay items, such as extra monthly payments, where the agreement provides them Training and union rights These are the items US employers usually decide for themselves. In Italy, much of that decision is already made.
Why every job maps to one   Think of the CCNL as a lookup. You start with the real work the person will do and the sector your business operates in. From that, you identify the agreement that applies. Then you place the role at a level inside it.
The level matters because it drives the minimum pay and many related terms. A junior analyst and a senior manager can sit under the same agreement. They will sit at different levels, with different minimums.
So the question is never whether a CCNL applies. The question is which one fits, and at what level the role belongs. Every employee ends up with an answer to both.
Why it sets the baseline   The CCNL is a floor, not a ceiling. You can offer more than the agreement requires. You cannot offer less on the points it covers.
This has practical effects:
Salary. Your offer must be at or above the minimum for the level. Many employers pay above it to attract talent. Cost. Leave, extra payments and notice rules all add to the real cost of an employee. The headline salary is only part of the picture. Termination. Notice terms come from the agreement. Planning an exit means reading it first. Disputes. If an employee challenges their treatment, the CCNL is usually the first document checked. A contract that ignores the right agreement creates risk. The employee can claim the difference, and the gap can build over time.
Choosing the right agreement   The choice is not based on your preference or on the cheapest option. It follows the sector of the business and the nature of the activity. A software company and a retail chain will not land on the same agreement, even if both hire an accountant.
There can also be more than one plausible agreement for a business. Some sectors have competing agreements signed by different organizations. Picking between them needs care. Check which one matches your activity, and confirm the terms before you issue an offer.
An error here is easy to make and slow to notice. It tends to appear later, in a payroll audit or a dispute.
What this means for your hiring plan   For founders, HR, finance and legal ops teams, a few habits help:
Map the role first. Decide the sector, the agreement and the level before you set the salary. Read the agreement. Do not rely on a summary from a different country’s practice. Budget the full cost. Include leave, extra payments and employer contributions, not just base pay. Put it in writing. Your offer letter and contract should name the CCNL and the level. Recheck when roles change. A promotion can change the level and the minimums that go with it. Why this helps you   The system can feel rigid at first. But it also gives you a clear starting point. Terms are known, comparable and public. You do not have to invent a leave policy or a notice period. You can plan against a fixed baseline, then decide where to offer more.
Once you know which CCNL applies, most of the structure of the hire follows from it.

## Italian Employment Contract Checklist: What to Include Before a Hire Signs
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/italian-employment-contract-checklist.html
Summary: A plain checklist of the mandatory and recommended clauses in an Italian employment contract, for US founders, HR, finance and legal ops teams.
An Italian employment contract is not a blank page. The national collective agreement (CCNL) for your sector sets many terms before you write a word. Your contract has to sit on top of it. This checklist covers what must be in the contract and what you should add.
Start with the collective agreement   Pick the right CCNL first. It sets minimum pay levels, job grades, working hours, leave, notice periods and often extra pay such as a thirteenth month. Many US teams skip this step and draft from a US template. That is the most common mistake.
Name the CCNL in the contract. Name the grade and level too. If the contract and the CCNL conflict, the more favorable term for the employee usually wins.
Mandatory content   Italian law requires the employer to give the employee written information about the main terms of the job. Put all of the following in the contract itself so nothing depends on a separate notice.
Parties. Full legal details of the employer and the employee. Place of work. The office address, or a clear statement that work is remote or mobile. Start date. And whether the contract is permanent or fixed-term. If fixed-term, state the end date and the reason where the rules require one. Job title, grade and duties. Use the CCNL grade. The grade drives pay, and it is hard to change later without consent. Probation period. If you want one, it must be in writing before work starts. Its length is capped by the CCNL and by law. Pay. Gross base salary, how often it is paid, and every pay element: allowances, bonuses, extra monthly payments. Working hours. Full-time or part-time, the weekly schedule, and rules on overtime. Paid leave. Annual holiday and other leave as set by law and the CCNL. Notice. The notice period for both sides, as set by the CCNL. Collective agreement. The CCNL that applies, as noted above. Social security and insurance. The institutions that receive contributions, and the severance fund arrangement (TFR). A contract that is not in writing, or that leaves these items out, invites disputes and possible penalties. Do not rely on a verbal offer.
Recommended clauses   These are not always required. They protect both sides and avoid arguments later.
Confidentiality. Define what is confidential and that the duty continues after the job ends.
Intellectual property. State that work product belongs to the employer. For inventions, Italian rules give the employee certain rights, so have a local lawyer check the wording.
Exclusivity. If you need the employee to work only for you, say so. Without a clause, moonlighting rules are limited.
Non-compete. Italian non-competes are enforceable only if they meet strict conditions. They need a defined scope, a time limit, a geographic limit and separate payment. A copy-paste US clause will not hold.
Remote work. Set out where the employee may work, what equipment you provide, and how you reach them. Cover data security and working hours.
Company equipment. Laptop, phone and software: who owns them, how they may be used, and when they are returned.
Data protection. Include the privacy notice for employee data. Italy applies EU data rules, and monitoring staff is tightly restricted.
Company policies. Reference the code of conduct, IT policy and disciplinary code. Employees should receive them and confirm receipt.
Expenses and travel. Say what you reimburse and how to claim.
Language and format   Write the contract in Italian. Add an English version for your own team if it helps. State which version prevails. If the employee does not read Italian well, a bilingual contract reduces the risk of a later claim that they did not understand it.
What not to copy from the US   At-will language. It does not exist in Italy. Dismissal needs a valid reason and a set procedure. Broad termination clauses. You cannot contract out of the dismissal rules. Unpaid bonus promises. Anything you pay regularly can become part of fixed pay. Be exact about what is discretionary. Vague titles. A loose title can lead to a claim for a higher grade. Before signing   Run a short final check.
Does the contract name the correct CCNL, grade and level? Are probation, notice and pay stated exactly as the CCNL allows? Is every pay element written down? Are the non-compete and IP clauses reviewed by an Italian lawyer? Has the employee received the privacy notice and company policies? Is the contract registered with the authorities as required before the start date? If you do not have an Italian entity, an Employer of Record can issue the contract under its own entity. It then handles registration, payroll and contributions. You still direct the daily work. The contract checklist above applies either way.

## Italy's Employer Calendar: Key Filings by Quarter
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/italy-employer-calendar-key-filings-by-quarter.html
Summary: A quarter-by-quarter view of the annual filings Italian employers must plan for, including the CU certificates and the Modello 770, with dates.
If you hire in Italy, your obligations do not stop at payroll. Some filings come once a year, and they cluster at predictable points. This guide groups the annual ones by quarter so finance and HR can plan around them.
The dates below come from a secondary source that tracks the 2026 deadlines. Treat them as a planning baseline. Confirm each one with your payroll provider before you commit resources.
What this calendar covers   This article covers two annual items: the Certificazione Unica (CU) and the Modello 770. The CU is the annual certificate of income paid and tax withheld. The Modello 770 is the annual withholding tax return that the employer files.
It does not cover every recurring duty. Periodic payments and other routine tasks also exist. Your payroll provider should keep a full list for your setup.
First quarter: CU for employees   The first big date is March 16. By then the CU for employees must be delivered to the workers. The same date applies to sending the CU data to the Italian tax authority (Agenzia delle Entrate).
In practice, one date drives two tasks:
Give each employee their CU. Transmit the CU data to the tax authority. The CU depends on clean payroll data for the whole prior year. Corrections made late in the process are harder. Review your year-end payroll records well before March 16.
Second quarter: CU for self-employed workers   The next date is April 30. It applies to CU filings for self-employed workers, not employees.
This matters if you work with freelancers or other independent contractors in Italy. Many foreign companies track only their employees and miss this one. If you engage independent professionals, add April 30 to your calendar and make sure someone owns it.
Third quarter: no annual date in this calendar   The verified dates for this guide do not include any in the third quarter. Use this window as working time.
Good uses of it:
Check your payroll data against your contracts. Confirm who is responsible for each upcoming filing. Agree on a timeline with your payroll provider for the year-end close. A quiet quarter is the right time to fix process gaps. Do not leave that work for the final stretch of the year.
Fourth quarter: CU for exempt income and the Modello 770   The year closes with two items.
First, October 31 is the deadline for CU filings covering exempt income. This is a narrower category, but it has its own date. Check with your provider whether it applies to you.
Second, the Modello 770 is due on October 31 as well. In 2026 that date falls on a Saturday. The deadline therefore moves to the next working day, November 2. Plan for the earlier date internally. Treat November 2 as a buffer, not a target.
A simple way to use this calendar   Put each date in a shared calendar, not in one person’s inbox. Name an owner for each filing, with a backup. Set internal deadlines ahead of the official ones. Keep year-end payroll data reconciled so the CU and the Modello 770 draw on the same numbers. The filings are linked. The CU you issue in the first quarter feeds the data you rely on in the fourth. Errors in one tend to show up in the other.
If you do not have an Italian entity   Many foreign companies hire in Italy without setting up a local company. In that case, these filings still exist. The question is who handles them. An employer of record (EOR) takes on the employer’s local filings, so you do not have to track them yourself. Whichever route you choose, you should know the calendar and ask who is responsible for each date.

## Italy's Employment Tax Credits in 2026: Why Net Pay Rises Faster on Lower Salaries
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/italy-employment-tax-credits-2026-net-pay-lower-salaries.html
Summary: How Italy's employee tax credit and payroll wedge relief work, and why lower salaries see net pay grow faster than higher ones. A guide for US teams.
If you hire in Italy, you will see something that surprises many US finance teams. Net pay does not move in a straight line with gross pay. At lower salaries, each extra euro of gross turns into more net than you might expect. At higher salaries, it turns into less.
The reason is a set of tax credits and relief measures built into Italian personal income tax, called IRPEF. This article explains how they work, in plain terms.
The base: three tax brackets   IRPEF is progressive. The rates are:
23% on income up to EUR 28,000 33% on income from EUR 28,000 to EUR 50,000 43% on income above EUR 50,000 On their own, these brackets would give a steady rise in tax as pay grows. But three other mechanisms change the picture for employees.
1. The employee tax credit   Every employee gets a tax credit that reduces the tax owed. Its size depends on annual income. It is largest at low income and shrinks as income grows.
Here is how it works:
Up to EUR 15,000 of income, the credit is EUR 1,955. There is a floor of EUR 690. For fixed-term contracts, the figure is EUR 1,380. From EUR 15,000 to EUR 28,000, the credit is EUR 1,910 plus a variable part. The variable part is EUR 1,190 multiplied by (28,000 minus income), divided by 13,000. The higher the income, the smaller this part. From EUR 28,000 to EUR 50,000, the credit is EUR 1,910 multiplied by (50,000 minus income), divided by 22,000. It falls steadily toward zero. Above EUR 50,000, the credit is zero. For incomes between EUR 25,000 and EUR 35,000, there is an extra EUR 65. Now think about what this does. A raise in the 28,000 to 50,000 range is taxed at 33%. It also shrinks the credit. So the employee loses twice: more tax on the raise, and a smaller credit. The effective burden on that slice of income is higher than the headline rate suggests.
At low income the credit is large and stable, so a raise is mostly taxed at 23% and little else.
2. The payroll wedge relief: income that is not taxed   Italy also applies a relief aimed at the gap between gross pay and net pay. For lower earners, a share of employment income is simply not taxable. The share depends on the income band:
Up to EUR 8,500 of income: 7.1% From EUR 8,500 to EUR 15,000: 5.3% From EUR 15,000 to EUR 20,000: 4.8% This is a direct boost to take-home pay. It applies to employment income and it is strongest at the bottom of the scale.
3. The additional credit for middle incomes   A further tax credit of EUR 1,000 applies for incomes between EUR 20,000 and EUR 32,000. Between EUR 32,000 and EUR 40,000, it declines gradually to zero.
This matters for hiring plans. Many mid-level roles sit in this range. Net pay for these roles is supported up to EUR 32,000, then the support fades.
Why net pay rises faster at lower salaries   Put the three pieces together.
At the low end, the 23% rate is the only bracket in play. The employee tax credit is at or near its maximum. The untaxed share of income is at its highest percentage. Each extra euro of gross is cushioned on all fronts. In the middle, the 33% bracket starts at EUR 28,000. At the same time, the employee credit starts to shrink and the additional EUR 1,000 credit fades out between EUR 32,000 and EUR 40,000. The net gain from each extra euro of gross drops. At the top, above EUR 50,000, the 43% rate applies and the employee credit is zero. There is no relief left to offset the rate. The result is a net pay curve that is steep at lower salaries and flatter at higher ones. A given gross raise produces a larger net improvement for a junior employee than for a senior one.
What this means for you   For US founders and finance teams, three practical points follow.
Do not scale net pay linearly. If you know the net figure for one salary, you cannot extrapolate it to another. Each salary needs its own calculation. Offers near the thresholds need care. The points around EUR 28,000, EUR 32,000 and EUR 50,000 are where relief changes fastest. A small difference in gross can mean a larger difference in net than you expect, or a smaller one. Fixed-term contracts are treated differently. The employee credit floor for fixed-term roles is EUR 1,380, against EUR 690 for others at the lowest incomes. Contract type can affect net pay. The figures here come from a secondary source. Before you sign off on an offer, confirm the numbers with your payroll provider.
Summary   Italian tax is progressive, and the relief for employees is front-loaded. The employee credit, the untaxed share of income and the additional credit all favor lower salaries. Together they explain why net pay grows faster at the bottom of the scale than at the top.

## Italy's payroll calendar: the dates US finance teams need
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/italy-payroll-calendar-dates-us-finance-teams.html
Summary: Key Italian payroll dates for US finance teams in 2026: the employee tax certificate in March and the Modello 770 filing moved to November 2.
US finance teams plan around a familiar year-end rhythm. Italy has its own. The names are different and some deadlines fall at other times. If you hire in Italy, you need to know which dates matter and what each one asks of you.
This article covers the 2026 dates we have confirmed from a published source. It also tells you which date we have not confirmed, so you do not plan around a guess.
A note on how we checked these dates   Both dates below come from a secondary source, an Italian tax news site. We have not yet matched them against an official notice. Treat them as a strong guide, not as final. Before you commit to a close calendar, ask your payroll provider or Italian accountant to confirm each one.
March 16, 2026: employee tax certificates   The first date is March 16, 2026. This is the deadline for the Certificazione Unica for employees, known as the CU.
The CU is the annual statement of what an employee earned and what was withheld during the year. A US team can think of it as the Italian counterpart to the year-end wage and tax statement you give US staff. Each employee receives one. The tax authority receives the data as well.
What this means for your team:
Payroll data for the prior year must be final well before the deadline. Any corrections to pay, benefits or withholding need to be settled early. The people who prepare the CU need clean records from you. If your Italian hires are on payroll through a local provider, the provider usually prepares the CU. Your job is to make sure the inputs are right and to ask for confirmation that the certificates went out on time.
November 2, 2026: the Modello 770   The second date is the Modello 770. The nominal deadline is October 31, 2026. That day is a Saturday, so the filing moves to November 2, 2026.
The Modello 770 is an annual return filed by the party that withholds tax. It reports the withholding taxes applied during the year. In practice it ties back to the same payroll records behind the CU. If those records do not agree, you will find out at this stage.
Two points for finance teams:
The shift from a Saturday to the next working day is a standard rule for Italian deadlines. Do not assume it applies in every case, and confirm with your accountant. The 770 should match what you reported on the CU. Reconcile the two before filing. One date we cannot confirm: the workplace insurance settlement   Italy’s workplace injury insurer, INAIL, runs an annual settlement of premiums. A date for it circulates online for 2026. We could not verify it against any source. For that reason we are not printing it here.
Do not put an unconfirmed date in your close calendar. Ask your provider for the exact date. Then add it yourself once you have it in writing.
How to use this in your calendar   A simple approach works well.
Add the CU date and the Modello 770 date to your finance calendar now. Set internal reminders ahead of each date, so data review is not left to the last day. Assign one owner on your side who talks to the Italian payroll provider. Ask the provider to confirm every date in writing, including the insurance settlement. Keep a record of what was filed and when. Why the calendar matters for a US team   Most US founders and finance leads are used to a single payroll system and a few federal and state dates. Italy adds its own certificates, its own returns and its own rules about what happens when a deadline falls on a weekend. None of this is hard once it is on a calendar. The risk comes from learning about a date after it has passed.
The two confirmed dates give you a base. March 16, 2026 sits early in the year. November 2, 2026 sits near the end. Add the confirmed insurance date once you have it, and you have the core of an Italian payroll calendar.
