## Part-Time Contracts in Italy: Hours, Scheduling and Changes
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/part-time-contracts-italy-hours-scheduling-changes.html
Summary: What an Italian part-time contract must state about hours and schedule, and how employers can change them later without creating legal risk.
Part-time work is common in Italy. It is also one of the easier contract types to get wrong. The reason is simple: the contract has to say much more about working time than a US offer letter does. And once it is signed, you cannot adjust the schedule on your own.
This guide covers what the contract must specify and how to change hours later.
Put it in writing   A part-time contract should be in writing. Do not rely on an email thread or a verbal agreement about “roughly half days.” The written contract is the document an inspector, a court or the employee will look at if there is a dispute.
If the working time is missing or vague, you invite problems. The employee can ask a court to fix the hours. The court may also treat the missing detail as a defect in the part-time arrangement. That can change the economics of the hire.
What the contract must specify   The contract needs to describe the working time clearly. At a minimum, plan to state:
The reduced hours, compared with full-time hours under the applicable national collective agreement (CCNL). How those hours are spread across the day, the week, the month or the year. The specific days and times when the employee works, or a clear rule for setting them. The rules for extra hours, if you want the option to ask for them. Whether any clause allows you to move the schedule, and under what conditions. The point of the distribution requirement is predictability. An employee with a part-time contract often has another job, family duties or studies. They need to know when they are expected to work.
Three common structures   Italian practice usually describes part-time in three forms.
Horizontal. The employee works fewer hours each working day. For example, mornings only, every weekday.
Vertical. The employee works full days, but only on some days of the week, month or year. For example, three full days each week.
Mixed. A combination of both. Some days are full, others are shorter.
Pick the structure that matches the real need and write it down. Do not leave this to a later conversation.
The CCNL matters   The national collective agreement for your sector fills in many details. It may set limits on extra hours, rules for schedule changes, minimum notice and the pay for additional work. Two companies hiring the same role under different agreements can end up with different rules.
Before you draft anything, confirm which CCNL applies to the role. Then check what it says about part-time. Your contract should follow it, not repeat generic wording.
Extra hours   Sometimes you need more time from a part-time employee without changing the contract. Italian rules distinguish between additional hours within the full-time limit and overtime beyond it. The details depend on the CCNL and the contract.
Three practical points apply:
Say in the contract whether you may ask for extra hours. Check whether the employee’s consent is needed each time. Pay extra hours at the rate the CCNL requires, and record them in payroll. Do not treat unrecorded extra hours as a favor. Unpaid work is a common source of claims.
Changing the schedule later   This is where US teams are most often surprised. In the US, a manager can usually change a shift with a message. In Italy, the schedule in a part-time contract is part of the agreement. Changing it needs a legal basis.
There are generally three routes.
Agreement with the employee. The simplest path. Both sides agree to the new schedule and sign a written amendment. Keep a copy in the personnel file.
A flexibility clause in the contract. Some contracts include a clause that lets the employer move the time slot of the work, or extend its duration, within set limits. Such a clause has to be written clearly, and the CCNL may require specific safeguards. These usually include advance notice and some form of compensation for the employee. Without a valid clause, you cannot rely on this route.
Statutory or contractual rights of the employee. Certain employees have rights tied to their personal situation. These can include requests to move between full-time and part-time, or to change hours for health or family reasons. If an employee makes such a request, do not ignore it. Check the CCNL and get advice before you answer.
Moving between full-time and part-time   A change in the number of hours is a change to the contract. Treat it as a formal amendment. Put the new hours, the new distribution and the start date in writing, and have both parties sign.
If you want to cut hours because business is slow, you generally cannot impose it. You need the employee’s agreement or another valid basis. Proposing a reduction and a pay cut unilaterally is likely to be challenged.
Payroll and benefits follow the hours   Pay for a part-time employee is proportional to the hours worked. Many benefits and contract terms also scale with the working time, though the exact treatment depends on the CCNL. Every change in hours therefore has a payroll effect. Notify your payroll provider before the change takes effect, not after.
A short checklist   Confirm the applicable CCNL. Choose horizontal, vertical or mixed. State the hours and their distribution in the contract. Decide whether you need extra hours and write the rule. Add a flexibility clause only if it meets the CCNL conditions. Document every later change in a signed amendment. Tell payroll about each change in advance. The practical takeaway   In Italy, the schedule is part of the deal. Specify it carefully at the start, and treat every later change as a contract matter, not a scheduling matter. That keeps both the employee and the company on solid ground.

## Performance Reviews for Italian Employees: A Fair Process
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/performance-reviews-italian-employees-fair-process.html
Summary: How to run performance reviews in Italy: clear criteria, written records, employee response and links to the CCNL. A practical framework for US teams.
US performance reviews often rest on manager judgment, a rating and a quick conversation. In Italy that approach can create problems. Employees expect a clear process. Records matter if a dispute ever arises. This guide gives a framework that fits both.
Why Italy is different   Italian employment is built on written rules and documented fairness. Dismissal needs a justified reason, and poor performance is hard to prove after the fact. A vague review file will not help you. A clean record of expectations, feedback and support will.
The national collective agreement (CCNL) that applies to your employee also matters. It can set job levels, duties and disciplinary steps. Your review process should respect it, not sit beside it.
Employees also tend to expect a direct and honest conversation, with reasons given. A rating with no explanation feels arbitrary and reduces trust.
Start with the job, not the score   A fair review needs a fixed reference point. Before any review:
Check the employment contract and the job level under the CCNL. Write down the duties and goals for the period. Make sure the employee has seen and acknowledged them. If you rate someone against goals they never received, the review has no weight. Goals should be specific and within the person’s control. They should also match the role the contract describes. Assigning duties far outside the contracted level can create its own legal risk.
A review cycle that works   Set expectations in writing   At the start of the period, send the goals by email or through your HR system. Ask the employee to confirm receipt. Keep this confirmation.
Hold regular check-ins   Short, frequent conversations beat one annual surprise. After each, send a brief written summary. Two sentences are enough: what was discussed, what was agreed. This builds a trail that shows steady feedback and real support.
Run the formal review   Use the same template for everyone in similar roles. Cover:
Results against the agreed goals. Specific examples, not general impressions. Strengths and gaps. Support or training offered. Goals for the next period. Share the draft before the meeting if you can. Italian employees often value time to prepare.
Let the employee respond   Give space for comments in the form itself. Ask the employee to add their view in writing and to sign that they received the document. A signature should confirm receipt, not agreement. Say that clearly.
Keep the file   Store the signed review, the goals and the check-in notes together. Limit access to people who need it. Employee data is covered by European privacy rules, so keep only what you need and be able to explain why.
Keep reviews separate from discipline   A review is a development tool. A disciplinary process is a formal procedure with its own rules. In Italy the disciplinary route usually requires a written notice of the issue, a chance for the employee to respond and a reasoned decision. The CCNL often adds details.
Do not use a review meeting to deliver a sanction. Do not call a conversation a review and then treat it as a warning. If performance problems are serious, speak with local counsel or your employer of record before you act. The order of steps matters.
Be careful with tools and data   Many US teams use dashboards, activity trackers and automated scoring. In Italy, tools that can monitor employees raise rules on consent, union agreement and privacy. Using output metrics that come from normal work is safer than tracking behavior. Before you roll out any measurement system, check that it is allowed and that employees have been properly informed.
Avoid common mistakes   Surprise ratings. If the employee hears the problem for the first time at the review, the process failed. Forced ranking. Comparing people against each other fits poorly with an Italian framework of fixed duties and fair treatment. Bias and unequal treatment. Keep criteria objective. Be careful with comments linked to age, sex, family status, health or other protected traits. Linking pay to unclear ratings. If a review affects pay or bonus, explain how. Check what the contract and CCNL already guarantee. Missing records. If it is not written down, it is hard to prove later. A short checklist   Goals are written and acknowledged. Criteria match the contract and CCNL level. Check-ins are summarized in writing. The review uses a standard template. The employee can respond in writing. Records are stored securely. Discipline follows its own separate process. Final point   A fair review in Italy is a documented, two-way conversation tied to the real job. Done well, it supports development and protects the company. Done poorly, it gives you a record that does not help when you need it most.

## Permanent vs Fixed-Term Contracts in Italy: Choosing the Right One
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/permanent-vs-fixed-term-contracts-italy.html
Summary: A decision guide for US employers hiring in Italy: when a fixed-term contract fits, when a permanent one wins, and how each affects cost and retention.
US employers often arrive in Italy with an at-will mindset. You hire, you adjust, you let people go if the plan changes. Italy does not work that way. The contract type you choose shapes your risk, your cost and your ability to keep good people.
This guide helps you pick between a permanent and a fixed-term contract. It does not replace advice on your specific case. It gives you a way to think about the choice.
The starting point: permanent is the norm   In Italy, the open-ended contract is the default. The law treats it as the standard form of employment. Fixed-term work is the exception, and it comes with rules.
That matters because many US teams assume a fixed-term contract is a simple way to stay flexible. It is not as simple as it looks.
What fixed-term really gives you   A fixed-term contract has an end date. When it ends, the relationship ends, and you do not need to justify a dismissal.
That is the real benefit. You avoid the process and the exposure that come with ending a permanent contract.
But the flexibility has limits:
There is a cap on total duration. Renewals are restricted. Beyond an initial period, you generally need a documented reason for using a fixed term. If you break the rules, the contract can be converted into a permanent one. Employees on fixed terms keep the same core rights as permanent staff. They are not a cheaper tier. The last point surprises many founders. You cannot offer a fixed-term hire fewer protections just because the contract is short.
Check the current limits with your advisor before you rely on them. Thresholds and conditions change, and the details matter.
What permanent gives you   A permanent contract has no end date. It ends by resignation, by mutual agreement, or by dismissal that meets legal grounds.
Dismissal in Italy needs a justified reason. You cannot end a permanent contract simply because the business case weakened or you want a different profile. There are procedures to follow and notice to give. The more senior the role and the longer the tenure, the more it can cost to exit.
In exchange, you get stability. The employee knows the role is secure. That shapes how they behave. They invest in the job, take ownership and plan their life around it.
The retention question   This is where the decision often turns.
In a tight market, strong candidates compare offers. A fixed-term offer signals that you are not sure about them. Senior engineers, finance leads and sales people with options will often decline it. Even if they accept, they keep looking.
For Italian workers, a permanent contract is also tied to practical things like mortgages and rentals. Banks and landlords read the contract type. A fixed-term hire may feel they cannot commit to a major purchase.
If retention is your priority, permanent is the safer signal.
A simple decision guide   Ask yourself these questions.
Is the work truly temporary? A defined project, a seasonal peak, or a cover for someone on leave fits a fixed term well. If the need will continue, a fixed term is usually the wrong tool.
Are you testing the market? If you are entering Italy and do not yet know whether the business will hold, a fixed term can limit your exposure. But think about whether you are testing the market or just avoiding a commitment you will need to make anyway.
How senior is the hire? For leadership and hard-to-replace skills, a fixed term damages the offer. For junior or support roles with a clear scope, it is less of a problem.
How long do you need them? If the answer is longer than the rules allow for a fixed term, you will end up with a permanent contract by default. Plan for that from the start.
Can you absorb an exit later? If a permanent hire does not work out, you will need a justified process or a negotiated exit. Budget for that possibility, not only for the salary.
Common mistakes   Chaining short contracts. Renewing again and again to avoid commitment is the fastest way to trigger conversion and a dispute.
Using fixed term to avoid probation decisions. Permanent contracts can include a probation period. If your concern is whether the person is a fit, that tool exists and is often better.
Ignoring the collective agreement. The national collective agreement for your sector sets terms that apply on top of the law. It can affect notice, pay and how fixed terms are handled. Always check it.
Treating cost as the only factor. A fixed-term contract does not make the person cheaper in a meaningful way. Social contributions and statutory rights still apply. The saving is in exit risk, not in monthly cost.
A practical way to decide   Start with the business need. If the work has a clear end, use a fixed term and document the reason. If the work is ongoing, use a permanent contract and manage risk through a probation period and clear performance expectations.
When in doubt, lean permanent for roles that matter and fixed term for work that is truly bounded.
If you hire through an Employer of Record (EOR), the EOR is the legal employer and handles the contract, payroll and compliance. You still decide the structure of the role, so the same logic applies. A good EOR will tell you early if a fixed-term plan does not hold up.

## Probation Periods in Italian Employment Contracts: How They Differ From At-Will
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/probation-period-italy-vs-us-at-will.html
Summary: How the trial period works in Italy, what it requires in writing, and why it is not a substitute for US-style at-will termination.
US founders often ask the same question when they plan a hire in Italy. Can we just use a trial period and let the person go if it does not work out? The short answer is that the trial period helps, but it is not at-will employment. Here is how it works and where the gap is.
What a probation period is in Italy   A probation period (periodo di prova) is an early phase of an open-ended employment contract. During it, both sides can test the fit. The employee sees the job and the company. The employer sees whether the person can do the work.
The employee is a full employee from day one. Pay, social contributions, leave accrual and health and safety rules all apply. Probation does not create a lighter category of worker.
It must be agreed in writing   This is the rule that catches foreign employers most often. Probation exists only if the written contract says so, and it must be signed before the employee starts work. If the clause is missing, or added after the start date, the probation is generally treated as void. The employee is then covered by the full dismissal protections from the start.
The clause should also describe the duties that will be tested. A vague clause that names no tasks is open to challenge. If the role changes after hiring, the clause may not cover the new duties.
How long it can last   The length is not free. National law sets an outer limit, and the applicable collective agreement (CCNL) usually sets the working limit for each job level. Senior roles tend to get longer periods than junior ones. The contract cannot go beyond what the collective agreement allows.
Check the CCNL that applies to your sector before you draft the clause. The same job title can carry a different maximum under a different agreement.
Ending the contract during probation   This is where probation looks closest to at-will. During the trial, either side can generally end the contract without the notice period that would apply later. The employer does not need to prove just cause or a justified reason in the usual way.
That said, it is not a blank check. A few limits matter in practice:
The employer cannot end the contract for a discriminatory reason or in retaliation. The trial must be real. If the employee was never given a fair chance to perform the tasks named in the contract, a court may find the termination unjustified. Protected situations, such as pregnancy or illness, can limit the employer’s freedom to terminate. The employee must actually be allowed to do the work. Leaving someone idle and then ending the trial invites a dispute. In most cases, a clear and documented termination within the probation window is low risk. The risk rises when the reason looks unrelated to performance.
What happens when probation ends   If neither side ends the contract by the last day of the trial, the employment confirms automatically. Time spent in probation counts toward length of service. From that point, the full Italian dismissal framework applies. Ending the relationship now needs a lawful reason, a proper procedure and, in many cases, notice. This is the real difference from the US.
In the US, at-will is the default for the whole relationship. In Italy, flexibility is front-loaded. It sits in the probation window and then mostly disappears.
How it differs from US expectations   Three points deserve attention from HR, finance and legal ops teams.
The default is reversed. In the US, you need a reason to restrict termination, such as a contract. In Italy, you need a reason to terminate, except in the probation window.
Paperwork decides the outcome. A missing signature or a late clause can erase the protection you thought you had. Treat the contract as a compliance document, not a formality.
Probation is a decision point, not a formality. Teams should schedule a real review before the window closes. Waiting until the last days leaves little room to act, and silence confirms the hire.
Practical steps for a foreign employer   Identify the CCNL that applies to the role before you draft. Put the probation clause in the signed contract before day one of work. List the duties that the trial will cover. Give the employee real work and real feedback during the period. Hold a documented review well before the end date. Decide in time, because the contract confirms by default. If you hire through an Employer of Record (EOR), the EOR is the legal employer and handles the contract, the clause and the CCNL choice. You still manage the work and the evaluation. The decision on the trial is a joint one in practice, so agree on the review timeline at the start.
The bottom line   Probation in Italy gives you a window of real flexibility, but only if you set it up correctly and use it on time. After the window closes, you are no longer in at-will territory. Plan the hire with that in mind.

## Productivity Bonuses in Italy: The 1% Flat Tax Explained
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/productivity-bonuses-italy-1-percent-flat-tax.html
Summary: Italy taxes qualifying productivity bonuses at a 1% substitute tax, up to a 5,000 EUR cap. Here is what US employers should know before they budget.
If you hire in Italy, you will hear about the productivity bonus. It is one of the few pay tools where the tax treatment is clearly better than a normal salary increase. This article explains the basics in plain terms.
What the 1% rate is   Italy lets employers pay certain performance-linked bonuses under a substitute tax. Substitute tax means the bonus is not added to the employee’s regular taxable income and taxed at the normal progressive rates. Instead, a flat rate applies.
The rate in the verified source is 1%. That is very low compared with the marginal income tax rates most employees face on ordinary pay.
The Italian name for this kind of bonus is premio di risultato. You will see that term in payroll documents and in union agreements.
The cap   The flat rate does not apply to an unlimited amount. The cap is 5,000 EUR per employee. The 1% rate covers the bonus up to that amount.
The source does not say how the tax works on any amount above the cap. Do not assume. Ask your payroll provider how the excess is treated before you design a bonus plan.
The income limit   The benefit is also tied to the employee’s earnings. The figure reported for 2025 is an income limit of 80,000 EUR.
We could not find confirmation that the same limit applies in 2026. Treat the 80,000 EUR figure as the last confirmed value. Check it again before you commit to a plan for the current year.
This matters for senior hires. A US startup that brings in an experienced engineer or finance lead may find that person sits above the limit. In that case the flat rate may not be available to them.
Why it matters for a US employer   US teams are used to discretionary cash bonuses. In Italy, the tax treatment changes the math.
A bonus that qualifies is worth more to the employee after tax than the same amount paid as ordinary salary. That makes it a useful retention tool. It also lets you reward results without raising the fixed monthly cost.
The employee sees more of each euro. You can offer a competitive package without pushing base pay up.
What to check before you promise a bonus   Do not copy a US bonus letter into an Italian contract. A bonus only gets this treatment if it meets the conditions of the regime. A vague promise to pay something at your discretion is a weak starting point.
Before you commit, confirm these points with your payroll provider:
Does the planned bonus qualify for the substitute tax? Is the employee under the income limit? How are amounts above the cap taxed? Is the limit for the current year the same as the last confirmed one? This article covers the income tax side only. Social contributions are a separate question. Ask about them explicitly so your cost model is complete.
Planning the budget   Build the bonus into your cost model from the start. Model two cases for each hire: the bonus qualifies, and the bonus does not qualify. The gap between them can be large for the employee and meaningful for your own budget.
Keep the facts dated. The 80,000 EUR limit is a 2025 figure with no 2026 confirmation found. Write that into your assumptions, so nobody treats it as settled later.
Bottom line   Italy offers a 1% substitute tax on qualifying productivity bonuses, up to 5,000 EUR. An income limit of 80,000 EUR was reported for 2025, and we have not found confirmation for 2026. Used well, the regime helps you reward performance at a low tax cost. Used carelessly, it leaves you with a promise the tax rules do not support.

## Recognition and Retention in Italy: Keeping Employees Engaged Beyond Salary
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/recognition-retention-italy-non-salary-levers-bonus-structures.html
Summary: How US employers keep Italian staff engaged: non-salary retention levers, plus how to structure results-based bonuses with a reduced flat tax rate.
US founders often assume retention is a pay question. In Italy it is rarely only that. Salary scales are shaped by national collective agreements, so you have less room to win people with a bigger base number. The levers that work are different. Most of them cost little, and some cost nothing.
What Italian employees tend to value   Stability matters. Predictability matters. People want to know their role, their manager and their schedule will not change on short notice. A US-style culture of constant reorganization reads as a warning sign.
Respect for time off matters too. Italian employees expect real rest and a clear line between work hours and personal hours. Messages at night and on weekends erode trust fast. If your team sits in a US time zone, set rules for meeting hours early and keep to them.
Non-salary levers that work   Clear growth paths. Say what the next role looks like and what it takes to get there. Vague promises of future promotion do not hold people. A written path does.
Flexibility with structure. Many Italian professionals value flexible hours and remote days. Offer them as a stated policy, not as a favor granted case by case. A policy feels fair. A favor feels fragile.
Training and certification. Pay for courses, language classes and professional qualifications. This signals investment in the person, and it builds skills you need.
Welfare benefits. In Italy, employers can provide benefits such as meal vouchers, supplementary health cover, transport support and family services. Employees often prefer these to a small raise, because they feel tangible and can be tax-efficient. Your payroll provider or EOR can tell you which benefits fit your contracts and your collective agreement.
Recognition that is specific. Generic praise lands flat. Name the work, name the result, and say it in public when the person is comfortable with that. Italian teams often value direct, personal acknowledgment from a senior leader more than a company-wide email.
A manager who is present. Many exits trace back to the direct manager. Regular one-to-one conversations, honest feedback and visible support do more than most perks.
Bonus structures: keep them tied to results   A bonus works best when it is linked to a measurable result. Think of team output, revenue targets, quality indicators or project delivery. Fixed, discretionary bonuses with no stated logic tend to become expected, and then resented when they stop.
Italy offers a tax advantage for this kind of structure. Results-based bonuses can qualify for a substitute tax of 1% instead of ordinary income tax rates. The cap on the bonus amount that benefits from this rate is 5,000 EUR. The income limit for eligible employees is 80,000 EUR. That figure is from 2025. We could not find confirmation for 2026, so check the current threshold before you build your plan.
This makes the bonus more valuable to the employee than the same gross amount paid as ordinary pay. For you, the cost stays the same. The employee keeps more of it.
A few practical points:
Define the targets in writing before the period starts. Choose indicators the team can influence. Measure and communicate results on a fixed schedule. Confirm with your payroll provider that your plan meets the conditions for the reduced rate, since the rules for eligibility are specific. The figures above come from a secondary source. Treat them as a starting point and verify them before you commit to a plan.
Combine the pieces   No single lever carries retention alone. A workable package looks like this:
A base salary that meets the collective agreement and sits at a fair market level. A results-based bonus with clear targets. Welfare benefits that employees actually use. A written growth path and a training budget. Respect for working hours and time off. A manager who gives regular, specific feedback. None of this requires a large budget. It requires consistency. Italian employees notice whether the promises made at hiring still hold a year later.
Common mistakes   Treating Italy like the US market is the most frequent one. Equity-heavy offers, at-will thinking and aggressive performance cycles do not translate well. Another mistake is skipping the local context. Collective agreements set rules on pay, benefits and working time, and your plan must fit inside them.
A third mistake is waiting until someone resigns. By then the decision is made. Ask early what people value, and adjust the package while it still matters.
Build the package, test the numbers and see what each hire really costs. Try the cost calculator.

## Relocating a US Employee to Milan: From Decision to First Payslip
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/relocate-us-employee-to-milan-first-payslip.html
Summary: Follow a US hire from the decision to move to Milan through to the first Italian payslip, including the Milan local income tax surcharge.
A US software company decides to send a senior engineer to Milan. The engineer, call her Dana, wants to stay on the same team. The company has no Italian entity. Finance asks a fair question: what happens between the decision and the first payslip?
This is the path, step by step.
The decision   The team agrees on the role, the start date and the pay. At this stage, most founders think about salary and housing. The better question is who will be the employer in Italy.
Dana will live and work in Milan. Italian rules apply to her employment from the day she starts working there. That means an Italian contract, Italian payroll and Italian social security registration. A US payroll run will not cover it.
There are two ways to handle this. You can set up a local company, or you can use an Employer of Record (EOR). A local company means incorporation, a bank account, a payroll provider and a legal representative. An EOR hires Dana in Italy on your behalf, while you direct her daily work. For a single relocation, the EOR route is usually faster and cheaper to run.
The paperwork before she lands   Dana is a US citizen, so she needs the right to live and work in Italy before she starts. This is the longest and least predictable part. Do not book flights until the permit path is clear.
In parallel, the employer side prepares:
The employment contract under the applicable national collective agreement. Registration with the Italian social security institutions. Payroll setup, including the tax withholding that Italy requires from the employer. Dana also needs an Italian tax code. She will need it for almost everything: the bank account, the lease, the phone contract.
Arrival and start date   Once the permit is in place, Dana arrives and signs her documents. The EOR confirms her start. From this day, payroll runs monthly in Italy.
Help with housing and registration at the local registry office makes the first weeks easier. Dana is more productive when the basics are handled. Plan for this support. It is part of the relocation, not an extra.
Reading the first Milan payslip   The first payslip surprises many US managers. In the US, you see gross pay, a few taxes and net pay. An Italian payslip lists many lines. Some are paid by Dana, and some are paid by the employer on top of her gross salary.
One line is specific to where she lives: the municipal income tax surcharge, called the addizionale comunale. Each city sets its own. Milan applies a single rate of 0.8%. According to the source we checked, it also has an exemption threshold of EUR 23,000.
In practice:
The surcharge is calculated on taxable income, not on the whole cost of employing her. Below the EUR 23,000 threshold, the surcharge does not apply. Dana’s senior salary will likely be above that threshold, so expect to see the line on her payslip. The rate is small next to the other deductions, but it is a real line item. Dana should know it is coming. One caution. The figures above come from a secondary source, not from the city itself. Municipalities can change their rules. Ask your payroll team to confirm the rate and how the threshold is applied before you quote net pay to Dana. Do not promise her a net figure based on a general estimate.
The surcharge is also not always collected in a simple monthly amount. Italian payroll often spreads local surcharges across the year and settles them at year end. Your payroll provider can show you how it appears in the first months. Dana should not read an early payslip as the final picture.
What to tell Dana before the first payday   A short briefing prevents most questions:
Gross and net pay will differ more than she is used to. Her payslip will include national and local taxes, including the Milan surcharge. The employer pays additional contributions that she will not see as deductions. Net pay can change slightly during the year as withholding adjusts. Share a sample payslip with her early. It removes anxiety and builds trust with the new employer setup.
What to tell finance   Finance cares about total cost, not net pay. The cost of Dana is her gross salary plus employer contributions, plus the EOR fee, plus relocation support. The Milan surcharge is paid out of her income, so it does not add to your cost directly. It does affect what she takes home, and that affects how she judges the offer.
Build the model from gross salary upward. Then check net pay with Italian payroll before you finalize the offer letter.
The short version   Decide on the employing structure first. Clear the permit path before booking travel. Set up Italian payroll before the start date. Explain the payslip, including the Milan surcharge, before the first payday. Verify local rates with your payroll team and not with a blog post, including this one.
Do this in order and the first Milan payslip will hold no surprises.

## Relocation Checklist for Employees Moving to Italy
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/relocation-checklist-employees-moving-to-italy.html
Summary: A practical checklist for employees moving to Italy: housing, tax code, bank account, healthcare registration and schools, in the order that works.
Moving an employee to Italy goes well when the steps happen in the right order. Many of them depend on each other. A bank wants a tax code. Healthcare registration wants proof of residence. Residence wants an address. If one step slips, the rest stall.
This checklist covers the five areas that matter most: housing, tax code, bank, healthcare and schools. Use it as a working plan for the employee and for your HR and finance teams.
1. Housing   Housing comes first because almost everything else needs an address.
Start with a short-term stay. Book temporary housing for the first weeks. This gives the employee time to see neighborhoods before signing a long lease. Expect a formal lease. Italian rental contracts follow set rules. The employee should get a written, registered contract. Ask the landlord or agent to confirm the registration. Check what is included. Utilities, building fees and furnishings vary a lot. Ask in writing what the rent covers. Keep the paperwork. The lease is the main proof of address for the steps below. Keep a copy ready. If the employee is bringing family, factor in space and school location before choosing the area.
2. Tax code (codice fiscale)   The codice fiscale is the personal tax identification number. Nearly every formal act in Italy needs it: opening a bank account, signing a lease, activating utilities, registering for healthcare, and being set up on payroll.
Get it early. Some people can request it before arrival through an Italian consulate. Others get it from the tax authority after landing. Check which route applies to the employee’s situation. Bring valid ID. A passport is the base document. Visa or permit documents may also be needed. Do it for family too. Spouses and children need their own codice fiscale for healthcare and school. Send it to payroll. Your payroll provider needs the number to run the first salary correctly. This is the step that unlocks the rest. Make it the first task after arrival, or before it if possible.
3. Bank account   An Italian account makes daily life easier. Salary, rent and utilities usually run through it.
Bring the standard documents. Expect to show a passport, the codice fiscale, proof of address and often the employment contract or permit. Compare account types. Traditional banks and online banks both operate in Italy. Online banks can be faster to open. Branch banks may handle in-person needs better. Ask about the language. Not every branch works in English. Check before the appointment, and bring a translator if needed. Plan for a gap. Opening an account can take time. Make sure the employee has a way to pay for rent and living costs in the meantime, such as a foreign card or a relocation advance. Finance teams should confirm the account details early so the first payroll run is not delayed.
4. Healthcare registration   Italy has a national health service. Registering gives access to a family doctor and public care.
Register with the local health authority. This is usually done at the local office covering the employee’s address. Residence status and permit type decide the route and the cost. Choose a family doctor. After registration, the employee picks a general practitioner. This doctor is the entry point for referrals and prescriptions. Keep the health card. The card is used for visits, tests and pharmacies. Consider private cover. Many employees add private insurance for faster access to specialists or English-speaking doctors. Check what your benefits plan offers. Until registration is complete, the employee needs a bridge. Travel or private insurance can fill that gap.
5. Schools   Families with children need to plan schooling as early as housing.
Choose the type of school. Options include public schools, private schools and international schools. Each has different language, curriculum and cost. Check the enrollment process. Public school enrollment follows a national procedure and calendar. Arriving mid-year can limit choices. International schools set their own rules and may have waiting lists. Prepare records. Bring school reports and ID. Some documents may need translation or official recognition. Think about language. A child who does not speak Italian will need support. Ask each school how it helps new students. Link school to housing. Public school placement often depends on where the family lives. Settle the address first. The order that works   Secure temporary housing, then a lease. Obtain the codice fiscale for every family member. Register residence at the local municipality. Open the bank account. Register with the health service and choose a doctor. Enroll children in school. Residence registration at the municipality sits between the lease and healthcare. Do not skip it. It confirms the employee lives at the address and feeds into other registrations.
What employers can do   You do not need to run every step yourself. You do need to know who owns each one. Assign a clear owner for housing, documents, payroll data and family needs. Give the employee a written list with the order above. Check progress at set points, so small delays do not turn into missed payroll or gaps in coverage.
A clear plan reduces stress for the employee and reduces risk for your company.

## Retirement Age in Italy and What It Means for Long-Term Hires
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/italy-retirement-age-long-term-hires.html
Summary: Italy's retirement age rises in 2027 and 2028. See the old-age and early-retirement thresholds and how they affect workforce planning for your Italian hires.
If you hire in Italy, you hire for the long run. Italian employment is built around stable, open-ended contracts. So the age at which your employee can retire matters for your planning, even if that date is decades away.
This article covers the retirement thresholds reported for 2026, 2027 and 2028. It explains how they affect succession, retention and budgeting.
Old-age pension: age and contributions   The standard route is the old-age pension. It has two conditions: a minimum age and a minimum contribution history.
The requirements reported for the coming years are:
Year Minimum age Minimum contributions 2026 67 years 20 years 2027 67 years and 1 month 20 years 2028 67 years and 3 months 20 years The contribution minimum stays flat. The age moves up. Your employees will not all retire at the same age, and the date depends on the year they reach the threshold.
Early retirement: contributions only   Italy also has an early pension. It is based on contribution history alone, with no age condition. The thresholds differ for men and women.
Year Men Women 2026 42 years and 10 months 41 years and 10 months 2027 42 years and 11 months 41 years and 11 months 2028 43 years and 1 month 42 years and 1 month The requirement rises each year. Anyone planning to leave early needs a longer contribution record than the year before.
What this means for your workforce plan   Plan for later exits   The age thresholds are going up. A person who started work in their twenties can reach the early route in their sixties. The old-age route needs them to stay past their mid-sixties. Do not assume a fixed exit age when you build a long-term headcount plan. Model a range instead.
The gap between the two routes   An employee with a very long contribution record can leave before the old-age age. One with a shorter record will stay until the age requirement is met. Two people of the same age in the same role can have very different exit dates. Ask about contribution history early in the relationship when it affects your plans. Your payroll provider or advisor can help you read it correctly.
Succession and knowledge transfer   Rising thresholds mean senior people stay longer. That helps with continuity. It can also slow promotion paths for younger staff. If you run a small Italian team, the same senior hire may stay in the role through most of a decade. Make sure you have a clear development path for the people below them.
Retention for senior hires   Senior hires near the early-retirement threshold have a real choice to make. They can leave once they meet the contribution requirement, or stay. Roles that offer flexibility, meaningful work and fair pay are easier to keep filled. Roles that feel like a countdown are not. Talk with senior staff about their plans before the date arrives, not after.
Budgeting   A longer working life means a longer payroll commitment. Salary, social contributions and benefits continue for each additional month. When you model the total cost of a hire over many years, use the thresholds above and revisit them each year. They are updated on a regular schedule, and the figures here are for 2026 to 2028 only.
A note on sources   The figures above come from a press review of the new requirements for 2027 and 2028. They are secondary reporting. Check them against official guidance before you make a binding decision, and again each year when the next set of thresholds is published.
Practical checklist   Do not assume one retirement age for all Italian employees. Separate the old-age route from the early route in your planning. Ask your advisor to check each senior employee’s contribution record. Review the thresholds every year. Build succession plans before senior staff become eligible. ## Salary Negotiation with Italian Candidates: What to Expect
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/salary-negotiation-italian-candidates-what-to-expect.html
Summary: How salary talks with Italian candidates usually go, why net pay drives the conversation, and what Italians value beyond the number on the offer.
Salary talks in Italy follow patterns that can surprise US hiring teams. Candidates often think in net pay. They care about stability and time as much as cash. And the first number you hear is rarely the last.
This article covers what to expect and how to prepare.
Candidates think in net, not gross   In the US, people usually compare gross salary. Italian candidates tend to ask what lands in their bank account each month. Your offer letter will state gross annual pay, but the conversation will drift to net quickly.
This matters because Italian income tax is progressive. IRPEF, the national personal income tax, applies these rates to annual taxable income:
23% up to EUR 28,000 33% from EUR 28,000 to EUR 50,000 43% above EUR 50,000 These are marginal rates. Each rate applies only to the slice of income inside its bracket. Employee social contributions and local taxes come on top, so the full picture is more complex than the table.
The practical effect is simple. A raise that pushes a candidate into a higher bracket feels smaller than they expect. A candidate near the EUR 50,000 line will notice that extra gross pay is taxed at 43% on the part above it. Be ready to explain this, and ready to talk about benefits that do not hit the same tax curve.
Common negotiation patterns   The candidate asks about the full package first. Expect questions about the contract type, the collective agreement that applies, notice periods and the way pay is spread across the year. Many Italian contracts include extra monthly payments on top of the regular ones. If your offer is a single annual figure, say how it breaks down. Confusion here kills trust fast.
The first counter is often modest. Italian candidates tend to negotiate in small steps rather than in one big jump. They may ask for a bit more, then ask for something else. Do not read this as weakness. Read it as a conversation that is still open.
Candidates compare you with local employers. They know what established Italian companies offer. A foreign company that is new to the market has to explain itself. Your brand may be unknown to them, and a strong US name does not carry the same weight it does at home.
Current salary is a reference point. Candidates will usually anchor to what they earn now. Ask about expectations, not just history, and explain how your range is built.
What Italians value beyond pay   Cash is only part of the decision. These points often tip the balance.
Job security. A permanent contract is the standard that most candidates want. A short fixed-term offer from a company with no local presence can look risky. If you hire through an employer of record, explain clearly who the legal employer is and what that means for the candidate’s rights.
Time and flexibility. Time off, predictable hours and the ability to work remotely some of the time carry real weight. Candidates value the right to disconnect. A US-style expectation of late calls across time zones should be raised early and honestly.
Family and place. Many candidates have strong ties to their city or region. Remote or hybrid work that lets them stay near family is a real benefit. So is flexibility around family needs.
Benefits that reduce cost of living. Meal vouchers, health coverage, supplemental pension contributions and similar items can be worth more to a candidate than the same amount in taxable salary. Ask your local payroll provider which benefits are tax-efficient before you offer them.
Growth and respect. A clear role, a named manager and a path to progress matter. So does how you treat people during the hiring process. Slow replies and vague answers hurt your offer more than a lower number would.
How to prepare   Know your range before the first call. Build it from local market data, not US bands converted to euros. Model net pay. Be able to show a candidate a realistic estimate of take-home pay at your offered gross figure. Decide what you can trade. If you cannot move on base pay, know which benefits, schedule terms or review dates you can offer instead. Put the whole offer in writing. Include the contract type, the collective agreement, the pay structure and any benefits. Be direct about the process. Say when you will answer and then do it. A note on tone   Italian candidates tend to value a personal, respectful exchange. A fast, transactional pitch can feel cold. Take time to explain the role and the company. Listen to what matters to the person. Often the best deal is not the highest salary but the best fit of pay, security and time.
That approach also protects you. A candidate who accepts after an honest discussion is less likely to leave when a local competitor calls.

## Same Salary, Different City: How a Job Offer Nets in Milan Versus Rome
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/same-salary-different-city-milan-vs-rome-net-pay.html
Summary: Hiring in Italy at the same gross salary? Milan and Rome differ only in the municipal surtax. Here is what changes for your employee's take-home pay.
You have an offer at a fixed gross salary. The candidate asks if it is the same in Milan and in Rome. The short answer: almost, but not quite. Most of the net pay calculation is identical in both cities. One local item is not.
What is the same in both cities   Two deductions do not depend on where the employee lives or works.
Social security. The employee’s pension contribution (INPS IVS) is 9.19% of taxable pay. The rate is national. Milan and Rome treat it the same way.
National income tax (IRPEF). IRPEF is progressive and uses the same brackets everywhere in Italy:
Income up to €28,000 is taxed at 23%. Income from €28,000 to €50,000 is taxed at 33%. Income above €50,000 is taxed at 43%. Each rate applies only to the slice of income inside its bracket. A salary above €50,000 does not get taxed at 43% in full. Only the part above €50,000 does.
So for a given gross salary, the pension contribution and the national tax are the same in Milan and Rome.
What is different: the municipal surtax   Every city can add its own surtax on income (addizionale comunale). It is a flat rate, and it comes with an exemption threshold.
Milan Rome Flat rate 0.8% 0.9% Exemption threshold €23,000 €14,000 Two things stand out.
Rome has a higher rate. At 0.9% against 0.8%, Rome takes a little more from every euro of taxable income once the surtax applies.
Milan has a much higher exemption. The Milan threshold is €23,000. The Rome threshold is €14,000. An employee with income between those two figures pays the surtax in Rome and does not pay it in Milan.
What this means for a typical offer   Most professional hires in Italy earn above €23,000. For them, both cities apply the surtax. The comparison then comes down to the rate. Rome is slightly higher, so the same gross salary nets slightly less in Rome.
The gap is small. It will not change the decision for a senior engineer or a finance manager. It is not a reason to move a role from one city to the other.
For lower-paid roles the picture shifts. Think of junior, part-time or entry-level positions with income between €14,000 and €23,000. Milan applies no surtax to them. Rome does. In that range the difference is larger in relative terms, because one city takes the surtax and the other takes nothing.
How to use this when you make an offer   Quote gross, but show net. Candidates in Italy compare offers by net monthly pay. If you only state gross, they will run their own numbers and may find that Rome nets less than they expected.
Do not adjust gross for the surtax difference. The gap is small enough for most roles that a different gross for each city is hard to justify. Keep one salary band and let the net differ.
Check lower-paid roles separately. If you hire in the range between the two exemption thresholds, run the numbers for both cities before you set the band.
Remember the scope of this comparison. This article covers the municipal surtax, the national income tax brackets and the employee pension contribution. Other items on a payslip, such as regional taxes or other contributions, are outside this comparison. A full net calculation needs all of them.
The takeaway   Same gross salary, same national tax, same pension contribution. The city changes one line: the municipal surtax. Milan charges 0.8% and exempts income up to €23,000. Rome charges 0.9% and exempts income up to €14,000.
For most hires, Rome nets a little less. For lower-paid roles, the difference can be more visible.
Run your own offer through the HiringItaly cost calculator to see the full picture for Milan, Rome or any other city.

## Sick Leave in Italy: What Managers Need to Know
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/sick-leave-italy-what-managers-need-to-know.html
Summary: How sick notes work in Italy, what a manager can ask an employee on sick leave, and what to leave alone. A practical guide for US teams hiring in Italy.
A US manager hears “I’m sick today” and expects a text, maybe a doctor’s note later. Italy works differently. The process is formal, it runs through the state, and managers have less room to ask questions than they might think.
This guide explains how sick notes work and where the limits are.
How the sick note works   In Italy, the employee does not hand you a paper note. The doctor issues a medical certificate electronically. It goes straight to the national social security institute, INPS. The employee gets a protocol number for the certificate.
The employer does not receive the diagnosis. That is the key point. The certificate you can access shows that the employee is certified unfit for work and for what period. It does not show the illness.
So your role is narrow. You do not collect medical paperwork. You check that a valid certificate exists and you record the absence.
What the employee must do   The employee still has to tell you about the absence. Do not wait for the system to do it. Most contracts and collective agreements expect the employee to notify the employer promptly, usually before the start of the working day. Many also expect the employee to share the certificate protocol number.
Your onboarding documents should say this in plain words. Name the channel (email, phone, a team chat) and the person to contact. If you leave it vague, you will end up chasing people.
How you find the certificate   Employers can retrieve the certificate data through INPS channels, using the protocol number from the employee. Most companies with an Italian payroll provider let that provider handle it. If you work with an Employer of Record, we do this step for you and flag anything unusual.
If you manage payroll yourself, make sure someone owns this task. A missing certificate is a real issue, but you need to confirm it before you act on it.
What managers can ask   You can ask for what the business needs to run:
Whether the employee has notified the absence and through which channel. The certificate protocol number, so HR or payroll can verify it. Whether urgent work or handovers need coverage. When the certified period ends, as shown on the certificate. You can also ask, kindly, to be told if the return date changes. Keep it short and practical.
What managers should not ask   This is where US managers get into trouble.
The diagnosis. Health data is among the most protected categories under European data protection rules. You do not need it and you should not request it. Symptoms or details. “What do you have?” is not a friendly question here. It can be treated as an intrusion. Proof beyond the certificate. Do not ask for extra notes, photos or lab results. Whether they are really sick. Doubts go to HR and, if needed, to the formal checks described below. They do not go in a chat message. Work while on leave. Do not ask a certified-sick employee to answer emails or join calls. It undermines the leave and creates risk for the company. A good rule: if the answer would not change how you plan the work, do not ask.
Home visits and checks   Italy has a system of medical control visits. The employee must be reachable at their declared address during set daily time bands. The employer can request a check, and INPS can also order one. There are rules on when an employee is exempt, for example for certain conditions or medical appointments.
If you suspect abuse, do not confront the employee. Talk to HR or your EOR first. A check is a formal step with its own procedure. An unsupported accusation can turn a small issue into a dispute.
Pay during sick leave   Sick pay is split between the employer and the state. How much each side pays depends on the national collective agreement (CCNL) that applies to the role, and on the length of service and the type of absence. Some agreements require the employer to top up what the state pays.
This is a cost many US teams miss when they budget an Italian hire. Salary is only part of the picture. Sick pay obligations sit on top of it, and they vary by sector.
Practical steps for your team   Write a short sick leave policy that reflects Italian practice, not US PTO habits. Tell managers what they may and may not ask. Name one person who verifies certificates and keeps the records. Store absence records separately from health information. In most cases you should never hold health information at all. Check your CCNL for notice rules, sick pay top-ups and any special provisions. Train managers to respond with support and a handover plan, not questions. The bottom line   Italian sick leave is simple once you accept the structure. The doctor certifies, INPS holds the record, and the employer confirms and plans. Your job is to keep the business running and stay out of the employee’s medical life.

## Smart Working Agreements in Italy: What the Written Contract Must Cover
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/italy-smart-working-agreement-lavoro-agile.html
Summary: Italian remote work (lavoro agile) needs a written agreement with the employee. See what it covers, why it is required and what US teams should prepare.
If you hire in Italy and want your team to work remotely, you cannot rely on a Slack message or an offer letter clause. Italian law treats remote work, called lavoro agile or smart working, as a formal arrangement. It needs a written agreement between employer and employee.
This guide explains what that agreement covers and why it matters.
What lavoro agile means   Lavoro agile is a way of performing an employment relationship. Part of the work happens outside the company premises. The employee is not tied to a fixed workplace for that part. Work is organized by phases, cycles and objectives, not by strict physical presence.
It is not a separate type of employment. The employee keeps the same contract, the same pay rules and the same rights as colleagues who work on site. The agreement only sets how the remote part works.
This is different from classic telework, where the employee works from a fixed remote location. Lavoro agile is more flexible. That flexibility is exactly why the rules need to be written down.
Why the written agreement is required   The agreement is not a courtesy. Italian law requires it for administrative purposes and for proof. In practice it does several jobs.
It shows that both sides agreed to the arrangement. It defines the limits of the employer’s control over a worker who is out of sight. It supports the mandatory communication to the authorities about the remote work arrangement. It protects you in a dispute about hours, tools, safety or discipline. Without a clear document, you carry the risk. If a claim arises, you will have little to show on what was agreed. A US-style remote work policy is usually not enough, because it does not address the points Italian law expects.
What the agreement covers   How the work is performed outside the premises   The agreement must describe how work is done away from the office. This includes which activities can be done remotely, how the employee reports in and how the employer directs the work. It also covers the use of technology for the job.
The employer’s power of control   In Italy, monitoring employees is limited. The agreement must state how the employer exercises supervision over remote work. It must also respect the rules on remote control of workers. If you plan to use monitoring software, check this point first. Vague wording here creates risk.
Disciplinary conduct   The agreement identifies behaviors outside the premises that may lead to disciplinary action. This gives the employee notice of the rules. It also gives you a clear basis if you ever need to act.
Working tools   Specify who provides the laptop, phone and other equipment. State who pays for maintenance and who is responsible for security. If the employee uses personal devices, say so and set the conditions.
Rest time and the right to disconnect   The agreement must set the employee’s rest periods. It must also set the technical and organizational measures that make disconnection from work devices possible. This is a core feature of Italian remote work. A team that expects replies at all hours will conflict with it.
If your headquarters is in the US and your clients are there too, plan for this. Define windows of availability and escalation rules in the agreement itself.
Duration and ending the arrangement   The agreement can be open-ended or for a fixed period. It must also set the notice needed to end the remote arrangement. Rules on withdrawal are stricter in some cases, such as for employees with disabilities. Do not copy a generic template here.
Health and safety   The employer stays responsible for safe working conditions. The employer must give the employee, in writing, information on the risks tied to working outside the premises. The employee must cooperate in applying the prevention measures. Include this information with the agreement.
Equal treatment   A remote employee must receive treatment no worse than colleagues doing the same work on site. This covers pay under the applicable collective agreement. It also covers training and career opportunities. Do not set lower terms because someone works from home.
Common mistakes US teams make   Treating remote work as a perk that can be granted by email. Using one global remote policy for every country. Skipping the right to disconnect. Adding monitoring tools without checking the limits on remote control. Forgetting to give the written safety information. Not filing the required communication to the authorities. Practical steps   Decide which roles can work remotely and how often. Draft the agreement in Italian, with an English reference version for your team. Align it with the applicable collective agreement for the role. Set clear availability windows and disconnection rules. Define equipment and cost responsibilities. Hand over the safety information in writing. File the required communication and keep proof. If you hire through an Employer of Record (EOR), the EOR is the legal employer in Italy. It prepares the agreement, files the communication and keeps the paperwork current. You direct the daily work. The EOR handles the formal side.
Bottom line   A smart-working agreement is a legal requirement and a risk tool. It sets what remote work looks like, protects the employee’s rest and protects you in a dispute. Write it before the first remote day, not after a problem appears.

## Social Security in Italy: Employee Rate, the Extra 1% and the Earnings Ceiling
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/italy-employee-social-security-rate-extra-1-percent-ceiling.html
Summary: How Italian employee social security works: the 9.19% pension rate, the extra 1% above 56,224 EUR and the 122,295 EUR contribution ceiling.
If you hire in Italy, part of each employee’s gross pay goes to INPS, the national social security body. The employee’s share is withheld from the paycheck. This article covers three numbers that shape that share: the base rate, the extra 1%, and the earnings ceiling.
The base employee rate   The employee’s pension contribution (called IVS in Italian) is 9.19% of taxable pay. Taxable pay here means the gross amount that INPS counts as the contribution base.
This is the rate that appears on most Italian payslips. It is taken from gross pay every month. The employee never has to pay it separately.
For your finance team, the practical point is simple. The 9.19% reduces the employee’s net pay. It does not add to your cost. Your own employer contributions are a separate line, and they are not covered in this article.
The extra 1% above a threshold   An additional rate of 1% applies to pay above a set threshold. The threshold is:
56,224 EUR per year 4,685 EUR per month The extra 1% only applies to the part of pay that goes over the threshold. Pay below the threshold is not affected.
This matters for senior hires. A US-style compensation package for a director or a senior engineer will often pass the annual threshold. For those roles, the effective employee rate on the upper slice is higher than the base rate. Junior and mid-level salaries may stay below the threshold and never see the extra 1%.
Payroll usually checks the threshold month by month, which is why the monthly figure exists. If you pay variable pay, such as a bonus in one month, that month can cross the monthly figure even when the annual picture looks modest. Ask your payroll provider how they handle this, so the numbers on the payslip do not surprise anyone.
The earnings ceiling   Italian social security has a ceiling on the pay that counts for contributions. For employees enrolled in the system from 1996, with no earlier contribution history, the ceiling is 122,295 EUR per year.
Above that amount, the pay no longer counts for the pension contribution. In practice, contributions stop growing once an employee’s annual pay passes the ceiling.
Two cautions apply here.
First, the figure is for employees enrolled from 1996 with no earlier seniority. Employees with a contribution history before that date can fall under different rules. Most people you hire from abroad will not have this history, but you should confirm each case. Someone who worked in Italy earlier in their career may be the exception.
Second, the ceiling is a limit on the contribution base. It is not a limit on salary. You can pay more than 122,295 EUR. The extra just stops generating further pension contributions under this rule.
How the three numbers work together   Think of the pay of one employee as a line that grows over the year.
Up to 56,224 EUR, the employee pays 9.19%. Above 56,224 EUR, the employee pays 9.19% plus the extra 1%. Above 122,295 EUR, the pay stops counting for contributions, for the employee group described above. So the burden is not a flat percentage across the whole salary. It has a base slice, a slightly heavier slice, and a point where it stops.
What to check before you make an offer   Decide whether you quote salaries as gross. In Italy, gross is the standard. Net pay depends on social security and income tax. Estimate where the salary sits against the 56,224 EUR threshold. Include bonuses. Check whether the employee has any contribution history in Italy from before 1996. This changes which ceiling applies. Keep these figures under review. Rates and thresholds are set by INPS and can change from year to year. A note on the figures   The numbers in this article come from published Italian payroll guides, which are secondary sources. They are consistent with each other, but you should confirm them against current INPS guidance or with your payroll provider before you finalize a contract or a budget.

## Supplementary Health Insurance in Italy: Why Private Plans Still Matter
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/supplementary-health-insurance-italy-employees.html
Summary: Italy has public health care for residents. Here is why supplementary private health plans still matter for employers hiring staff in Italy.
Italy has a public health system. Residents can use it, and employees contribute to it through payroll. So a US founder often asks a fair question: why add private health insurance on top?
The short answer is that the public system and a private plan do different jobs. Most Italian employees use both. If you want to hire and keep good people in Italy, you should understand the gap between them.
What the public system does well   The national health service, the Servizio Sanitario Nazionale, covers a broad range of care. Family doctors, hospital treatment, emergency care and many specialist services are available to people who are registered. For serious illness, the public system is a core part of the safety net, and many Italians trust it.
You do not need to replace it. A private plan is not a substitute for it. It sits next to it.
Where the friction shows up   The pain points are practical, not medical.
Waiting times. For non-urgent specialist visits and diagnostic tests, waits can be long. How long depends on the region, the local health authority and the type of exam. An employee with a nagging problem may wait weeks or months for an appointment.
Regional differences. Health care is organized at the regional level. Quality, speed and access are not the same everywhere in the country. A team member in one city may have a very different experience from a colleague in another.
Choice of doctor and facility. In the public system, you often go where you are assigned or where there is space. Private plans let people pick a specialist, a clinic and a time that fits their working day.
Time away from work. Long waits and slow scheduling can pull people out of work for longer than needed. A faster route to a diagnosis helps the employee and the business.
Language. Foreign hires and relocated staff may be more comfortable with providers who speak English. Private networks often make that easier to find.
What supplementary plans typically cover   Plans vary by insurer and by contract, so read the terms before you commit. In general, supplementary plans help pay for things like:
Specialist visits and diagnostic exams Private hospital stays and surgery Dental care and some vision care Maternity-related services Prevention checks and screening Some plans extend to the employee’s family. Some do not. Coverage limits, exclusions and waiting periods differ, so compare them line by line.
Where collective agreements come in   Italian employment is shaped by national collective agreements, known as CCNL. Many of them provide for sector health funds or other welfare benefits for employees. Which agreement applies to your hire depends on the sector and the role.
This matters for two reasons. First, a benefit may be expected or required under the agreement, so you cannot treat it as optional. Second, if the agreement already provides a baseline, a company plan can top it up instead of duplicating it.
Check the applicable agreement before you design a benefits package. Do this before the offer, not after.
Why it matters for hiring and retention   Italian candidates know the system. They know what the waits can be like. A solid supplementary plan reads as a real signal that you take care of your people.
For foreign companies entering Italy, this is a cheap way to stand out. You may not match local brand names on salary or prestige. You can match them on benefits that people use.
A plan also helps with relocation. Someone moving to Italy from abroad is often unsure how to find care. A plan with clear access and English support removes a worry at the moment they need it most.
How to approach it   Keep the process simple.
Identify the collective agreement that applies to the role. Find out what health benefits it already provides. Decide what you want to add on top, and for whom. Compare insurers on coverage, exclusions, provider networks and claims process. Explain the benefit clearly in the offer and in onboarding. Finance teams should also check how the benefit is treated for payroll, since tax and contribution treatment of welfare benefits has its own rules. Get that confirmed locally before you roll out the plan.
The bottom line   Public care in Italy is real and valuable. It is not always fast, and it is not the same everywhere. Supplementary health insurance closes part of that gap. It gives employees speed, choice and peace of mind, and it gives you a stronger hiring offer.
The cost depends on the plan, the collective agreement and the size of your team. Before you decide, see what it adds to your total cost of employment. Try the cost calculator.

## The Italian CU: What Employees Receive at Tax Time and When
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/italy-cu-annual-tax-certificate-employees.html
Summary: The Certificazione Unica (CU) is Italy's W-2 equivalent. See what it contains, who gets it, and the dates that matter to employers and employees.
If you run payroll in the US, you know the W-2. Italy has a close equivalent. It is called the Certificazione Unica, or CU. Every employee in Italy should receive one after the tax year closes.
This article explains what the CU is, what it shows, and which dates matter. If you hire in Italy through an Employer of Record (EOR), this is a document your team will see and your employees will ask about.
What the CU is   The CU is the annual statement of income and withholding. The employer issues it. It reports what the employee earned in the previous year and what was withheld on their behalf.
The parallel to the W-2 is real, but not exact. The W-2 is mainly a document for the employee’s own tax return. The CU does that job too. It is also a filing the employer sends to the tax authority, the Agenzia delle Entrate. So the same data goes to two places.
What it contains   A CU for an employee typically covers:
The employer’s details and the employee’s details Gross employment income for the year Income tax withheld at source Social security contributions paid by the employee Regional and municipal surtaxes withheld Certain deductions and tax credits applied during the year The employee uses these figures to check their position and, where needed, to file a return. Many Italian employees do not file a full return, because the employer already handles withholding and adjustments through payroll. Even so, the CU is the reference document if they do file, or if they need proof of income for a bank, a landlord, or a visa renewal.
The dates that matter   For the 2026 cycle, a secondary source that tracks the fiscal calendar lists these deadlines:
March 16, 2026: the CU must be delivered to employees. March 16, 2026: the same date applies to sending the CU data to the Agenzia delle Entrate. April 30: the later deadline for CUs covering self-employed income. October 31: the deadline for CUs covering income that is exempt from tax. For employment income, one date does most of the work. March 16 is both the delivery date to the employee and the filing date with the tax authority. There is no gap to plan around. Payroll needs to close the prior year cleanly and produce the file in time.
The April 30 and October 31 dates are not about regular employees. They matter if your company also pays freelancers or other types of income in Italy. Those are tracked separately.
Deadlines in Italy can shift. The authorities sometimes adjust them by decree or by calendar rules. Confirm the date with your payroll provider or tax adviser each year before you commit to an internal schedule.
What employers should do   A few practical points for US founders and finance teams:
Treat it as a year-end close task. The CU depends on correct payroll data for the whole year. Errors in withholding, benefits, or contributions show up here. Review the year before the file is generated, not after.
Expect employee questions. Employees often ask what each box means. A short internal note explaining the CU in plain terms saves time. If you work with an EOR, the provider usually produces and delivers the document for you.
Keep terminations in mind. If someone leaves during the year, they still need a CU for the period they worked. Make sure your process covers former employees, not only current ones.
Do not confuse it with the payslip. The monthly payslip shows each pay period. The CU is the annual summary. They should reconcile, and when they do not, that is a signal to investigate.
What employees should do   Employees should check that the name, tax code, and income figures are correct when the CU arrives. If something looks wrong, they should contact the employer or payroll provider quickly. A corrected CU is possible, but it is easier to fix before the data is used for a return or another application.
They should also keep the document. Banks, landlords and immigration offices often ask for it as proof of income.
The takeaway   The CU is Italy’s W-2 equivalent, with one extra role: it is also the employer’s filing to the tax authority. For employees, the key date is March 16, 2026. Other income types follow later dates. Build the year-end close around that, and the process is routine.
