## The Italian employer withholding return (Modello 770) in plain English
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/modello-770-employer-withholding-return-explained.html
Summary: What the Modello 770 is, who files it, and what your Italian employer of record handles for you, explained for US finance teams.
If your company hires in Italy, you will hear the term Modello 770 at some point. It sounds like a tax form your team has to prepare. In most setups it is not. This article explains what it is, why it exists, and what finance should expect to see.
What the Modello 770 is   The Modello 770 is the annual return filed by the party that withholds tax at source. In Italy, an employer does not pay salary in full and leave the tax to the employee. The employer holds back income tax from each payslip and pays it to the state. Social security contributions follow a similar path.
The 770 is the yearly summary of all that. It reports what was withheld, what was paid over, and to whom. Think of it as the year-end reconciliation between payroll and the tax authority.
It does not cover your corporate income tax. It does not replace your own US filings. It only covers amounts withheld from people and professionals the Italian employer paid.
Who files it   The withholding agent files it. That is the entity acting as employer on the Italian side.
If you hire through an Employer of Record (EOR), the EOR is the legal employer in Italy. It runs payroll, withholds the tax, and files the return. Your US company does not file the 770 for those employees. You do not need an Italian filing account for it.
If you instead hire directly through your own Italian entity, then your entity is the withholding agent. In that case the filing sits with your local accountant or payroll provider.
When it is due   For 2026, the published deadline calendars list the Modello 770 for October 31, 2026. That date falls on a Saturday, so it moves to Monday, November 2, 2026. This date comes from a secondary source, not from the tax authority itself. Your EOR will confirm the date it works to.
How it connects to other year-end documents   The 770 is the last step in a chain. During the year, payroll produces payslips with withheld tax. After year end, employees receive a statement of what they earned and what was withheld. That statement is called the Certificazione Unica. The 770 then reports the same data to the authority in aggregate.
This matters for one reason. The numbers must match across payslips, the employee statement, and the return. If they do, the process is boring. That is the goal.
What US finance actually sees   You will not receive a draft 770 to approve line by line. That is normal. Here is what to expect instead:
Monthly invoices from the EOR that show gross pay, employer contributions, and the service fee. A year-end confirmation that the annual filings were completed. A copy of the employee statements on request. Answers when your auditors ask how Italian withholding is handled. If an auditor asks who is responsible for withholding and reporting, the answer is the EOR as legal employer. Keep the service agreement and the filing confirmation on file.
Questions worth asking your EOR   You do not need to learn the form. You do need to know the process is covered. Ask these:
Do you file the annual withholding return for all employees placed with us? Can you share confirmation once it is filed? How do you handle corrections if an amount was wrong? Who is the contact if the tax authority sends a notice? How are costs for any late filing penalties allocated if the error is yours? Good answers are short and specific. Vague answers are a warning sign.
What can go wrong   Most problems come from data, not from the form. A wrong tax code for an employee. A bonus paid late and booked in the wrong period. A mid-year change in role that was never updated in payroll. Each of these creates a mismatch that someone must fix.
You can reduce the risk on your side. Send compensation changes to the EOR before the payroll cut-off. Tell them about one-off payments, equity events, and relocation allowances early. Clean inputs make a clean annual return.
The short version   The Modello 770 is the employer’s yearly report of tax withheld from payroll. Under an EOR model, the EOR files it. Your job is to supply accurate inputs, keep the confirmation, and know the date it is due.

## The Italian Payslip (Busta Paga) Decoded for US Managers
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/italian-payslip-busta-paga-explained-us-managers.html
Summary: A section-by-section tour of the Italian busta paga, so US managers can answer employee questions about gross pay, deductions, leave and severance.
Your Italian employee brings you a payslip and asks why the net looks small. You open it and see a wall of Italian abbreviations. This guide walks through the document section by section, so you can answer most questions without calling payroll.
The payslip is called the busta paga or cedolino. It is a legal document. The employer must give it to the employee every pay period. It is usually dense, and layouts differ by payroll provider. The same blocks appear on all of them.
1. The header: who, where, what contract   The top of the page identifies the employer and the employee. You will see the employer’s tax and social security registration data, the employee’s tax code (codice fiscale), and the payroll period.
The key field here is the collective agreement, the CCNL. Italy sets many employment terms by sector-wide agreements. The CCNL defines the minimum pay for each job level, notice periods, leave rules and more. Next to it you will see the employee’s livello (job level) and qualifica (category, such as employee, manager or executive).
If an employee asks why their salary “must” be at least a certain amount, the answer starts here. The CCNL and level set the floor.
2. Pay items: the gross side   This block lists everything the employee earns before deductions. Common lines:
Paga base or minimo tabellare. The minimum pay set by the CCNL for that level. Superminimo. Pay above the CCNL minimum. This is where your negotiated salary usually shows up. It can be absorbed into later CCNL increases unless the contract says otherwise. Scatti di anzianità. Seniority increments, if the CCNL provides them. Straordinari. Overtime, paid at rates the CCNL sets. Indennità. Allowances, for example for travel, role or shifts. Premi. Bonuses. The sum is the totale competenze or gross pay. Your offer letter number should reconcile with this total once you account for how your payroll provider annualizes it.
3. Time and leave   A separate block tracks days worked and leave balances. Italian employees accrue several types:
Ferie. Paid vacation. The slip shows accrued, used and remaining balances. ROL and ex-festività. Reduced-hours leave and compensation for former holidays, depending on the CCNL. Not every contract has these. Malattia. Sick leave. Pay during sickness follows a mix of social security benefits and employer top-ups set by the CCNL. Managers get many questions here. “How much vacation do I have left?” is answered by this block. Approving time off without checking it creates payroll corrections later.
4. Employee social security   Next come the deductions. The first is the employee’s share of social security, paid to INPS. It is withheld from gross pay and sent to the authority by the employer.
This is different from the employer’s own contributions. Those do not appear as a deduction. They sit on top of the gross salary and are a real cost to the company. Many US managers miss this. The payslip shows what the employee pays, not what the company pays in total. That is why the total cost of an Italian hire is higher than gross pay.
The result of this step is the imponibile fiscale, the taxable base for income tax.
5. Income tax withholding   The employer withholds income tax at source, much like US payroll. The lines to know:
IRPEF lorda. Gross personal income tax, calculated on the taxable base using progressive brackets. Detrazioni. Tax credits that reduce the tax due. They depend on income level, family situation and dependents. Two employees with the same salary can have different net pay because of these. Addizionale regionale and comunale. Regional and municipal surcharges. They depend on where the employee lives, not where the company is. Conguaglio. An adjustment. It trues up the tax withheld against what is actually due, often at year end or when the employee’s situation changes. If an employee says their net changed with no salary change, check detrazioni and conguaglio first.
6. The net   At the bottom you find the netto in busta, the amount transferred to the employee’s bank account. It is gross pay minus employee social security, income tax and surcharges, adjusted for credits and any other items such as union fees or salary advances.
7. TFR: the severance accrual   The slip also reports TFR (trattamento di fine rapporto). This is a severance amount that builds up during employment and is paid when the contract ends. It is not an extra deduction from the employee. It is a company liability that grows each period. The slip shows the accrual, and the employee may have chosen to direct it to a pension fund instead.
Expect questions here from employees who think the company holds back their money. Explain that TFR belongs to them and is paid at exit or moved to a pension fund.
8. Extra monthly payments   Many CCNLs provide additional salary payments during the year, often paid at set times. In Italy, this is part of normal annual compensation, not a bonus. When an employee asks why one payslip looks larger, check whether one of these payments falls in that period.
How to use this   When an employee questions a payslip, work through it in order. Check the CCNL and level. Check the pay items. Check leave balances. Check deductions and credits. Then look at the net.
Most questions have a simple answer in one of these blocks. For anything involving a conguaglio or a legal interpretation, send it to your payroll provider.

## The Italian Social Security Ceiling and What It Means for Senior Employees
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/italy-social-security-ceiling-senior-hires-employee-side.html
Summary: Italy caps the pay on which social security contributions are calculated. Here is what the ceiling means for the take-home and pension of a senior hire.
You are hiring a senior leader in Italy. The salary is high. You expect social security costs to rise in line with it. They do not, past a certain point. Italy has an annual earnings ceiling for social security contributions. This article looks at what that ceiling means for the employee.
What the ceiling is   The ceiling is called the massimale contributivo. It is the maximum annual pay on which INPS contributions are calculated. For employees enrolled in the system from 1996 with no earlier contribution history, the figure is EUR 122,295 per year.
Pay up to that amount is subject to contributions. Pay above it is not subject to the same contributions.
This figure comes from a secondary source. Treat it as a planning number and confirm it with your payroll provider before you quote it in an offer.
The employee side in plain terms   Every employee in the Italian system pays a share of social security out of gross pay. The employer pays a separate share on top. The ceiling limits the pay that both shares are applied to.
For a senior hire, this has a direct effect.
The employee’s contribution is calculated on pay up to the ceiling only. Once gross pay passes the ceiling, the employee’s contribution stops growing. Extra salary above the ceiling is not reduced by further social security deductions. So a raise for someone already above the ceiling is not eroded by additional contributions on that raise. The rest of the deductions still apply.
What the ceiling does not change   The ceiling covers social security contributions. It does not cap income tax.
Income tax applies to the full taxable income, including the part above the ceiling. A senior employee will still see a large share of each additional euro go to tax. The ceiling softens only one layer of deductions.
It also does not cap pay. You can offer any salary you like. The ceiling only decides how much of it counts for contributions.
The pension side   There is a trade-off that many high earners overlook. Contributions build the pension. If pay above the ceiling is not subject to contributions, it also does not add to the pension base in the same way.
For the employee, this means two things:
Lower deductions on the slice above the ceiling, so more take-home pay. A public pension that tracks capped pay, not total pay. A person on a very high salary should not expect the state pension to follow their last salary. The gap grows with the size of the salary above the ceiling. Many senior hires know this. Some will ask about supplementary pension or other savings as part of the package. Be ready for that question in negotiation.
Who the ceiling applies to   The figure above applies to people enrolled from 1996 with no earlier contribution history. This describes many younger professionals and people who started their career in Italy after that point.
It may not describe every candidate. A person with contributions before that point can fall under different rules. An executive who worked in Italy years ago and is now returning should have their position checked. Ask for their contribution history before you model the cost.
What this means for your offer   For a US founder or HR lead, a few practical points follow.
Do not scale costs in a straight line. A salary offer that is much higher does not carry much higher social security cost on the employee side. The cost curve flattens above the ceiling.
Present net pay carefully. If a candidate asks for a net figure, income tax still moves with gross pay. Work from gross, apply the contribution cap, then apply tax. Do not skip a step.
Expect pension questions. Senior candidates may compare your offer with a package that includes extra retirement benefits. Know the answer before they ask.
Check the individual case. The ceiling depends on the employee’s contribution history. One senior hire may be capped. Another may not be.
A short checklist   Confirm the current ceiling with your payroll provider. Ask the candidate when they first entered the Italian system. Model contributions on pay up to the ceiling only, where the cap applies. Model income tax on the full gross amount. Decide whether to add supplementary pension to the offer. Bottom line   The ceiling is good news for the cost of a senior hire. Contributions stop at a fixed pay level. It is also a fact the employee should understand, because it shapes both take-home pay and the future pension. Be clear about both when you make the offer.

## The Low-Income Tax Supplement on Italian Payslips: What the Line Means
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/italy-payslip-trattamento-integrativo-explained.html
Summary: Employees on lower salaries in Italy see a line called trattamento integrativo. Here is what it is, why it appears, and what employers should tell staff.
If you hire in Italy, sooner or later an employee on a lower salary will ask about a payslip line called trattamento integrativo. It is a tax supplement for low earners. It adds money to the net pay. It is not a bonus from you, and it is not a discretionary benefit.
This article explains what the line is, why it shows up, and how to answer the question without a call to your accountant.
What the line is   Italian income tax (IRPEF) is withheld from salary each month. For people on lower incomes, the law adds a supplement on top of the net pay. On the payslip it appears under the name trattamento integrativo. Some payroll systems label it with a short form or a code, but the idea is the same.
The supplement is capped. The verified figure we use here is a maximum of 1,200 euros per year. It applies to employees with income up to 15k euros, and only under conditions. The conditions matter. Not everyone below the income threshold receives the full amount, and some receive nothing.
Because the source for this figure is a secondary one, treat it as a guide to the order of magnitude. Your payroll provider should confirm the exact rules for each employee.
Why employees ask about it   There are three common reasons.
It is a positive line. Most payslip lines reduce pay. This one adds to it. People notice, and they want to know whether it will continue.
It can change month to month. The supplement depends on the employee’s income and tax position. If pay changes, the supplement can change too. A new hire who starts mid-year, or someone who works fewer hours, may see a different amount than a colleague.
It can disappear. If an employee’s income rises above the limit, or the conditions are no longer met, the line goes away. That can look like a pay cut when it is not one. The gross salary is the same. The supplement just no longer applies.
Who pays for it   The employee receives it through payroll, so it is the employer who pays it out with the salary. In practice the employer then recovers the amount by offsetting it against the taxes and contributions it already owes the state. So the supplement should not be a net cost to you, but your payroll team has to handle it correctly.
This is one reason to work with a payroll provider that knows Italian rules. A wrong calculation means either an underpaid employee or an amount that has to be corrected later.
What happens at year end   The supplement is based on the employee’s expected income for the year. Final eligibility is checked at year-end adjustment. If the employee turns out not to meet the conditions, the amount already paid may have to be returned, usually through the final payslips.
This surprises people. An employee who received the line all year may see a deduction later. It is worth telling staff in advance that the supplement is provisional until the year is closed.
This tends to happen when:
the employee had other income during the year the employee started or left a job mid-year the pay was higher than first estimated How to explain it to an employee   Keep the message short. Something like this works:
This line is a tax supplement the state gives to employees with lower income. It is added to your net pay. Whether you get it, and how much, depends on your income and your situation. It can change, and it is checked again at year end.
Then add what you cannot promise. You cannot guarantee the amount. You cannot guarantee it will stay on the payslip. You can only say that payroll applies the rule as written.
What this means for your cost planning   If you are a US founder or finance lead, there are two practical points.
First, the supplement does not change the cost of the employee to you in a major way. It changes what the employee takes home. When you compare offers, look at the net pay and not only the gross salary. Two roles with the same gross can leave different amounts in the employee’s pocket if one of them qualifies for the supplement.
Second, this affects how a raise lands. If a salary increase pushes someone above the income limit, part of the raise can be offset by losing the supplement. The employee may feel the raise is smaller than expected. Warn people before the change shows up on a payslip.
What to check with payroll   When onboarding someone on a lower salary, ask your payroll team or provider these questions:
Does this employee qualify, and on what basis? Is the line calculated correctly in the first payslips? How will year-end adjustment work if eligibility changes? What do we tell the employee in writing? A clear answer to each one prevents most of the questions later.
Summary   The trattamento integrativo is a tax supplement for lower earners. It adds to net pay. The cap we use is 1,200 euros per year, for income up to 15k euros, under conditions. It can change or stop, and it is verified at year end. Explain it early and keep the wording plain.

## The Non-Taxable Wage Component for Lower Earners in Italy: How It Works in Payroll
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/italy-non-taxable-wage-component-lower-earners.html
Summary: How Italy's tax-wedge relief for lower earners works in payroll: a non-taxable share of income at low bands, plus an extra deduction in the middle bands.
Italy has a relief for lower earners that works inside payroll. It is often called the tax-wedge relief. It has two parts. One is a non-taxable share of employment income. The other is an extra tax deduction for the next income band. This article explains how each part works and what it means for your payroll process.
What the tax wedge is   The tax wedge is the gap between what an employer pays and what the employee takes home. Taxes and contributions sit in that gap. The relief described here narrows it for people on lower pay. The employer does not claim anything. The relief is applied in the monthly payroll run.
Part one: the non-taxable amount   For lower earners, a share of employment income is treated as non-taxable for personal income tax (IRPEF). The share depends on the income band:
Employment income Non-taxable share of that income Up to EUR 8,500 7.1% EUR 8,500 to EUR 15,000 5.3% EUR 15,000 to EUR 20,000 4.8% The share is a percentage of employment income. It is not a flat sum. The lowest band gets the highest share. The share steps down as income rises.
For a founder, the practical point is simple. The employee’s taxable base is smaller than the gross pay. Net pay goes up. Your gross cost does not change.
Part two: the additional deduction   The second part covers the band above the first. Employees earning between EUR 20,000 and EUR 32,000 receive an additional deduction of EUR 1,000 per year. Above EUR 32,000 the deduction shrinks. It reaches zero at EUR 40,000.
This is a phase-out, not a cliff. The amount falls gradually across the range between EUR 32,000 and EUR 40,000. A raise inside that range still increases net pay, but by less than the same raise would elsewhere.
What this means at payroll level   Payroll handles both parts, so you rarely touch them directly. Still, a few points matter for planning.
Gross pay drives the result. The relief depends on the level of employment income. When you set a salary, the band decides which treatment applies. Two offers that look close on paper can produce different net amounts if they fall on opposite sides of a threshold.
Net pay is not a straight line. In the lower bands the non-taxable share changes as income crosses a threshold. In the upper range the extra deduction fades out. Both effects mean that net pay does not rise evenly with gross pay.
Income is measured on the year. The thresholds refer to annual amounts. A mid-year hire or a mid-year raise needs a payroll provider that can estimate the annual figure and adjust. Otherwise the relief may be over- or under-applied during the year and corrected later.
Offers should be shown as gross and net. Candidates in Italy compare net pay. If you only quote gross, the relief is invisible to them. Showing both avoids confusion in the first payslip.
What to check before you rely on this   The figures above come from a secondary source. The rules can be updated by each annual budget law, and payroll software applies the official tables. Before you build a salary offer around a threshold, confirm the current figures with your payroll provider or an Italian labor consultant.
Also confirm how the relief interacts with other items in the payslip. Those items include other deductions and any regional or municipal taxes. Each of them has its own rules. The relief described here is one layer in the calculation, not the whole result.
A simple way to work with it   Start from the target net pay for the role. Work backward to the gross salary. Check which band that gross falls in. Then check whether a small change in gross would move the employee into a different treatment. If it would, decide whether the move is worth it for both sides.
This takes a few minutes with the right tool. It prevents surprises when the first payslip arrives.

## The Residence Permit After Arrival: Your Employee's First Weeks in Italy
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/residence-permit-after-arrival-italy.html
Summary: The visa gets your hire into Italy. The permesso di soggiorno lets them stay and work. Here is what happens next and what your team should track.
The visa gets your new employee into Italy. It does not let them stay. The residence permit, called the permesso di soggiorno, does that. Most delays in a relocation happen in the weeks right after landing, not before.
This guide walks through what happens next and what your HR and legal ops teams should watch.
The visa is an entry document   A work visa lets your employee enter Italy for the purpose of working. Once they arrive, they must convert that entry into a permit to stay. The permit is a separate document, issued by the local police headquarters (the questura) after an application.
The steps start almost immediately. Deadlines after arrival are short and strict. Confirm the exact window for your employee’s case before they travel, and tell them on day one.
Step 1: Declare presence   A person arriving from outside the Schengen area must declare their presence in Italy. In most cases the border stamp or a form handled by the hotel or host covers this. Keep a copy. The questura may ask for it later.
Step 2: Get a tax code   The codice fiscale is the Italian tax ID. Your employee needs it for the employment contract, payroll, a bank account, a lease and a phone plan. Often it is requested before arrival or issued at the first appointment. If it is missing, payroll cannot start properly.
Step 3: Sign the stay contract   For most work visas, the employee and the employer must meet at the Immigration One-Stop Shop (Sportello Unico per l’Immigrazione) at the local prefecture. There, they sign the contratto di soggiorno. This document ties the permit to the job.
Your employer of record usually handles the employer side of this. The employee must attend in person with the right documents. Plan the trip so nobody is traveling when the appointment falls.
Step 4: File the permit application   The permit application is submitted through a postal kit, available at designated Post Office counters. The kit has forms, a copy of the passport and visa, and proof of the stay contract. The employee fills it in and returns it at the counter.
The post office gives a receipt. Keep it safe. It is the proof that the application is pending.
Mistakes here cost weeks. Common errors are:
Names that do not match the passport exactly. A missing signature. An address the employee cannot use for mail. Have someone who knows the process review the kit before submission.
Step 5: Attend the questura appointment   After filing, the questura calls the employee in. They give fingerprints and a photo. They also hand over or confirm the details of the application. Wait times depend heavily on the city. Some offices are quick. Others are slow.
The employee should check their mail and phone often. A missed appointment can reset the clock.
Can they start working before the permit arrives?   In many work cases, the postal receipt allows the employee to start work while the permit is being produced. This is a common point of confusion. Do not guess. Have your provider confirm that the receipt is enough for your specific visa category before the first day of work.
Step 6: Register residence and healthcare   Once settled, the employee registers their address with the local town hall (anagrafe). This is the residence registration. It matters for healthcare, a driving license, tax and many daily tasks.
They can then enrol in the national health service. Some employees also want private cover during the first weeks. Ask your benefits team what is included.
What the employer must do   Your company is not a bystander. In the first weeks, expect to:
Communicate the new hire to the authorities, as required for any employee in Italy. Provide the documents needed for the stay contract. Give the employee a stable address for mail, or help find housing quickly. Keep a record of the receipt, the permit and its expiry. Set a reminder well before the permit expires. Renewal should start early. An employer of record can run this checklist for you. You still need to know what is happening, since it affects start dates and onboarding.
Practical tips for founders and HR   Do not book the start date too tightly. Leave room for appointments and mail delays. Assign one contact. The employee will have questions in a new language and a new system. One person at your provider should own them. Share a plain timeline. A one-page list of steps and who does what removes most anxiety. Keep copies of everything. Passport, visa, receipt, stay contract, tax code, residence registration. Plan for family. If relatives join, they have their own paperwork and timelines. The short version   The visa opens the door. After that, the employee must declare presence, get a tax code, sign the stay contract, file the postal kit, attend the questura, and register their residence. Each step has a deadline and a document. Miss one and onboarding slips.
Good planning turns the first weeks from stressful to routine.

## Vacation and Public Holidays in Italy: How to Plan Team Coverage
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/italy-vacation-public-holidays-team-coverage.html
Summary: Why Italy slows down in August, how leave and public holidays work for employers, and how to plan coverage so your Italian team and clients stay supported.
If you hire in Italy, you will notice a pattern. Replies slow down in August. Some colleagues vanish for weeks. Clients and suppliers go quiet. This is normal, and it is predictable. You can plan for it.
This article explains why it happens and how to build coverage that works.
Why August slows down   Italy has a strong summer holiday culture. Many people take their main break in August, and they take it in a block. Schools are closed. Families travel together. The mid-August holiday, Ferragosto, sits in the middle of the period and anchors it.
Many Italian businesses also close entirely for part of the month. Factories, small firms and professional offices often shut down so everyone can rest at the same time. If your team works with Italian customers, partners or advisors, expect them to be away too.
So the slowdown is not only about your employees. It is the whole local ecosystem. Your accountant, your payroll contact, your landlord and your customers may all be out at once.
How leave works in practice   Italian employees have a legal right to paid annual leave. The exact entitlement and the rules on how it is used come from national law and from the collective agreement that applies to the role. Collective agreements vary by sector. Always check which one covers each employee before you write a leave policy.
A few points matter for planning:
Leave is a right, not a favor. You cannot ask people to give it up. Employers have a say in when leave is taken, but they must take employee needs into account. Part of the leave is expected to be used as a continuous break during the year. Summer is the usual choice. Unused leave does not simply disappear or get paid out in the normal course. Carrying it forward has limits. This means a US-style policy of “take it when you can” or “unlimited time off” does not map cleanly. You need a clear, documented process.
Public holidays   Italy has several national public holidays across the year. Some fall on fixed days. Others move, such as Easter Monday. Local patron saint days add more in individual cities. A team spread across several cities may not share the same calendar.
When a holiday lands on a weekday, the office is closed. When it lands on a weekend, the treatment depends on the contract and the collective agreement. Do not assume the US habit of moving the day off to a Friday or Monday.
Build a holiday calendar for each location at the start of the year. Share it with your whole company, not just the Italy team. Your US colleagues should know when Italian coverage is thin.
Plan coverage before the rush   The worst time to plan summer coverage is in July. Start early. A simple process works well.
Ask for leave plans in spring. Request preferred summer dates from everyone. Most people already know when they want to go. Asking early lets you spot clashes while there is still room to adjust.
Stagger the breaks. If a team has several people, avoid having everyone away at the same time. Agree a rotation. Be fair about it. Rotate who gets the most popular weeks from year to year.
Name a backup for each critical task. Payroll inputs, customer escalations, compliance deadlines and system access all need a second person. Write down who covers what. Do not rely on memory.
Document handovers. Before anyone leaves, ask for a short handover note. It should list open items, deadlines that fall during the absence, and who to call.
Set expectations with clients. Tell customers and partners in advance that response times will be longer. A short notice in June avoids frustration in August.
Do not plan around people on leave   A common mistake is to expect people to check email while away. In Italy this is poorly received, and in many cases it undermines the purpose of the break. Employees may also have rights about disconnecting. Treat time off as time off.
If you truly need an urgent decision from someone on leave, handle it as a rare exception. Plan so that it is not needed.
Align your global calendar   US founders often schedule product launches, board meetings and fiscal deadlines without thinking about Italy. Check your calendar against Italian holidays and the summer break. Avoid setting big deliverables for the quiet weeks. If a deadline cannot move, agree the coverage months ahead and confirm it in writing.
Payroll and statutory filings keep running even when people are away. Make sure the person who handles them, internally or through a provider, has a clear backup.
Get the terms right in the contract   Your employment contracts and internal policy should state how leave requests are made, how far ahead, and who approves them. They should also describe how public holidays are treated. A clear policy prevents disputes. If you use an Employer of Record (EOR), your provider can apply the correct collective agreement and keep leave balances accurate, so your managers focus on scheduling rather than rules.
The short version   Italy slows down in August because the whole country takes a break at once. Accept it. Collect leave plans early, stagger absences, name backups, document handovers and tell clients ahead of time. Do this and the quiet weeks cost you very little.

## What Americans Get Wrong About Italian Colleagues
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/what-americans-get-wrong-about-italian-colleagues.html
Summary: Long lunches, endless meetings, no sense of urgency? A plain look at common stereotypes about Italian coworkers and what working with them is really like.
Many US founders arrive with a picture of Italian work life. It comes from movies, holiday trips and a few stories from friends. Some of it has a grain of truth. Most of it leads to bad management choices.
This article looks at the common stereotypes and compares them with what US teams usually find once they hire in Italy.
Stereotype: Italians do not work hard   This is the most common one, and it is the least useful. Italian professionals tend to take pride in their craft. They care about doing a task properly, not just quickly. Engineers, accountants, designers and sales people on Italian teams often put in real effort and think hard about quality.
The difference is in how effort is shown. In the US, visible busyness is often read as commitment. Fast replies, packed calendars and late-night messages signal dedication. In Italy, a person may be less visible but still deliver strong work. Judge output, not noise.
Stereotype: Long lunches mean lost time   Meals matter in Italy. Many colleagues will step away to eat properly and talk. An American manager may see this as slack. In practice, the meal is often where relationships form and problems get solved informally.
If you schedule a call over the lunch break, expect friction. If you join the table now and then, expect trust to grow faster than it would over a dozen status updates.
Stereotype: Everything is relaxed and informal   This one surprises people. Italian workplaces can be quite formal. Titles are used. First names may not be offered right away. Emails often open with a polite greeting and close with a courteous line. Skipping this can come across as cold or careless.
The warmth is real, but it comes after respect is shown. A US manager who jumps straight to casual language may lose some goodwill without knowing it.
Stereotype: Italians do not respect deadlines   Deadlines are real in Italy. What differs is how they are negotiated. Italian colleagues often prefer to talk through a deadline and adjust it by discussion. An American team may treat a date as fixed once it is written down. An Italian teammate may treat it as a point to revisit if circumstances change.
The fix is simple. State which deadlines are firm and why. Ask directly whether the plan is realistic. Do this early, not on the day before delivery.
Stereotype: Meetings are chaotic   Meetings in Italy can feel looser than in US companies. People may speak at the same time. Side conversations are common. The agenda may not be followed to the letter.
This does not always mean a lack of focus. Discussion is often how people reach agreement. Decisions may be shaped before and after the meeting, in smaller conversations. If you want clear outcomes, send a written summary afterward and confirm owners for each action. Most teams welcome this.
Stereotype: Italians are not direct   Americans often say Italians talk around the point. The reality is more mixed. Italians can be very expressive and open about opinions. They may also soften bad news in a way that sounds vague to a US ear.
If you need a clear yes or no, ask for it in plain words. Ask what could go wrong. Ask what support is needed. People usually answer honestly when the question is specific.
Stereotype: Time off is treated as sacred, so nothing gets done   Italian workers value their time away from work, and they expect to disconnect. This is part of the culture and it is protected by the way employment is set up in the country. A US manager who expects replies during holidays or evenings will meet resistance.
This is not laziness. It is a different view of balance. Teams that respect rest often see steadier performance across the year. Plan around absences instead of fighting them.
What to do as a US employer   A few habits help most.
Define outcomes clearly and leave room for the person to choose how to reach them. Use polite, formal tone at the start, then let the relationship relax over time. Mark firm deadlines as firm, and explain the reason. Follow every meeting with a short written summary. Ask specific questions when you need a direct answer. Respect time off and plan coverage ahead. None of this requires you to change your company. It asks you to read the signals correctly. Most conflicts between US managers and Italian staff come from misreading style as substance.
The practical side   Culture is one part of hiring in Italy. Pay, contributions and employer obligations are another. Understanding both helps you make a fair offer and plan your budget before you commit.

## What an Italian Employee Really Costs: The Employer Pension Share on Top of Gross Salary
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/italian-employee-cost-employer-pension-contributions.html
Summary: Employer pension contributions in Italy sit on top of gross pay. See the 23.81% share finance teams should add to an offer before setting a budget.
You agree a gross salary with a candidate in Italy. Finance builds a budget from that number. Months later the real cost is higher, and nobody can say why.
A large part of the gap is the employer pension contribution. It is easy to miss because it never shows up on the employee’s payslip as a deduction. It is a separate charge on you.
This article isolates that one item. It does not cover every cost of an Italian hire. It shows how big the pension share is and how to put it in the budget from day one.
Gross salary is not the cost of the hire   In the US, many teams think of salary as the base and benefits as the extras. In Italy, the employer’s social security charge is a core part of the cost. It is set by rule, not negotiated, and it is calculated on the employee’s taxable pay.
So an offer letter shows one number. The ledger shows that number plus the employer contributions. Finance needs to see both before the offer goes out.
The employer pension rate   The main pension charge is called IVS. It covers invalidity, old age and survivors’ benefits. The employer share is 23.81% of taxable pay.
That is the employer side only. It is separate from what the employee pays out of their own gross salary. The employee’s share reduces their take-home pay. Yours increases your cost.
The practical meaning is simple. Whatever gross salary you offer, add 23.81% of the taxable amount to get the cost of the pension line alone. This is before any other employer charge.
Where budgets go wrong   We see the same mistakes again and again.
Budgeting on gross only. The hiring manager approves a salary band. Finance books exactly that. The pension charge is not in the plan.
Treating it like a US payroll tax. The structure is different. The base is taxable pay, and the rate is much higher than many US teams expect. A rough mental shortcut from US payroll will understate the cost.
Forgetting it scales with every raise. The contribution moves with taxable pay. A salary increase raises the pension charge with it. A bonus that counts as taxable pay can do the same.
Comparing offers on the wrong basis. If you compare an Italian hire with a hire elsewhere, compare total employer cost, not gross pay. Gross pay hides the difference.
A note on the source   The 23.81% figure comes from a secondary source, a Italian tax and payroll information site. It is a reliable reference for planning. For a signed offer, have your payroll provider confirm the rate that applies to the specific role and contract. Rates can differ by employer category, so the confirmation step matters.
Other employer charges to keep on the list   Pension is not the only employer-side cost. There is also the workplace injury insurance premium paid to INAIL. The rate tables from 2019 remain in force. The way they are applied changed in 2026, so the premium your employer account pays may not match what an older guide tells you.
We do not put a figure on that premium here, because it depends on the type of work and on your own record. The point for finance is to keep it as its own line in the model, next to pension. Do not fold it into a generic percentage.
How to build the budget line   Use this order when you price an Italian hire:
Start with the gross salary you plan to offer. Identify the taxable pay base. Add the employer pension share of 23.81% of that base. Add the injury insurance premium as a separate line. Add the other employer charges your payroll provider lists. Compare the total with the budget the hiring manager was given. The gap between steps one and six is what finance needs to see. If the approved budget is close to the gross salary, the hire is under-funded from the first day.
What to do before the offer   Show the hiring manager two numbers side by side: the gross salary and the full employer cost. Get approval on the second one. This avoids a renegotiation after the candidate has already accepted.
Also ask your payroll provider for a written cost breakdown by line. You want pension, injury insurance and the remaining items separated. That makes variance reviews much easier later.
The pension share is predictable. It is a fixed rate on a known base. The surprise only happens when it is left out of the plan.

## What Italian Employees Expect From a US Employer
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/what-italian-employees-expect-from-us-employer.html
Summary: Italian hires judge a US employer on stability, clear communication and a visible path to grow. Here is what that means in practice for your first hires.
You found a strong engineer, designer or sales lead in Italy. They like the product and the pay is fair. Before they sign, they are asking themselves a quieter question: will this company still be here, and will it treat me well?
This article covers what Italian employees tend to expect from a US employer. It is not a legal guide. It is about the signals that decide whether a good candidate says yes and stays.
Stability comes first   US startup culture treats fast change as normal. Roles shift, teams reorganize, and people expect to move on after a few years. Many Italian professionals see work differently. A job is a long-term arrangement, and they weigh it against family, housing and local ties.
That does not mean they avoid risk. It means they want to understand the risk. A candidate who hears “we are moving fast, nothing is fixed” may hear “this job may vanish.”
What helps:
Say clearly how the company is funded and where it is heading, in plain terms. Put the employment terms in writing before the start date, in a form the candidate can read and check. Be open about how the role may change. Explain what is likely, not just what is possible. Avoid vague promises. A modest commitment you keep is worth more than a big one you drop. An open-ended employment contract signals that you see the person as part of the company’s future. A fixed or short arrangement can read as a lack of confidence, even when you do not mean it that way.
Pay and benefits must be predictable   Italian employees expect payroll to be correct, on time and easy to read. They notice mistakes, and they remember them. A late or wrong payslip damages trust faster than almost any other error.
Expect questions about the full package, not only the headline salary. Candidates often compare total compensation, time off, and the benefits that come with the role. If your offer is built around equity and a base that looks low next to local norms, explain the logic. Do not assume the candidate will fill the gaps in your favor.
If you hire through an Employer of Record, tell the employee how it works. Who is the legal employer on paper? Who do they call with a payroll question? Who manages their day-to-day work? Clear answers remove a lot of worry before it starts.
Communication: direct, but not careless   US teams often prize speed and informality. First names, short messages, quick calls. Italian colleagues usually adapt well, but a few habits matter.
Be explicit about expectations. Do not rely on hints. Say what good work looks like, who decides what, and how you will measure results.
Respect working hours. Your team may be spread across several time zones. Messages sent late in the Italian evening, with an expectation of an instant reply, wear people down. Agree on overlap hours and stick to them.
Give feedback in private, and give it early. Public criticism lands badly. Regular one-to-one conversations work better than a surprise review at the end of the year.
Explain decisions. If priorities change, say why. People accept hard news better than silence.
Watch the language gap. Many Italian professionals work well in English, but writing in a second language takes more effort. Keep your messages simple. Avoid slang and sports metaphors. Follow up a call with a short written summary.
Growth needs a visible path   A US employer with no local office can look like a place where a career stalls. The candidate may wonder who will notice their work, and whether the best roles go to people in the home country.
You can address this directly:
Name a manager who will advocate for them, not just assign tasks. Describe what progress looks like in this role and what the next step could be. Offer training, conferences or a learning budget, and honor it when the time comes. Include them in company meetings and decisions at a reasonable hour for their time zone. Let them work on projects that matter, not only on support tasks. Italian professionals often value expertise and craft. They want to be seen as skilled, not just as a cost-effective hire. Recognition of that skill matters as much as a title.
Respect for time off and life outside work   Paid leave and rest are taken seriously. A team member who disappears for a long summer break is not being lazy. That is a normal part of the work culture. Plan around it. Do not make people feel guilty for using what they are entitled to.
The same applies to sick days and family needs. A manager who handles these with calm and kindness earns lasting loyalty. One who pushes back creates quiet resentment.
Show that you understand the local setup   The fastest way to build trust is to show you did your homework. Know that Italy has its own rules for employment, payroll and benefits. You do not need to be an expert. You need to show respect for the process and a willingness to ask.
When something local comes up, say “let me check how that works in Italy.” Do not say “that’s not how we do it.” The first answer builds confidence. The second ends the conversation.
A short checklist for founders   Put the terms in writing early and keep them clear. Explain the structure of employment, including the role of any Employer of Record. Pay accurately and on time, every time. Set communication norms and working hours up front. Give regular, private feedback. Define a growth path with a named manager. Respect leave and personal time. Ask about local practice before you assume. None of this is complicated. It asks for consistency more than effort. Candidates who feel secure and respected stay longer, work better and recommend you to others.

## Where to Find Tech Talent in Italy: Channels That Actually Work
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/where-to-find-tech-talent-in-italy.html
Summary: Job boards, communities, universities and referrals compared. A practical guide for US teams hiring engineers in Italy.
Hiring engineers in Italy is not hard because talent is scarce. It is hard because US teams look in the wrong places. The channels that work in San Francisco or New York do not always work in Milan, Turin or Rome.
This guide compares four channels: job boards, communities, universities and referrals. Each has a clear use. Each has a clear limit.
Job boards   Job boards are the default starting point. They are fast to set up and they reach a wide audience.
LinkedIn is the main board for mid-level and senior engineers. Most Italian tech professionals keep a profile there. Recruiters from large firms and startups all post there, so you compete for attention. Expect many applicants and a lot of noise.
Local boards reach different people. Italian engineers also browse national job sites and tech-specific boards. Some candidates never update LinkedIn but do check these sites.
What works: A post written in both English and Italian. A clear salary range. A named hiring manager. Italian candidates often distrust postings that hide pay or the real employer.
What fails: A generic US job description with no mention of location, contract type or working hours. Candidates want to know if the role is remote, hybrid or on-site. They also want to know who employs them.
Best for: Volume hiring and roles with clear titles, such as backend, frontend or QA.
Communities   Communities are slower, but the quality is higher. Italy has active developer groups, meetups and online forums. Many cover specific stacks like Python, Rust, JavaScript, data engineering or DevOps.
You can find people through:
Local meetups in larger cities Slack and Discord groups for specific languages Open source projects with Italian maintainers Conferences and hackathons The rule is simple: contribute before you recruit. Answer questions. Sponsor an event. Share a technical blog post from your team. Members notice when a company only shows up to post a job.
Best for: Niche skills, senior engineers and passive candidates who are not actively applying.
Limit: It takes months to build a reputation. This channel does not fix an urgent vacancy.
Universities   Italy has strong technical universities, and several produce graduates with solid engineering fundamentals. Polytechnic schools in Milan and Turin are well known for this. Many other universities have good computer science and engineering programs.
How to work with them:
Contact career offices directly Offer internships that can convert to full-time roles Give a guest lecture or run a workshop Sponsor a student project or competition Universities are the best source of junior talent. Graduates are often eager to join international teams and learn English-speaking workflows.
Limit: Juniors need mentoring. If your Italian team will be one or two people, you may not have the capacity to train. Also, a US company with no local presence can look unfamiliar to career offices. Be ready to explain who you are and how the hire will work.
Best for: Junior hires and a steady pipeline over time.
Referrals   Referrals are often the best channel for quality. They work well in Italy because professional networks are tight. Engineers know who is good, and they know who is looking.
Start with your first hire. A strong first engineer in Italy will bring in others. Give them a clear process for introducing people. Make the interview fair and fast. Reward referrals in a way that fits local norms, such as a bonus paid after the new hire completes the probation period.
What works: Asking your existing Italian team, advisors and investors for introductions. Asking engineers in other countries if they know Italians who want to work with you.
Limit: Referrals depend on who you already have. If you have no one in Italy, you have no network to tap. They can also narrow diversity if you rely on them alone.
Best for: Senior roles and cultural fit after the first hire is in place.
How to combine them   No single channel is enough. A practical mix looks like this:
Start with a job board to get the first applicants and test the market. Join two or three communities in your stack while the search runs. Hire the first engineer and ask them for referrals. Add university contacts once you need junior roles and have someone to mentor them. This order matches how trust builds. Boards give speed. Communities give reputation. Referrals give quality. Universities give a pipeline.
The employer question   Candidates will ask who their employer is. A US company without an Italian entity cannot easily hire locally, and many engineers will hesitate to join without a proper Italian contract, local payroll and social contributions. Be ready with a clear answer before the first interview.
An Employer of Record (EOR) can employ the person in Italy on your behalf while you direct the daily work. This lets you hire without setting up a company first. Explain this early. It removes a common reason for candidates to drop out.
Practical tips   Write job posts in English and Italian. Publish the pay range and contract type. Reply to applicants quickly. Slow answers lose good people. Offer a technical interview in English, with an Italian-speaking interviewer if possible. Explain benefits in local terms. Italian employees expect things like paid leave and a statutory end-of-service payment. Summary   Channel Speed Quality Best for Job boards Fast Mixed Volume, standard roles Communities Slow High Niche, senior talent Universities Medium Good for juniors Junior pipeline Referrals Medium High Senior, cultural fit Pick the channels that match your timeline and your seniority needs. Then be clear about who the employer is and how the contract works.

## Why Italian Salaries Are Quoted Gross Annual (RAL) and How to Read Them
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/italian-salary-ral-gross-annual-explained.html
Summary: RAL is the gross annual salary Italian candidates quote and negotiate on. Learn how to read it, how monthly installments work, and what it means for cost.
If you hire in Italy, you will hear the term RAL early. It stands for Retribuzione Annua Lorda. In English, gross annual salary. Candidates use it in interviews, on CVs and in offer talks. Almost nobody quotes a net monthly figure.
This article explains what RAL covers, why the market works this way, and how to avoid common misreads.
What RAL means   RAL is the total gross pay an employee earns in a year, before income tax and before the employee’s share of social security contributions. It is the contractual base number. It is not what lands in the bank account.
RAL usually does not include the employer’s own costs. Employer social security contributions, severance accrual and insurance sit on top. So RAL is not the cost to the company either. It sits in the middle: higher than take-home pay, lower than total employer cost.
Why Italy quotes gross   Three reasons explain the habit.
The national collective agreement for the sector sets pay levels in gross terms. Job grades, minimum pay and many allowances are written as gross amounts. Candidates compare offers against that frame.
Net pay is personal. It depends on family situation, tax deductions, regional and municipal surcharges and other individual factors. Two people with the same RAL can take home different amounts. Gross is the only figure that is comparable across people.
Gross is also stable. Tax rules and contribution rates change over time. A gross figure written in a contract stays clear even when the net result moves.
Monthly installments are not always a simple split   US teams often divide the annual figure by the number of calendar months and call it the monthly salary. In Italy this can be wrong.
Many contracts pay the annual gross in more installments than there are calendar months. The extra installments are usually paid at set times of the year, often around the end-of-year holidays and in summer. The exact structure depends on the applicable collective agreement and the contract.
This matters for two reasons.
First, the monthly gross on a payslip can be lower than a simple division suggests. A candidate who says their RAL is a certain amount is describing the yearly total. The regular monthly payment is a fraction of that total, and the extra installments make up the rest.
Second, cash flow in the year is uneven for the employee and for the company. Payroll costs rise in the months when the extra installments are paid. Finance teams should model that in their forecast.
Always ask which installment structure the offer assumes. State it in the offer letter so there is no confusion.
Why candidates negotiate on gross   Negotiating on net sounds simpler, but it shifts risk. If the employer promises a net figure, any change in tax or contributions becomes the employer’s problem. Few companies accept that.
Negotiating on RAL keeps the conversation clean. The candidate asks for a gross number. The employer decides if it fits the budget. Net pay follows from the rules, and the candidate can estimate it with a simple tool.
It also helps to know that candidates often compare RAL across offers and against what peers earn. A gross figure that looks low next to the market will lose the candidate, even if the benefits package is strong. Benefits such as meal vouchers, health cover or a company car are usually discussed next to RAL, not inside it. Make clear whether a benefit is part of the gross figure or on top.
How to read an Italian offer   Use this short checklist.
Confirm the figure is gross annual. Ask how many installments the year is split into. Check which collective agreement applies and what it adds. Separate fixed pay from variable pay. A bonus is not part of the base unless the contract says so. List benefits and say if they are on top of RAL. Ask your payroll provider for the full employer cost, not only RAL. What this means for your budget   When a hiring manager says a candidate wants a certain RAL, that is only the start. The real cost to the company includes employer contributions, severance accrual, insurance and any benefits. Budgets built on RAL alone will fall short.
The reverse mistake is common too. Some founders convert RAL to a monthly figure, compare it with a US salary and conclude that Italy is cheap or expensive. The comparison only works when you place both on the same basis: total employer cost against total employer cost.
Key takeaway   RAL is a gross yearly figure. It is the shared language of Italian hiring. Learn to read it, ask about installments and benefits, and always convert it to full employer cost before you decide.

## Work Permit Quotas for Non-EU Hires in Italy in 2026
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/work-permit-quotas-non-eu-hires-italy-2026.html
Summary: Italy set 43,300 non-seasonal entry quotas for non-EU workers in 2026. See how they split and what US employers should plan for before hiring.
If you plan to hire a non-EU national to work in Italy, quotas may decide your timeline. Italy caps how many non-EU workers can enter each year under the flows decree. This article explains the 2026 numbers and what they mean for your hiring plan.
The decree behind the numbers   The current framework is DPCM 02/10/2025. It covers the period 2026-28. Each year in that period has its own quota. This article looks at 2026 only.
The figures below come from a secondary source that reports the split of non-seasonal quotas. Check them against the official text before you commit to a plan.
2026 non-seasonal quotas   The total for non-seasonal entries in 2026 is 43,300. The decree splits it into three groups:
25,000 for workers from countries covered by article 6, paragraph 2, letter a of the decree. 18,000 for workers from countries that have agreements with Italy. 300 for stateless persons and refugees. The three groups add up to 43,300.
Notice how the quota is divided. Most of it goes to two groups. The first depends on the country list in the decree. The second depends on bilateral agreements. The third group is very small.
What we could not confirm   The source we used does not give figures for seasonal work. It also does not give figures for entries outside the quota. We do not quote numbers for those categories. If your hire may fall into one of them, ask for the current official figures.
What this means for your hire   Your candidate’s nationality matters. It decides which group of the quota applies. Before you make an offer, find out where the candidate holds citizenship. Then check whether that country appears in the decree’s list or in the agreements group.
A candidate from a country outside both groups may face a harder path. Do not assume a quota place exists just because the total looks large.
Quotas are also a shared pool. Many employers in Italy compete for the same places. A late application can find the allocation used up. Plan early and prepare documents before the application window opens.
The quota is only one step. After entry approval, the worker still needs a visa and, after arrival, a residence permit. Each step has its own paperwork and waiting time. Build slack into your start date.
Practical steps for US founders and HR teams   Confirm the candidate’s citizenship and check it against the quota groups. Ask whether the role fits the non-seasonal category. Gather the employer and candidate documents early. Set a realistic start date that allows for visa and permit steps. Keep a fallback plan, such as hiring a candidate who already has the right to work in Italy. Why an Employer of Record helps   A US company usually has no Italian entity. That is a problem for work permit applications, which need an employer in Italy. An Employer of Record (EOR) can act as the Italian employer on paper. It handles the hiring, the payroll and the permit paperwork. You direct the daily work. The EOR carries the employer duties in Italy.
This does not remove the quota. A non-EU hire still needs a place under the decree. What an EOR changes is who submits the file and who answers to the Italian authorities. For a small team without local staff, that is often the difference between a hire that starts on time and one that stalls.
Bottom line   Italy has 43,300 non-seasonal places for non-EU workers in 2026. Most sit in two groups, 25,000 and 18,000. A small share of 300 is set aside for stateless persons and refugees. Know which group your candidate falls into, apply early, and verify every figure with the official text.

## Working for a Foreign Company in Italy: Answers for Candidates
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/working-for-foreign-company-in-italy-candidate-faq.html
Summary: A plain FAQ HR teams can share with candidates who would work in Italy for a foreign employer: contract, pay, benefits, leave, tax and who to call.
Candidates in Italy often hesitate when the employer is based abroad. They worry about who actually employs them, which rules apply and who they can call when something goes wrong. This FAQ answers those questions in plain terms. HR can share it as is.
It is general information, not legal advice. Your contract and the collective agreement that applies to your role set the details.
Who is my employer?   That depends on how the company hires in Italy. It may have its own Italian entity. It may use an Employer of Record (EOR). With an EOR, the EOR is your legal employer on paper. It signs your contract, runs payroll and handles social security. Your day-to-day work, goals and manager stay with the foreign company.
Either way, you get an Italian employment contract. Ask HR to tell you clearly which entity signs it.
Will I have a proper Italian contract?   Yes. Employment in Italy is built on written contracts that follow Italian law. Most roles also fall under a national collective agreement (CCNL). It sets things like minimum pay, working hours, leave, notice periods and extra benefits. Ask which agreement applies to your role. It tells you a lot about what to expect.
Does Italian labor law still protect me if the company is foreign?   Yes. If you work in Italy, Italian rules on working time, leave, termination and workplace safety apply. A foreign headquarters does not change that. The contract cannot take these protections away.
Who pays my salary, and in what currency?   You are paid in euros into an Italian bank account. Payroll is run under Italian rules, whether by the Italian entity or by the EOR. You receive a payslip that shows your gross pay, deductions and net pay. Salary offers are often quoted as gross annual pay. Ask HR to confirm whether a number is gross or net, and how many payments per year the contract uses.
What about taxes and social security?   The employer withholds income tax and social security contributions from your pay and sends them to the Italian authorities. You usually do not file the same way a freelancer does. Your payslip shows what was withheld. If you have other income or special circumstances, a local tax adviser can help. Your employer’s payroll provider can explain how your own payslip is built.
What benefits can I expect?   Italian employment comes with statutory protections, including health coverage through the national system, pension contributions and a severance fund that builds up while you work. Many contracts add benefits through the collective agreement. Companies can also offer meal vouchers, supplementary health insurance, equity or bonuses. Ask HR for a full list in writing.
How does leave work?   You are entitled to paid annual leave, public holidays, sick leave and protected family leave. The exact amounts come from the law, your collective agreement and your contract. A foreign company’s home policy does not replace these. If the company offers more generous leave than Italian rules require, the better terms apply.
Can I work remotely?   Often yes, but agree it in writing. Remote work arrangements should state where you work, which equipment you get and how working hours are tracked. If you plan to work from another country for long periods, tell HR first. It can change your tax and social security position.
What language will work be in?   Many foreign companies work in English. Your contract and official documents will usually be in Italian, sometimes with an English version. Ask for a copy in a language you are comfortable with before you sign, and ask which version prevails if they differ.
What if I need a visa or work permit?   Citizens of the European Union can work in Italy without a permit. Other candidates may need authorization before they can start. Your employer should explain the process, who handles the paperwork and what the timeline looks like. Do not resign from your current job or relocate until the right to work is confirmed.
Who do I call when I have a problem?   Ask this before you accept. You should know who handles payroll questions, who handles contract questions and who is your day-to-day manager. With an EOR, payroll and contract questions go to the EOR. Work questions go to your manager at the foreign company. A good employer can name these contacts on the first call.
What happens if the arrangement ends?   Termination follows Italian rules, including notice and final settlement. If the company changes how it employs people in Italy, for example by opening its own entity, your rights should carry over. Ask HR how that transfer would work.
What should I ask HR before signing?   Which entity is my legal employer? Which collective agreement applies? Is the offered pay gross or net, and how is it paid out over the year? What benefits are included, and where are they written down? What are the notice terms? Who is my contact for payroll and contract issues? What are the remote work terms? A clear answer to each question is a good sign. Vague answers are worth a follow-up.

## Working Hours, Overtime and the Right to Disconnect in Italy: Scheduling Across US and Italy Time Zones
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/working-hours-overtime-right-to-disconnect-italy.html
Summary: How working hours, overtime and disconnection work for Italian employees, and how to schedule a team that spans US and Italy time zones without breaking the rules.
US teams often hire in Italy and then run it like a US team. Calls land late in the Italian evening. Slack pings arrive at night. Overtime is treated as a favor. This causes friction fast.
This article explains how to think about working hours in Italy and how to set norms that work across the Atlantic. It is a practical guide, not legal advice. Specific limits depend on the national collective agreement (CCNL) that applies to the role, so always check it.
Hours are set by law and by the CCNL   Italy regulates working time through national law and then fills in the details through the CCNL. The CCNL decides many things you would expect to find in an offer letter:
The normal weekly schedule. How overtime is defined and paid. Rest breaks during the day. Rules for night work, weekends and holidays. Whether time off can be banked instead of paid. The practical point is simple. Do not copy your US handbook. Find out which CCNL covers your employee, and read the working time chapter before you agree on a schedule.
Overtime is not informal   In the US, exempt employees absorb extra hours without a second thought. In Italy, extra hours are a defined category. They usually need to be requested or authorized, tracked, and compensated in the way the CCNL says. That can mean extra pay, a pay premium, or time off in lieu.
Three habits help:
Ask for approval before overtime, in writing, even by a short message. Record the hours. Do not rely on memory at month end. Tell the employee how extra hours will be compensated before they happen. If your company culture expects regular after-hours work, say so in the contract terms and price it into the cost of the hire. Surprises here become disputes later.
Rest is a protected value   Italian employment law gives real weight to rest between working days and to weekly rest. A manager in New York who schedules a late call for an Italian employee and then expects an early start the next day may be creating a rest problem. This is not just a courtesy issue. It can become a compliance issue for the employer.
The lesson for cross-border teams is to plan the whole day, not only the call. If the Italian employee works late for you on Tuesday, the Wednesday schedule has to account for it.
The right to disconnect   Italy has recognized disconnection mainly in the context of remote work, often called smart working or agile work. The idea is that an employee can step away from digital tools outside working hours without penalty. In practice, the written remote work agreement is where employers describe rest periods and the technical and organizational measures that make disconnection real.
You do not need a long policy. You need clear norms that your US managers will follow:
Define core hours when the employee is expected to be reachable. State that messages sent outside those hours do not require an answer until the next working period. Do not reward or punish people based on out-of-hours responsiveness. Use scheduled send for messages written in the US evening. The last point matters most. Many US managers write at the end of their day, which is the middle of the Italian night. A scheduled send costs nothing and removes the problem.
Scheduling across time zones   The overlap between the US and Italy is narrow. For East Coast teams, it sits in the Italian afternoon. For West Coast teams, it is smaller still, and it pushes into the Italian evening. This is where most problems start.
Use these norms:
Protect the overlap. Put live meetings in the shared window and keep that window for work that truly needs a conversation. Make the rest asynchronous. Status updates, reviews and decisions should work through written documents. Record important calls and share notes. Rotate the pain. If a recurring meeting must fall outside normal hours for one side, alternate which side bears it. Do not make the Italian employee the permanent late-night participant. Set an end time for the Italian day. Agree on the latest hour a regular call can run. Treat exceptions as exceptions. Be careful at clock changes. The US and Europe shift their clocks on different dates, so the gap between the two changes for a short period. Check recurring invites during those weeks. Respect local holidays. Italy has public holidays that do not match US ones. Keep a shared calendar so no one schedules a launch on a day when the Italian team is off. Put it in writing   A short working-time note, attached to the employment documents or shared as an internal guide, prevents most conflicts. It should cover core hours, the meeting window, how overtime is approved and paid, and the disconnection norm. Keep it to a page.
This also helps your finance team. Predictable hours mean predictable overtime cost, and fewer disputes mean fewer legal expenses. If you use an Employer of Record (EOR), ask your provider to confirm the CCNL rules for the specific role so your policy matches what the contract requires.
The short version   In Italy, working time is structured, tracked and tied to the CCNL. Overtime needs a process. Rest is protected. Disconnection is expected, especially in remote work. For US teams, the fix is mostly habit: protect a small overlap, work asynchronously, and stop treating after-hours availability as a default.
