## Workplace Health and Safety Duties in Italy for Remote and Office Staff
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/italy-workplace-health-safety-remote-office-employees.html
Summary: What a foreign employer must do in Italy on risk assessment, safety training and remote work, and how an Employer of Record helps you stay compliant.
If you hire in Italy, you take on health and safety duties from the day your employee starts. This applies to office staff and to people who work from home. Italy treats safety as an employer obligation, not a favor. The rules are broad, and the paperwork is real.
This article explains what US founders, HR teams and finance and legal ops leads need to know. It covers risk assessment, training and the specific duties for remote work.
Who carries the duty   The employer carries it. That means the legal entity that holds the employment contract. If you have no Italian entity, you cannot easily meet these duties on your own. The employer of record model solves this because the EOR is the legal employer in Italy. It owns the safety obligations on paper and in practice, while you direct the daily work.
You still have a role. You must give accurate information about how and where the person works. You must also follow the safety instructions the EOR passes on to you.
Risk assessment   Italian law requires a written risk assessment. The employer must identify the hazards in the workplace, judge how serious they are, and set out measures to reduce them. The document must be kept and updated when work conditions change.
For a typical office job, the hazards are familiar. They include screen work, posture, lighting, electrical equipment, fire safety and stress. The assessment should cover each of these in plain terms.
The law also expects the employer to name a few key roles. These include a head of the prevention and protection service, workers’ safety representatives, and people trained for first aid and fire response. Depending on the risks, an occupational physician may also be needed. That physician runs health surveillance for workers whose roles call for it.
A foreign company rarely has any of this in place. An EOR usually does, and it can attach your employee to its existing structure.
Safety training   Every employee must receive safety training. The training must match the real risks of the job. A software engineer and a warehouse operator do not need the same course.
Training has a general part and a part specific to the role. It must be delivered at hiring, and it must be refreshed when duties change or when new risks appear. The employer must keep records of who was trained and when.
Training is not optional, and a signed document alone is not enough. Inspectors and courts look at whether the training was real and suited to the person. If an accident happens, missing training records weigh heavily against the employer.
Practical points for your team:
Tell your EOR early about the actual tasks the person will do. Flag any travel, equipment or site visits that change the risk profile. Make sure the employee has time to complete training during working hours. Keep proof of completion in the personnel file. Remote work and smart working   Many US companies hire Italians to work from home. Italy has a framework for this, usually called smart working or agile work. It does not remove safety duties. It changes how they are met.
The arrangement is set in a written agreement between employer and employee. That agreement should cover how the work is done, the tools used, and how the employer can give instructions. It should also address rest periods and the right to disconnect.
On safety, the employer must give the remote worker a written information notice. The notice explains the general risks tied to working outside the company premises. It also gives guidance on how to set up a safe workspace and how to work safely. Employers are expected to update it when the situation changes, and to deliver it on a regular basis.
The employee has a duty too. They must cooperate in applying the safety measures and follow the instructions in the notice. Employers do not inspect a private home the way they inspect an office. So the law relies on clear information and on the worker’s cooperation.
Equipment matters. If you provide a laptop, monitor or chair, the employer is responsible for supplying equipment that is safe and fit for use. Define who supplies what in the agreement, and keep it in writing.
Accidents and insurance   Work accidents are reported to the Italian national insurer for work injuries. The employer registers the employee with this insurer and pays the contributions. Accidents on the way to work and accidents in a remote setting can also raise questions about coverage. Your EOR handles registration and reporting. You should tell them quickly if anything happens.
Common mistakes   Foreign companies tend to make the same errors:
Assuming remote staff fall outside the safety rules. Skipping the written risk assessment because the team is small. Treating training as a one-time task. Leaving the remote-work notice out of the onboarding pack. Failing to pass on changes in the job to the legal employer. Each of these can lead to penalties and, in a serious case, personal liability for the people responsible. The fix is simple. Keep documents current, train people properly and keep communication open with the legal employer.
What to do now   Before your first Italian hire starts, ask your EOR for the risk assessment that covers the role. Confirm who the safety officers are. Schedule training for the start date. For a remote hire, sign the smart-working agreement and send the safety information notice with the contract.
Do this once, and the process repeats for every hire after that.

## Year-End Checklist for US Companies With Italian Employees
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/articles/year-end-checklist-us-companies-italian-employees.html
Summary: A practical year-end checklist for US companies with Italian staff: bonuses, leave balances, performance reviews and employee data. Plain steps, no surprises.
Year-end in a US company usually means bonus approvals, review cycles and a payroll cleanup. With Italian employees, the same tasks follow different rules. Some deadlines come earlier than you expect. Some payments you never planned for are already owed.
This checklist covers the four areas that cause the most trouble: bonuses, leave balances, reviews and data. Use it as a starting point for a conversation with your payroll provider or employer of record.
Bonuses and extra pay   Start with what is already promised. Italian employment contracts sit under a national collective agreement (CCNL). Many of these agreements require extra salary payments on top of the regular monthly pay. Your US team may not know they exist. If you hired through an offer letter written in the US style, check that these payments were budgeted.
Then look at discretionary bonuses.
Confirm whether the bonus is contractual or truly discretionary. If it was paid repeatedly and employees expect it, it may be treated as part of pay. Decide the amount and the payment month before the payroll cut-off, not after. Ask how the bonus is taxed and what social contributions apply. The employer cost is higher than the amount the employee sees. Keep a written record of the criteria. Vague criteria lead to disputes. A US-style equity or stock grant needs its own review. Tax and reporting treatment in Italy can differ from the US, for both the employee and the employer. Do not wait until the vesting date to find out.
Leave balances   US companies often treat unused vacation as use-it-or-lose-it, or they pay it out under a policy. Italy works differently. Employees have a statutory right to paid leave, and unused leave does not simply disappear because the calendar turns.
Before year-end:
Pull the current leave balance for each Italian employee. Check what your CCNL and the employment contract say about carry-over. Look at other kinds of paid time off, such as permits and special leave. These are often tracked separately from vacation. Plan time off with managers now. Leave pushed into the new year builds up and creates cost and scheduling problems later. If an employee leaves, accrued leave and other deferred pay are settled in the final payment. Track them throughout the year so the figure is never a surprise.
Performance reviews   Reviews are fine in Italy. The risk is in how they are used.
Keep reviews factual and tied to the role and agreed goals. Do not use review scores as the sole basis for a pay cut or a demotion. Changes to duties or pay need a proper legal process. Write down feedback and share it with the employee. Documented, consistent feedback protects both sides if a dispute ever arises. Keep forced ranking and anonymous peer scoring under review. They can raise data protection and fairness questions. If a raise follows the review, check whether the collective agreement sets minimum pay levels for the role. A raise may be needed just to stay compliant. Deliver the review in a language the employee is comfortable with. A rushed video call from a different time zone is not a good setting for hard feedback.
Employee data   Year-end is when HR data gets exported, copied and emailed. For Italian employees, that data falls under EU data protection rules.
Limit who in the US can see Italian payroll files, review notes and medical or leave information. Use secure systems, not email attachments or shared spreadsheets. Make sure employees know what data you hold and why. Update notices if you added a new HR tool this year. Check that the legal basis for transferring data to the US is in place. Delete data you no longer need, according to a retention rule you can explain. Also confirm that basic records are current: address, tax details, bank account, emergency contact and any change in family status. Errors here lead to payroll corrections in the new year.
Other items to close out   Review each employee’s contract against actual duties. Drift over the year is common. Check that expense reimbursements and benefits are documented and processed correctly. Confirm any filings and payments your payroll provider needs from you before the holiday period. Italian offices slow down around year-end, so late requests wait. Set the budget for next year with the full employer cost in mind, not just base salary. A simple way to work   Do not try to handle all of this in one meeting. Assign each area to one owner. Finance takes bonuses and budget. HR takes leave and reviews. Legal or your provider takes data and contract checks. Set a date for each, and leave buffer time before payroll closes.
Most year-end problems in Italy come from assuming US practice applies. A short review now costs far less than a correction later.

## Employing in Italy vs the US
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/italy-vs-us.html
Summary: How employing someone in Italy differs from the US: termination, notice, leave, health care, payroll taxes, severance, 13th month and non-compete.
 Payroll guide Employing in Italy vs the US The main differences a US company runs into when it hires its first person in Italy. Most of the rules come from the national collective agreement for the sector, not from the employment contract.
TopicUnited StatesItaly Ending employmentAt-will in most states: either side can end it at any time, for any lawful reason.Dismissal needs a valid reason: just cause, or a justified objective or subjective reason. Unfair dismissal can lead to compensation or reinstatement.Notice periodNot required by federal law.Set by the collective agreement (CCNL), based on level and seniority. Typically from a few weeks to several months.ProbationNo legal concept; at-will applies from day one.Allowed if written in the contract. Length set by the CCNL, up to 6 months. Either side can end it without notice.Paid vacationNo federal minimum.4 weeks per year minimum, at least 2 taken in the year they accrue. CCNLs often add paid leave hours (ROL).Sick leaveNo federal paid sick leave; some states and cities require it.Paid sick leave with a medical certificate, covered partly by INPS and partly by the employer as set by the CCNL. Job protected for a period set by the CCNL.Parental leaveFMLA: 12 weeks unpaid, for eligible employees only.Maternity: 5 months mandatory, paid. Paternity: 10 working days, paid. Additional optional parental leave, partly paid.Health insuranceUsually employer-provided and a major cost.National health service for everyone, funded by general taxation. Not an employer cost. Some CCNLs add a supplementary health fund.SeveranceNone required by law.TFR: about 6.91% of annual pay set aside every year and paid when employment ends, for any reason.13th month salaryNot required.Mandatory under every CCNL, paid in December. Some CCNLs add a 14th, paid in June or July.Working hoursFLSA: overtime after 40 hours for non-exempt staff; no cap on hours.Normal week is 40 hours. Average including overtime cannot exceed 48 hours. Many CCNLs set fewer normal hours.Non-competeVaries by state; some ban it.Valid only if written, paid, and limited in time (max 3 years, 5 for executives), place and activity. General comparison for orientation. US rules vary by state. Italian figures depend on the CCNL applied to the role.
What this means for your budget In the US the big extra costs are health insurance and benefits. In Italy they are social contributions, the 13th month and the TFR. Health care is not on your bill. Put together, the total cost of an Italian employee is usually well above gross salary, and it is predictable: it follows the CCNL tables.
What this means for planning Italian employment is designed to be stable. Ending it takes a reason and follows a procedure. Use the probation period properly, write clear role descriptions, and plan notice periods into any change of plans.

## FAQ for US Companies
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/faq.html
Summary: 25 answers for US companies hiring in Italy through an Employer of Record: process, costs, employment rules, equity, benefits and data.
 FAQ Questions US companies ask us Short answers. For anything specific to your role, ask us directly.
How it works What is an Employer of Record?A company that legally employs someone on your behalf. We hold the Italian employment contract and run payroll. You direct the work.
Do we need an Italian entity?No. That is the point of the service.
Who manages the employee day to day?You do: tasks, schedule, goals, tools, reviews.
How fast can someone start?Usually within days of a signed offer for EU citizens. Visa cases take longer, depending on the permit.
Can we convert an existing contractor?Yes. We move them to an employment contract, typically within 30 days.
Can we hire part-time or fixed-term?Yes. Both are standard in Italy, with limits on fixed-term duration and renewals.
Costs and billing What does it cost?€250 per employee per month, plus the employment cost billed monthly on actuals.
What is in the employment cost?Gross salary, employer social contributions, 13th month (and 14th where applicable), TFR, CCNL funds, and any benefits or expenses you approve.
What currency do you invoice in?US dollars, from our US company.
How much more than salary does an employee cost?It depends on salary and CCNL. Employer contributions are around 30%, plus 13th month and TFR. Use the calculator for a specific number.
Is there a deposit?What about visas?€2,500 per case for the work permit and visa process.
Can you run payroll if we already have an Italian company?Yes, at €55 per payslip.
Employment rules Can we terminate at will?No. Dismissal needs a valid reason and a procedure. Probation, up to 6 months depending on the CCNL, is the period when either side can end it freely.
How much vacation do employees get?At least 4 weeks a year, plus public holidays. CCNLs often add more paid hours off.
Do we need to provide health insurance?No. Italy has a national health service funded by taxes. Some CCNLs include a supplementary health fund, which is part of the cost.
What is the TFR?Severance pay set aside every year (about 6.91% of pay) and paid when employment ends.
What is a CCNL?The national collective agreement for the sector. It sets minimum pay, levels, hours, notice and many benefits.
Can we include a non-compete?Yes, if it is written, paid, and limited in time, place and scope.
Who owns the employee's work?Your company. Our contracts include an IP assignment and confidentiality clause.
Equity, benefits and data Can the employee join our stock plan?Which benefits are common?Meal vouchers (tax-free up to €10 a day if electronic), company car, supplementary pension and health, and fringe benefits up to €1,000 a year (€2,000 with dependent children).
Where is employee data stored?On our servers in the EU, under GDPR.
Can the employee work from another country?Short trips are fine. Working from another country for longer changes where tax and contributions are due, so tell us first.
What happens if we later open our own entity?We transfer employees to it without losing seniority, and help with the company setup through our partners.

## For Employees Hired Through HiringItaly
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/employees.html
Summary: For people hired in Italy through HiringItaly: your Italian contract, payslip, INPS, TFR, 13th month, leave, and answers to common questions.
 For employees You have been hired through HiringItaly A company abroad wants you on its team and has asked us to employ you in Italy. You work for them. We make sure you are paid and protected like any employee in Italy.
Italian contractA written employment contract under the CCNL for your sector, with your level, salary, hours and probation period.
Monthly payslipPaid every month, with tax and contributions already withheld. You get a clear payslip you can use for loans or rentals.
INPS contributionsYour pension and social security build up in Italy. You are covered for sickness, maternity and unemployment.
TFRAbout 6.91% of your yearly pay is set aside as severance and paid when you leave, or moved to a pension fund if you choose.
13th monthAn extra month's pay in December. Your CCNL may add a 14th in summer.
LeaveAt least 4 weeks of paid vacation, public holidays, paid sick leave, maternity and paternity leave.
Questions employees ask Who is my employer?EmployItaly is your legal employer in Italy. You work day to day for the company that hired you: they set your tasks, team and goals. We handle your contract, payslip, taxes and contributions.
Is this a real Italian employment contract?Yes. Same contract type, same national collective agreement (CCNL) and same rights as any employee of an Italian company.
When do I get paid?Every month, by bank transfer to your Italian or EU account, with a payslip. The pay date is in your contract.
Do I pay taxes myself?No. Income tax and your share of contributions are withheld from your pay. Every year you receive the CU certificate. You file a tax return only if you have other income or want to claim deductions.
Does my pension build up?Yes. Contributions go to INPS like for any Italian employee and count toward your pension.
What happens when I leave?You receive your TFR, unused leave and the accrued share of the 13th month. If you are dismissed you may be entitled to unemployment benefit (NASpI) under the usual rules.
Can I work from home?Yes, if agreed with the company. We put the remote work agreement in writing.
Who do I call if something is wrong with my payslip?Us. You get a direct contact in our payroll team, in Italian or English.
What if I am not an EU citizen?We handle the work permit and visa together with your employer.

## Hire in Bologna, Italy
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/hire-in-bologna.html
Summary: Hiring employees in Bologna: main sectors, universities, local income tax surcharges, take-home pay and practical notes for US companies.
 Hiring by city Hire in Bologna Bologna sits at the centre of one of the richest manufacturing regions in Europe. Machine makers, motor brands and food groups surround it, and the oldest university in the western world feeds them.
Main sectorsPackaging and automatic machinery (the "Packaging Valley"), motorcycles and sports cars, mechatronics, food processing, logistics, and high performance computing around the Tecnopolo and CINECA.
Talent poolsThe Università di Bologna, one of the largest in Italy, for engineering, computer science, economics and agriculture. Nearby universities in Modena, Reggio Emilia, Ferrara and Parma add mechanical and automotive engineers.
Local income tax in Bologna On top of national IRPEF, employees pay a city surcharge and a regional surcharge. We withhold both through payroll.
Item2026 valueStatus City surcharge rate0.8%Source: pmi.it, 730/2026 table, read 27 Oct 2026. secondary source City council resolution for 2026 not yet checked. City exemption threshold€15,000Same source. Regional surcharge (Emilia-Romagna), first bracket1.33% up to €15,000Source: quifinanza.it, read 27 Oct 2026. unverified Higher brackets to confirm on finanze.gov.it. Other brackets not read. What it means for net pay Bologna pairs a low flat city rate with a moderate exemption, and the Emilia-Romagna starting regional rate is among the lower ones. For the same gross, take-home pay is close to Milan and above Rome and Naples. Upper regional brackets still need checking before you compare senior salaries.
Practical notes Commuting. Buses and suburban rail. Many industrial employers are outside the city, so a car or a company shuttle is often needed. Travel. Bologna is the main high-speed rail hub: about one hour to Milan and Florence, about two and a quarter hours to Rome. The airport has European flights. Time zones. Italy is UTC+1, UTC+2 in summer: 6 hours ahead of New York and 9 ahead of San Francisco. A team working 9:00 to 18:00 has three shared hours with the East Coast (9:00 to 12:00 New York time). With the West Coast there is no overlap in a standard day, so plan a late afternoon slot in Italy or async work. Start hiring in Bologna Estimate the full employer cost, then tell us about the role.

## Italian Employment Contracts
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/italy-employment-contracts.html
Summary: Employment contracts in Italy: the CCNL, contract terms, leave, sickness, parental leave, public holidays and termination.
 Payroll guide Contracts, leave and termination in Italy How a contract is set up under the collective agreement and what employees are entitled to.
Contracts and the CCNL Every employment contract is written and sits under a national collective agreement, the CCNL, chosen according to the job and the sector. The CCNL sets the minimum pay for each job level, working hours, overtime rates, leave, probation and notice periods.
The contract states the job title and level, place of work, salary, hours, start date, probation and whether it is permanent or fixed-term. Changes such as a raise, a promotion or a move to part-time are made with a written amendment.
For non-EU nationals, the work permit (nulla osta) must be granted before the employee starts. See visas.
Ending employment follows set rules: a valid reason, the notice period of the CCNL and the payment of TFR and any unused leave in the final payslip.
Leave and absences Annual leave: at least 4 weeks a year by law, often more under the CCNL, plus extra paid hours off (ROL) in many agreements. Sick leave: the doctor sends the certificate online to INPS; pay during sickness is shared between INPS and the employer according to the CCNL. Maternity and paternity: mandatory maternity leave of 5 months and paternity leave of 10 working days, mostly paid through INPS. Public holidays: 12 national holidays plus the local patron saint's day. We track every absence and reflect it in that month's payroll and invoice.

## Italian Salary Components
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/italy-salary-components.html
Summary: What an Italian salary is made of: RAL, 13th and 14th month, allowances, benefits in kind, INPS and INAIL contributions, income tax and surcharges.
 Payroll guide What makes up an Italian salary From the RAL in the offer letter to the net pay in the employee’s account.
From gross to net Offers in Italy state the RAL, the annual gross salary. It is split into 13 monthly installments, or 14 under agreements such as Commerce and services: the 13th is paid in December, the 14th in June or July.
From each gross installment the employer withholds:
the employee's social security share, around 9–10% of gross pay; national income tax, IRPEF, which is progressive and reduced by employment tax credits; the regional and municipal income tax surcharges, which depend on where the employee lives. On top of gross pay, the employer pays its own social security share (roughly 30%), INAIL insurance and the TFR severance accrual. See the cost calculator for a worked example.
13th, 14th month and bonuses 13th month (tredicesima): mandatory for all employees, paid in December. 14th month (quattordicesima): paid only where the CCNL provides it, such as Commerce and services, usually in June or July. Performance and seniority bonuses: set by the CCNL, a company agreement or your own policy. All of these are part of taxable pay and carry contributions like the regular salary. Both the 13th and 14th month accrue month by month, so an employee who joins or leaves mid-year receives the part they have accrued.
Pay elements on the payslip ElementWhat it is Base salary (minimo tabellare)The minimum for the job level under the CCNL Above-minimum pay (superminimo)Any amount you agree on top of the CCNL minimum Seniority increments (scatti di anzianità)Automatic raises every few years of service, set by the CCNL OvertimePaid with the surcharges of the CCNL, higher at night and on holidays Shift and night allowancesFor night, weekend or rotating shifts Hazard payFor roles with specific risks Commissions and variable payFor sales and target-based roles; taxed as salary Performance bonusProductivity bonuses under a company agreement can qualify for a reduced flat tax In 2026 productivity bonuses up to €5,000 a year are taxed at a flat 1% instead of normal rates.
Benefits in kind Meal vouchers (buoni pasto): exempt from tax and contributions up to €10 a day for electronic vouchers, €4 for paper ones (2026). Company car for business and private use: taxed on a flat share of a standard cost that depends on the car’s emissions. Health insurance: contributions to supplementary health funds, often set by the CCNL, are exempt up to €3,615.20 a year. Housing: rent paid or reimbursed by the employer, common in relocation packages. Fringe benefits (gift cards, utility bills, fuel): tax-free up to €1,000 a year, €2,000 for employees with dependent children (2026). Supplementary pension: the employee can send the TFR and extra contributions to a pension fund. Contributions and other deductions INPS funds pensions, unemployment, sickness, maternity and family allowances. The employee pays around 9–10% of gross pay; the employer around 30%, depending on sector, size and contract type. Contribution ceiling: for employees first insured from 1996 onwards, pension contributions stop above a yearly earnings ceiling: €122,295 in 2026. The employee rate also rises by 1 point on pay above €56,224 a year. INAIL is paid by the employer only, at a rate set by the job’s risk class. Trade union dues are deducted from pay for members who ask for it. Pension fund contributions chosen by the employee. Income tax (IRPEF) IRPEF is progressive and withheld every month. Each band of taxable income is taxed at its own rate:
Taxable incomeRate Up to €28,00023% €28,000 – €50,00033% Above €50,00043% Taxable income is gross pay minus the employee’s social security share. Employment tax credits reduce the tax, mainly on lower salaries. The regional and municipal surcharges are added on top.
What the employer’s contributions pay for ItemCovers Pension (IVS)Old-age, disability and survivors’ pensions; the largest share Unemployment (NASpI)Unemployment benefit Sickness and maternityINPS benefits during sick and maternity leave (not for all categories) Family allowances (CUAF)Family support schemes TFR guarantee fundPays severance if an employer cannot Wage guarantee fundsShort-time work schemes, depending on sector and size INAILWorkplace injury and occupational disease TFR accrual6.91% set aside for severance (not a tax, it is the employee’s) State pension in brief Contributions build the employee’s state pension. The standard old-age pension starts at 67 with at least 20 years of contributions. Early retirement is possible regardless of age after 42 years and 10 months of contributions for men, one year less for women.
From 2027 both requirements go up by one month, and by three months from 2028.
More in the guide EOR, entity or contractors? The payroll calendar and filings What makes up an Italian salary Contracts, leave and termination Outsourcing payroll and choosing a provider Get a quote

## Italy Employment Cost Calculator
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/calculator.html
Summary: What an employee in Italy costs: gross salary, employer contributions, INAIL and severance accrual for two example collective agreements, plus how regional and municipal taxes change net pay.
 Cost calculator What an employee in Italy really costs You pay the actual employment cost of your employee plus our monthly fee. Here is what the employment cost is made of, using two example collective agreements.
Annual gross salary, RAL (EUR) Collective agreement (CCNL)Commerce and services (CCNL Terziario, Distribuzione e Servizi)Engineering and manufacturing (CCNL Metalmeccanico Industria) Pay 13th and 14th month pro-rata in each monthly payslip Pay TFR monthly into the employee’s chosen fund USD per EUR ItemPer month (avg)Per year Example figures, rates updated 2026-10-26. Contribution and insurance rates are indicative estimate and depend on the exact sector, company size and job risk class. We confirm them in your quote.
Your monthly invoices over a year The annual cost is the same either way. The options change when you pay it: with both options on, every month costs the same and nothing accumulates for later.
MonthSalaryINPS + INAILTFRFeeInvoice What the employment cost is made of RALAnnual gross salary. The figure in the offer letter. It is paid in 13 or 14 monthly installments depending on the CCNL: the extra installments are the 13th month (December) and, in commerce and services, the 14th month (July). INPSEmployer social security. Pension, unemployment, sickness and maternity funds, roughly 29–32% of gross pay. The employee pays a further ~9% out of their gross salary; that part is not an extra cost for you. INAILWorkplace injury insurance. Mandatory. Low for office jobs (well under 1%), higher for technical and production roles. TFRSeverance accrual. 6.91% of gross pay set aside every year and paid to the employee when employment ends, for any reason (Civil Code art. 2120). FeeOur EOR fee. €250 per employee per month. Billed on actuals, month by month The table above is an estimate. Each month we run the real payroll and invoice what it actually cost: overtime, bonuses, unpaid leave, sick days partly covered by INPS, salary changes and CCNL raises all show up in that month's figures. You receive the payslip summary with every invoice, so you can check every line.
Billing terms: one month's estimated cost as a refundable deposit at start, then each month paid in advance on the estimate and adjusted on the next invoice to the actual payroll.
Two collective agreements, compared On the same €50,000 RAL, an engineering contract under the Metalmeccanico agreement costs the employer roughly €1,500–2,000 a year more than an office contract under Commerce and services: social security rates are about 2–3 points higher and injury insurance is higher for technical roles. The Commerce agreement pays in 14 installments, so each monthly payslip is smaller, but the annual cost is the same RAL.
Which agreement applies is not a free choice: it follows the job and the sector of the work. We pick it in the contract draft and explain why.
Why the city changes net pay, not your cost On top of national income tax (IRPEF), every employee pays a regional surcharge (from 1.23% up to about 3.33% of taxable income, depending on the region and income band) and a municipal one (usually 0–0.8%; 0.9% in Rome, 1% in Naples, up to 1.2% in Turin; many cities exempt lower incomes). Both are withheld from the employee's gross pay.
They do not change what you pay. They change what the employee takes home: on a €50,000 RAL, the gap between the cheapest and the most expensive combination of region and city is in the order of €1,000–1,500 a year of net pay. Worth knowing when you compare offers for candidates in different cities.
Get an exact quoteSee the employee’s net pay

## Italy Net Pay Calculator
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/net-pay-calculator.html
Summary: From gross to net in Italy in 2026: employee social security, income tax (IRPEF) with employment credits, regional and municipal surcharges, for Milan, Rome, Turin, Bologna and Naples.
 Net pay calculator What your employee takes home in Italy Enter the annual gross salary and the city. The estimate applies 2026 rules: employee social security, income tax with employment credits and the local surcharges.
Annual gross salary, RAL (EUR) CityMilanRomeTurinBolognaNaples Paid in13 installments14 installments12 (13th/14th pro-rata) ItemPer year How the calculation works The employee pays 9.19% social security on gross pay, plus 1% on the part above €56,224 a year. Income tax (IRPEF) applies to what remains: 23% up to €28,000, 33% from €28,000 to €50,000, 43% above. Employment tax credits reduce the tax. They are largest on low salaries and reach zero at €50,000. Between €20,000 and €40,000 an extra credit of up to €1,000 applies. The regional and municipal surcharges are added, unless income is below the city's exemption threshold. None of this changes what you pay as employer: see the employer cost calculator.

## Italy Payroll Calendar
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/italy-payroll-calendar.html
Summary: The monthly payroll cycle in Italy: cut-off, payment date, F24 by the 16th, UniEmens, LUL, Certificazione Unica and annual returns.
 Payroll guide The Italian payroll calendar and filings What happens each month, and once a year, when you employ someone in Italy.
Italy payroll at a glance CurrencyEuro (EUR) Tax year1 January – 31 December Pay frequencyMonthly, plus 13th (and sometimes 14th) month Employer cost on top of gross payAbout 35–40% including severance accrual Taxes and contributions paidMonthly, by the 16th of the following month (F24) Time zoneCET (UTC+1), CEST in summer How Italian payroll works Payroll runs monthly. Each month the employer calculates gross pay under the employee's collective agreement, withholds the employee's taxes and contributions, adds the employer's own contributions, pays the employee and pays the authorities.
Before the first payslip, the employer must be set up with three bodies:
INPS, the national social security institute: pensions, unemployment, sickness and maternity. INAIL, the workplace injury insurer. Agenzia delle Entrate, the tax agency, for income tax withholding. The hire itself is reported to the labor authorities electronically the day before work starts.
With our Employer of Record service all of these registrations are already in place: we are the employer, so your hire can start without you registering anything in Italy.
The monthly payroll calendar Each pay period is one calendar month. A typical month looks like this:
Mid-monthCut-off for the month's variables: overtime, absences, bonuses, new hires and leavers. Third weekPayroll is calculated and the payslips are checked. End of monthNet pay is transferred; some employers pay in the first days of the next month, as the contract or CCNL allows. Payslips go out, usually digitally. 16th of next monthWithheld taxes, INPS and INAIL contributions are paid with the F24, and the UniEmens report is filed. Your invoice follows the same calendar, so the cost you see each month matches that month's payroll.
How we run each payroll month Collect changesHours, leave, overtime, new hires and leavers, salary and benefit changes, approved by you. CalculateGross pay, contributions, taxes and net pay under the CCNL and the law. CheckComparison with the previous month; anomalies explained before anything is paid. PayNet salaries by bank transfer, payslips to employees. FileF24, UniEmens and the LUL update. ReportSummary and invoice to your finance team. Monthly and yearly filings FilingWhat it isWhen Payslip (cedolino)Monthly statement of gross pay, deductions and net payEvery month F24Single payment form for withheld taxes, social security and surchargesBy the 16th of the following month LUL (Libro Unico del Lavoro)The official payroll and attendance registerUpdated every month UniEmensMonthly report of pay and contributions to INPSEvery month Certificazione Unica (CU)Annual certificate of income, tax and contributions; the employee uses it for their tax returnBy 16 March Modello 770Annual withholding agent returnBy 31 October INAIL self-assessmentAnnual premium calculationBy 16 February More in the guide EOR, entity or contractors? ## Italy Work Visas
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/visas.html
Summary: Work visas and EU Blue Card for non-EU hires in Italy. €2,500 per case.
 Visas and immigration Bring non-EU talent to Italy Hiring a US citizen or another non-EU national? The employee needs a work permit before moving. We act as the Italian employer and sponsor.
Two main routes EU Blue CardFor qualified roles above a minimum salary threshold. Not subject to annual quotas and leads to mobility within the EU.
Ordinary work permitUnder the annual quota system (Decreto Flussi, 2026–2028 planning). Timing depends on quota windows.
The process Eligibility checkDegree, salary and role against the route requirements. Work authorizationWe file the nulla osta with the Immigration Office (Sportello Unico). VisaThe employee applies at the Italian consulate in their country. ArrivalResidence permit, tax code, registration with the health service. Check eligibility

## Outsourcing Payroll in Italy
URL: https://hiringitaly.com/italy-payroll-outsourcing.html
Summary: Why outsource payroll in Italy, common mistakes of foreign employers, reporting to headquarters, and the questions to ask a provider.
 Payroll guide Outsourcing payroll in Italy What a provider takes off your hands, where foreign employers go wrong, and how to choose.
What a payroll and EOR service covers AreaWhat we do OnboardingContract under the right CCNL in English and Italian, hire notification, tax code, registration with INPS and INAIL Monthly payrollGross-to-net, payslips, F24 payments, UniEmens, LUL AbsencesLeave, sickness, parental leave, overtime Year endCU for every employee, annual returns, INAIL self-assessment HR administrationPersonnel files, amendments, renewals, terminations, benefits Your sideOne invoice in USD a month with the payroll summary Why outsource payroll in Italy Fewer errors and penalties. Rates, tax credits and CCNL tables change during the year; late or wrong F24 payments carry penalties and interest. No local setup. No Italian payroll software, no local accountant, no Italian entity if you use the EOR service. Expertise on call. Specialists follow INPS, INAIL and tax changes so your team does not have to. On-time pay. Employees are paid correctly and on time, which matters for retention. Where foreign employers go wrong Wrong CCNL or job level: pay below the agreement's minimum, or missing allowances it grants. Part-time and fixed-term contracts: contributions and leave calculated as for full-time. Late F24 payments: penalties and interest from day one. Forgotten accruals: 13th and 14th month and TFR not budgeted, so year-end costs come as a surprise. Mismatched calendars: Italian payroll closes on the calendar month, which may not match your fiscal periods. Missed changes: tax brackets, contribution rates and reporting formats change every year. Reporting to your headquarters Every month you receive, in English and USD:
the payroll summary for each employee: gross pay, employer costs, net pay; the accruals that build up during the year: 13th and 14th month, unused leave, TFR; a cost forecast for the rest of the year, for your budget; the leave and absence balance. The data comes in a format your accounting team can import, and stays available for auditors.
Choosing a provider: questions to ask, and our answers AskOur answer Who is the legal employer in Italy?We are, directly. No third-party subcontractor. Which CCNL will apply and why?Stated in the quote, chosen from the job and sector. What exactly is in the price?A flat €250 per employee per month, plus the actual employment cost billed month by month. Which currency do you invoice in?USD, at the EUR reference rate of the invoice date. Where is employee data kept?On servers in the EU, under the GDPR. How do you handle changes in the law?We apply them in payroll and tell you before they change your cost. Who answers the employee's questions?We do, in Italian and English. FAQ How often are employees paid in Italy?Monthly, with the 13th and, under some agreements, the 14th month on top.
What is the Certificazione Unica?The annual certificate of income, withheld tax and contributions. The employer gives it to the employee and files it with the tax agency by 16 March; the employee uses it for their tax return.
Do employees file their own tax return?Many do, especially to claim deductions such as medical expenses. The employer's withholding already covers most of the tax due.
How much are social security contributions?Roughly 9–10% of gross pay for the employee and about 30% for the employer, depending on sector and company size, plus INAIL insurance paid by the employer.
Can I hire a non-EU national?Yes, once the work permit is granted. We handle the application as the employer.

 Partner program Your clients want Italy. You keep the client. They hire within days, without setting up an Italian company, and you stay their advisor.
Become a partnerSee our pricing Why recommend an EOR to your clients An Italian subsidiary means a notary, a registered office, local bookkeeping and months of setup before anyone is on payroll. For one to ten people that rarely pays off. With HiringItaly the employee gets a compliant Italian contract under the right collective agreement, while your client directs the work. One price, €250 per employee per month, all included.

We handle employment in Italy; tax planning, corporate and legal matters stay with you, and we send any such question back to you.
Will you compete with my practice?No. We do not give tax or legal advice in the US, the UK or Italy. We run the employment and payroll, nothing more.
Is client information confidential?Yes. Client data is used only to deliver the service, under a confidentiality clause in the partner agreement and the GDPR.

When should my client open an Italian company instead?Usually once the team in Italy grows large or the client needs to sign contracts and invoice locally. At that point we help move the staff across and the incorporation goes to you.
